en: The *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra*, Volume One, contains nine causal narratives translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Ki-ka-ye (Gītakṣa) of the Western Regions during the Northern Wei Dynasty, together with Tanyao. The first is:
"The Narrative of King Daśaratha."

The story of the prince who saved his parents with his own flesh; the story of the parrot child who nourished his blind parents; the story of the abandonment of the kingdom of the old man; the story of the Buddha preaching the Dharma for Māyā in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; the story of the Buddha recounting the past life of his mother, Kātyāyanī; the story of the compassionate maiden; the story of Queen Padmāvatī; the story of Queen Mṛgajā; and (1) the story of King Daśaratha. (1) The Story of King Daśaratha: Long ago, when the human lifespan was ten thousand years, there was a king named Daśaratha who ruled over Jambudvīpa.
The King’s principal consort gave birth to a son named Rāma.
The second consort had a son named Ramaṇa. Prince Rāma possessed great martial prowess and the strength of Nārāyaṇa;
furthermore, he was endowed with the Śilavajra [weapon], which could inflict harm upon anyone who merely heard his voice or saw his form, such that no one could withstand him.
At that time, the third queen gave birth to a son named Bharata.
The fourth queen gave birth to a son surnamed Śatrujit.
The king held the third queen in great love and respect, and he said to her:
"I have no stinginess whatsoever regarding all my wealth and treasures; if you have anything you require, I shall grant it according to your wishes.
The lady replied, "I have nothing to ask for now;
if I later have a wish, I shall inform you again."

At that time, the king fell ill and his life was in peril; he immediately installed the crown prince Rāma to succeed him as king. Rāma bound his hair with silk, donned a celestial crown, and assumed the dignified bearing and ritual protocols of a monarch according to royal law.

At that time, the junior queen attended to the king’s illness until he had recovered slightly. Relying on this, and seeing that Rāma was to succeed his father to the throne, she conceived a heart of jealousy.
She then addressed the king, requesting her former wish: “I pray that you appoint my son as king and depose Rāma.”
When the king heard these words, he was like a person choking, unable to swallow and unable to spit out.
He wished to depose his elder brother, yet he had already established him as king;
he wished not to depose him, yet he had previously granted him his request.
"However, King Daśaratha has never violated his word since his youth;
furthermore, according to the law of kings, there is no such thing as double-tongued speech, nor does one go back on one's previous words."
Having reflected thus, he immediately deposed Rāma and stripped him of his robes and crown.
At that time, his younger brother Ramaṇa said to his elder brother, "Brother, you possess both valor and strength, as well as the *śakti*; why do you not employ them to avoid such humiliation?"
The elder brother replied to his younger brother, saying:
"To go against one's father's wishes is not called filial piety.

However, although this mother did not give birth to me, my father honors and treats her just as he does my own mother; furthermore, my younger brother Bharata is exceedingly harmonious and submissive, truly harboring no ill intent."
Just as I am now, though possessed of great strength and power, how could I possibly commit an act that ought not to be done against my parents and younger brother, such as seeking to harm them?
Upon hearing these words, the younger brother remained silent.
King Daśaratha then exiled his two sons to a remote deep mountain; only after twelve years had passed did he permit them to return to their kingdom.
The brothers Rāma and his kin, having received their father’s command, felt no resentment in their hearts; they took their leave of their parents and entered the deep mountains.
At that time, Bharata, who had previously been in another country, was summoned back to the kingdom and installed as king.
However, Bharata had always been harmonious, respectful, and submissive toward his two elder brothers, maintaining deep reverence and yielding to them.

Once he had returned to the kingdom, he learned that his father the King had already passed away and that his own mother had arbitrarily instigated the deposition and installation [of another]. He realized that she had banished his two elder brothers to a distant place; resenting the irrational conduct of his biological mother, he refused to bow or kneel before her, saying to her:
"What kind of perverse and rebellious act is this you have committed? You have utterly brought ruin upon my family!"
He bowed toward his mother, showing a degree of reverence and filial piety far exceeding the ordinary.
Then, Bharata immediately led his army to the foot of that mountain; leaving the host behind, he went forward alone.
When his younger brother arrived, Rāma said to his elder brother:
"Previously, you always praised my brother Bharata for his righteousness, humility, and obedience; yet today he has come leading an army, desiring to slaughter my brothers?"
The elder brother said to Bharata,
"Younger brother, why have you now brought this host of troops?
The younger brother replied to his elder brother:
"Fearing that we might encounter bandits and hardships on the road, I have brought these troops for my own protection; I have no other intention.
I pray that you, my elder brother, will return to the kingdom to govern its affairs."
The elder brother replied to his younger brother, saying:
"I previously received my father’s command to move far away and come here.
How could I now simply return on my own accord?"
"If one acts so arbitrarily, they cannot be called a benevolent son fulfilling the duty of filial piety toward their parents.
Thus he entreated him with earnestness, seeking his consent without ceasing; yet the elder brother’s mind remained firm, and his resolve grew even more steadfast.

The younger brother, knowing that his elder brother’s resolve could never be turned back, immediately followed him; having obtained the leather sandals, he returned to his own country with a heavy heart and deep regret, whereupon he took charge of the administration of state affairs.

He constantly placed his leather sandals upon the imperial throne, and in the morning and evening he performed the rites of salutation and inquiry as if toward an elder brother, no different from how he treated him in person.
He also frequently dispatched messengers to that mountain to repeatedly invite his brother.

However, his two elder brothers, because their father had previously commanded them to return after twelve years, did not dare disobey that mandate as the term was not yet complete; they were so filial and loyal.

Later, when the years had gradually run out and they learned that their younger brother had been earnestly sending messengers to summon them, and further realized that Jingxi was as devoted to them as he was to himself, they were moved by the depth of their brother’s affection and subsequently returned to their own country.
Having arrived at the kingdom, the younger brother returned the throne and yielded it to his elder brother.
The elder brother again declined, saying:
"My father previously gave it to you; it is not fitting for me to take it."
The younger brother again yielded, saying, "As the eldest son of the primary wife, you are the one to shoulder your father’s legacy; it is truly you who should be king.
Thus they continued to defer to one another in turn, until the elder brother, having no other recourse, finally returned to the throne as king.

Brothers were harmonious and respectful, and the influence of moral transformation spread widely; wherever the Way reached, the common people relied upon its benefits. Strengthened by loyalty and filial piety, people inspired themselves to encourage one another in serving their superiors with reverence and honoring their parents.
Although Māyādevī had committed great evils, she harbored no resentment whatsoever.

Due to these causes and conditions of loyalty and filial piety, the winds and rains arrived at their proper times, the five grains ripened in abundance, and there were no epidemics among the people. Within Jambudvīpa, all the inhabitants flourished and prospered, tenfold more than usual.
2. The Story of the Prince Who Saved His Parents with His Own Flesh (II). Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
At that time, Ānanda put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.
He saw a young boy whose parents were blind; having obtained food through begging, he offered the finer portions to his parents and ate the coarse portions himself.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This child is truly most rare!”
"I beg for fine food to offer to my parents, while selecting the coarse and poor-quality portions for myself.
The Buddha said, "This is not what is difficult;
rather, in my past lives, providing for my parents was what was truly difficult."
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the past world, what were the circumstances of making offerings to one’s parents?”
The Buddha said:
"In the distant past, there was a great king who ruled over a kingdom.
The king had six sons, each of whom governed a separate country."
At that time, there was a high minister named Rāhuṣa who, through his stratagems, raised an army and killed the Great King and his five sons.
Regarding the sixth youngest son, a spirit had previously come to him and said:
"Your father the Great King and your five elder brothers have all been slain by the high minister Rāhuṣa; it is now your turn."
Having heard this, the prince immediately returned home.
Seeing that his wife’s complexion was haggard and distressed, unlike its usual state, she asked her husband,
"Why are you like this?"
The husband replied to his wife, saying,
"Matters concerning men must not be spoken of to you.
The wife said:
“Prince! I am now one with you in life and death; why do you not speak to me when there is such urgency?
The husband replied to his wife:
"Just now a spirit came and spoke to me, saying:
'Your father, the Great King, and your five elder brothers have all been killed by another; it is now your turn.'"
Filled with such anxiety and fear, they did not know where to turn.
The husband and wife devised a plan and immediately took their child to flee to another country.
Carrying provisions for seven days, they calculated that they would reach their destination; however—
Driven by fear and terror, he took a wrong and circuitous path; though he traveled for ten days, he still had not reached his destination.
His provisions were completely exhausted, and he was so weakened by hunger that he was on the verge of death.
The prince reflected:
"If all three were to lose their lives together, the suffering would be especially intense; it would be better to kill one person so that the lives of two may be preserved.
He immediately drew his sword, intending to kill his wife.
The son looked back at his father, joined his palms, and said:
"I pray that you, Father, will not kill my mother now; it would be better for you to kill me instead, so that I may take her life in exchange."
The father followed his son’s words and intended to kill him.
The son spoke again, saying:
“Do not take my life; if you take my life, my flesh will rot and spoil, and I shall not be able to remain for long, which might prevent my mother from reaching her destination.”
"Do not end my life; cut and slice me for a moment, eating me little by little day after day.
Before they had reached a human village, there was only meat remaining on his body in three pieces.
The son said to his parents, "Eat these two pieces of meat, father and mother; there remains one piece left, which you may give back to me."
Having thrown the child onto the ground, the parents stepped forward.
At that time, Śakra-devānām-indra’s palace shook; he immediately observed it, wondering what the cause and condition were.
Seeing this child performing such a marvelous feat, he immediately transformed himself into a starving wolf and came to demand his flesh.
The child reflected:
"If I eat this meat, my life will surely end; yet even if I do not eat it, I shall die."
He then set aside this flesh and gave it to the starving wolf.
Śakra Devānām Indra immediately transformed himself into a man and said to the boy:
"Now that you have cut your own flesh to give to your parents, do you feel any regret?"
He replied,
"I do not regret it.
The deva said:
"You are now suffering; who would believe you when you say you have no remorse?
Thereupon, the child spoke these truthful words:
"If I do not harbor a heart of remorse, let the flesh of my body grow back and be restored as it was before."
"If there be any who feel regret, they shall die at this very moment.
Having spoken these words, his body was restored to its former state, no different from before.

Śakra Devānām Indra then brought the son together with his parents to one place so that they might see the king. The king’s heart was filled with great compassion and joy; moved by their supreme filial piety, he marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and immediately provided them with an army to escort them back to their own country.
Śakra Devānām Indra gradually protected him and became the king of Jambudvīpa.
The child at that time was my own self;
the parents at that time were today’s parents.
The Buddha said, "It is not only today that I have praised filial piety; throughout immeasurable kalpas, I have always praised it.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding the past lives, how did you provide for your parents?
The Buddha said:
"Formerly, within the realm of the King of Kāśī, there was a great mountain. Upon it lived a seer named Śyāmaka.
His parents were aged and both blind; he would constantly gather fine fruits, fresh flowers, and pure water to nourish them, placing them in a secluded and peaceful location free from fear."
In all that he did—whether moving, acting, or remaining still—he first informed his parents.
Having informed his parents, he would then go to fetch water.

At that time, King Brahmadatta was out hunting; seeing a deer drinking water, he drew his bow and shot it. By mistake, a poisoned arrow struck Śyāmaka’s body. Once pierced by the venomous shaft, he cried out in a loud voice:
"To kill three men with a single arrow—how cruel is such agony!
When the king heard these words, he immediately cast his bow and arrows to the ground and went at once to see who had spoken them.
"I have heard that in this mountain there is a rishi named Śyāmaka, who is compassionate, benevolent, and filial; he cares for his blind parents, and the whole world praises him."
"Are you not Śyāmaka now?
He replied, "I am indeed he."
He then addressed the king, saying:

"As for this body of mine, I do not take account of its pain; I only worry that my parents are aged and their vision is failing, and from now on they will suffer hunger and exhaustion with no one to provide for them."
The king asked again,
"Where are your blind parents now?
Śyāmaka pointed them out to the king, saying:
"He is in that grass hut.
The king then went to where the blind parents were.
At that time, Śyāmaka’s father said to his wife:
"My eyes are twitching; could it be that my filial son Śyāmaka is suffering some misfortune?
The wife spoke again to her husband:
"My breasts are also throbbing; could it be that there is some inauspicious matter concerning my son?"
At that time, the blind parents heard the rustling sound of the king’s footsteps and felt terror arise within them:
"This is not our son walking; who could this be?
When the king reached their presence, he called out and prostrated himself in greeting.
The blind parents said, "Our eyes see nothing; to whom do you pay homage?
He replied:
"I am the King of Kāśī. Then his blind parents commanded the king, saying, "Please be seated.
Had my son been alive, he would have offered you fine flowers and fruits."
"My son went this morning to fetch water, but he has not returned despite my waiting for a long time.
The king then wept with grief and spoke these verses:
"I am the king of this land, Hunting here upon this mountain; Now that my son has gone to fetch water, I fear he will not return."
I merely wished to hunt birds and beasts, Unaware that I was harming a human being.
I now renounce the royal throne To serve my blind parents;
I am no different from your own son— Pray, do not give way to grief or distress.
The blind parents replied to the king in verse:
“My son was compassionate, filial, and obedient; Such a one exists not among gods or men.
Though Your Majesty shows us pity, How could anyone equal my son?”
"May Your Majesty have compassion for us; we pray that you will show us the place where our son is.
To be by our child's side would satisfy both our lives and our hearts.
Thereupon, the king led the blind parents to the side of Śyāmaka.
Having arrived at his son’s place, he beat his breast in distress and wailed, saying:
"My son was compassionate and benevolent, filial beyond compare.
O gods of heaven, gods of earth, gods of the mountains, gods of the trees, gods of the rivers, gods of the lakes, and all you deities! He then spoke this verse:
“Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Kings—why do you not provide assistance?
Why let my filial son undergo such suffering?”
"I am deeply moved by my filial son, who has swiftly come to save my life.

At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra’s palace shook; hearing with his divine ear the pitiful cries of the blind parents, he immediately descended from heaven, went to where they were, and said to Śyāmaka:
"Did you give rise to an evil thought toward the king?"
He replied,
"Truly, I had no evil intent.
Śakra Devānām Indra said:
"Who would believe that you harbor no evil intent? Śyāmaka replied,
"If I harbored any evil intent toward Your Majesty, my body would be instantly pervaded by poison and I would die on the spot."
"If I harbor no ill will toward the king, may this poisoned arrow come forth and the wound on my body heal.
As soon as he spoke these words, the poisoned arrow came out of its own accord, and his body was restored to its former state.
The King was greatly delighted and leaped for joy beyond measure; he immediately issued a decree, proclaiming throughout the realm:
"One should cultivate loving-kindness and benevolence, and serve one's parents with filial piety."
"Since ancient times, Śyāmaka has been compassionate, benevolent, filial, and obedient, providing for his parents.
If you wish to know who the blind father was at that time, he is now King Śuddhodana."
At that time, the blind mother was Queen Māyā;
Śyāmaka was my own self in this life;
and the King of Kāśī was Śāriputra.
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra was Mahākāśyapa. 3.

The Story of the Parrot Boy Who Supported His Blind Parents (III) The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha and addressed the bhikṣus, saying: “There are two types of wrong conduct that are like a bouncing ball; they quickly fall into hell. What are these two? First, one who has no compassion for his parents, yet claims to be practicing the holy life.
Second, one who does not support his blind parents, yet claims to be practicing the holy life. These two types of wrong conduct are like a bouncing ball; they quickly fall into hell.”
What are the two?
First, failing to make offerings to one's parents;
second, performing various unwholesome deeds toward one's parents.
There are two forms of right practice that, like striking a ball, cause one to be swiftly reborn in the heavens.
What are these two?
The first is to make offerings to one’s parents.
"Second, performing various deeds of goodness toward one's parents.
The bhikṣus said,
"How rare, World-Honored One!"
"The Tathāgata is most capable of praising his parents.
The Buddha said, "Not only today;
in a past life, there was a parrot in the Snowy Mountains whose parents were both blind. He would constantly gather fine flowers and fruits, first offering them to his parents."
At that time, there was a landowner who, when first sowing grain, made this vow:
"The grain I sow shall be shared and eaten together with all sentient beings."
At that time, because the field-owner already possessed a mind of generosity, the young parrot would constantly gather rice from the field to provide for his parents.

At that time, the landowner was inspecting the rows of seedlings when he saw various insects and birds stripping the grain from the ears; filled with anger and distress, he set out a net and captured a parrot.
The parrot said, "The master of the field previously possessed a kind heart and was generous in giving things without stinginess; for this reason, I have ventured to come here to gather the rice."
How is it that you have now been caught in this net?
Furthermore, the field is like a mother, the seed is like a father, the true word is like a son, and the owner of the field is like a king; protection depends upon oneself.
Having spoken these words, the landowner was filled with joy and asked the parrot,
"For whom do you take this grain?
The parrot replied:
"I have blind parents; I wish to offer [this field] to them.
The landowner replied, "From this day forward, you may always take [what you need] from here; do not harbor any further doubts or difficulties."
The Buddha said:
"The parrot delighted in many kinds of fruit, and the farmer was likewise.
At that time, the parrot was my own self."
At that time, the landowner was Śāriputra;
at that time, the blind father was King Śuddhodana;
and at that time, the blind mother was Māyā.
4. The Story of the Abandonment of the Elderly (IV). The Story of the Abandonment of the Elderly. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these words:
“To revere the elderly brings great benefit.”
"Having heard matters never before heard, you have attained understanding; your fame has spread afar, and you are revered by the wise.
The bhikṣus said, "O Tathāgata, World-Honored One!"
"And he constantly praises and reveres his parents, elders, and senior citizens.
The Buddha said, "Not only today;
throughout immeasurable kalpas in the past, I have always revered my parents, elders, and senior citizens."
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Regarding the past veneration, what were the circumstances?
The Buddha said:
"In the distant past, there was a kingdom named Abandoning the Aged. Within that land, all those who were elderly were driven far away and cast out.
There was a high minister whose father had grown old; according to the laws of the kingdom, he was subject to being sent away."

The minister was filial and obedient; unable to bear it in his heart, he dug deep into the earth, constructed a secret chamber, and placed his father within it, providing for him with filial care at all times.
"At that time, a celestial deity seized two snakes and placed them upon the king's palace, saying:
'If you can distinguish the male from the female, your kingdom shall enjoy peace;
if you cannot, then you yourself and your nation shall both be utterly destroyed seven days hence.'"

Upon hearing this, the king was filled with distress; he immediately consulted with his ministers on this matter, and they each offered their apologies, declaring themselves unable to distinguish [the two].
He immediately issued a proclamation throughout the realm: "Whoever can distinguish [the true jewel], they shall be granted generous rank and reward.
The minister returned home and went to question his father.
The father replied to his son:
"This matter is easy to distinguish.
Place a fine, soft object upon them;
that which becomes agitated and restless should be known as the male."
"One who dwells without moving should be known as female.
Following these words, they indeed distinguished between male and female.
The celestial deity asked again:
"Who is it that, while others sleep, is called awake?
Who is it that, while others are awake, is called asleep?
The king and his ministers were again unable to resolve this; they further issued a proclamation throughout the kingdom, yet no one could provide an explanation.
The minister asked his father,
"What does this mean?
His father replied:
"This is called a learner.
Among ordinary people, he is called an awakened one;
among arhats, he is called one who sleeps."
He then answered exactly as he had been told.
The celestial deity asked again:
"What is the weight of this great white elephant?"
The ministers deliberated together, but none could know; they also issued a proclamation throughout the kingdom, yet still no one could know.
A minister questioned his father, who said: "Place the elephant on a boat and set it in a large pond;

mark the water level at the depth to which the boat sinks; then, using bricks or stones, weigh them against the boat until it sinks to that same marked depth. By measuring the weight of the bricks or stones, you will know the weight of the elephant."
"Simply take this boat, place stones inside it until the water reaches the mark, and you will know its weight.
He answered with this wisdom.
The deva asked again:
"Who can know that a single handful of water is greater than the great ocean?
The ministers deliberated together but could not resolve it; they issued a general call for inquiries, yet no one at all knew the answer.
The minister asked his father,
"What are these words?
The father replied:
"This statement is easy to understand.

If there is anyone who, with a mind of pure faith, offers even a single handful of water to the Buddha and the Sangha, or to their parents, or to those who are distressed and ill, by virtue of this merit, they shall enjoy inexhaustible blessings for many thousands of millions of kalpas."
The waters of the ocean are exceedingly vast, yet they do not last beyond a single kalpa.
Reasoning from this, a single handful of water is hundreds of thousands of millions of times greater than the great ocean.
He then used these words to answer the celestial deity.
The deity further transformed himself into a starving man, with his sinews and bones showing, and came forward to ask:
"In this world, is there perhaps anyone whose hunger, poverty, emaciation, and suffering are more severe than mine?"
The ministers deliberated, yet they were again unable to answer. The ministers once more went to ask his father about the matter, and the father immediately replied:

"In this world, there are those who are stingy, greedy, and envious; they do not believe in the Triple Gem and cannot provide for their parents, teachers, or elders. In a future life, they will fall among the hungry ghosts (preta). For hundreds of thousands of millions of years, they shall not even hear the names of water or grain. Their bodies are like Mount Tai, their bellies like vast valleys, their throats like fine needles, and their hair like awls or knives, wrapping from their bodies down to their feet. When they move or stir, their joints burst into flames."
"Such a person suffers from hunger a hundred thousand million times more than you.
With these words, he answered the celestial deity.

The deity then further manifested another person whose hands and feet were bound with shackles and whose neck was encircled by a collar; fire issued from his body, and his entire frame was scorched and withered. He then asked again:
"Is there perhaps anyone in the world whose suffering is more severe than mine?
The king and his ministers, taken aback, were unable to provide an answer.
The minister questioned his father again, and the father immediately replied:

"There are people in the world who are unfilial toward their parents, rebellious and harmful toward their teachers and elders, treacherous toward their husbands, and slander the Triple Gem. In future lives, they shall fall into hell—into the mountains of knives and trees of swords, the chariots of fire and glowing coals, the river of sinking and the boiling excrement, the path of blades and the path of fire."
Such sufferings are immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable;
compared to these, your present afflictions are but a hundred-thousand-millionth part.
He then answered the heavenly deity exactly as he had been told.
The deity further transformed herself into a woman, exquisite and magnificent, surpassing all those of the mortal world, and asked again:
"Is there anyone in the world as beautiful as I?"
The ruler and his ministers remained silent, none able to answer.
The minister questioned his father again, and the father then replied:

"There are people in this world who have faith and reverence for the Triple Gem, are filial and obedient to their parents, and delight in giving, patience, diligence, and the observance of precepts; they attain rebirth in the heavens with such exquisite and extraordinary beauty that it surpasses yours by hundreds of thousands of millions of times. Compared to them, you are like a blind monkey."
He then used these words to answer the celestial deity.
The deity then presented another piece of sandalwood that was square, straight, and perfectly symmetrical, and asked again:
"Which part is the head?"
"Neither the king nor his ministers possessed the wisdom to provide an answer.
The minister questioned his father again, and the father replied,
'It is easy to know.'"
"If one were to cast them into the water, the head would surely sink and the tail would surely float.
He then used these words to answer the celestial deity.
The deity then presented two white mares of identical appearance and color, and asked again:
"Who is mother and who is child?
Neither the ministers nor the subjects were able to answer.
He then questioned his father, and the father replied:
"Give him grass to eat; if she is his mother, she will surely push the grass toward her child.
When he had answered all such questions in this manner, the celestial deity was delighted and bestowed upon the king rare and precious treasures, saying to the king:
"I shall now protect your kingdom and ensure that no foreign enemies can cause you harm.
Upon hearing this, the king was filled with immense joy and asked his ministers,
"Did you know this yourself?"
"Was someone instructing you?
It is by virtue of your wisdom and talent that the land has attained peace; that we have obtained these rare treasures and that you have promised us protection—all this is due to your power."
The minister replied to the king, saying:
"This is not within my own wisdom; I pray that you grant me fearlessness, and only then shall I venture to explain it in detail.
The king said:
"Even if you were now guilty of ten thousand deaths, you would still not be interrogated, let alone for a minor offense.
The minister said to the king:
"The kingdom has a decree that does not permit the support of the elderly."
"I have an aged father whom I cannot bear to abandon; thus, defying the royal law, I concealed him within the earth.
All that I have said in response comes entirely from my father's wisdom, not from my own power."
"I only pray, Great King, that throughout all lands, you will once again permit the support of the elderly.

The King immediately praised him with admiration, his heart filled with joy; he provided for the minister’s father, honoring him as his teacher. "The benefit of saving all the lives of our nation in this manner is something beyond my own knowledge," [the minister said].
He even issued a proclamation, announcing throughout the world:
"The abandonment of the elderly shall not be tolerated; you are commanded to provide filial support and care.
Those who are unfilial toward their parents or disrespectful toward their teachers and elders shall be punished with the gravest crimes."
“At that time, the father was I myself.
The minister at that time was Śāriputra.
The king at that time was Ajātaśatru.”
"At that time, the heavenly deity was Ānanda. 5.
The Circumstances of the Buddha Preaching the Dharma for His Mother Māyā in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven (V) The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I now wish to go to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to observe the summer retreat and preach the Dharma for my mother."
“O bhikṣus! Whoever among you desires to go, let them follow me.

Having spoken these words, he immediately went to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and entered the summer retreat beneath a tree. There, he preached the Dharma for his mother Māyā and immeasurable devas; they all attained the vision of the Truths (satyadarśana), and he returned to Jambudvīpa.
The bhikṣus said:
"It is marvelous, World-Honored One!
You were able to remain in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven for ninety days for the sake of your mother."
The Buddha said:
"Not only today; in the past as well, I once acted as a mother and removed her from suffering and distress.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What was the nature of his past deeds?
The Buddha said:
"In the distant past, on the borders of the Snowy Mountains, there was a king of monkeys who led five hundred monkeys."
At that time, a hunter spread his nets to surround and capture them.
The monkey king said:
"All of you, do not be afraid today; I shall destroy those nets for you."
"You monkeys! All of you, follow me out!
Immediately, he broke through the net, and they all attained liberation.
There was an old monkey who, while carrying his young one, stumbled and fell into a deep pit.
The monkey king sought his mother but did not know her whereabouts; seeing a deep pit, he went to its edge and looked down, seeing his mother below.
He said to the other monkeys, "Each of you must exert yourselves and help me rescue my mother."
"At that time, the monkeys took hold of one another's tails down to the edge of the pit and pulled their mother out, freeing her from suffering and distress.
How much more so should I today rescue my mother from her suffering and distress?"
"At that time, he rescued her from the peril of the deep pit; now, he has again rescued his mother from the perils of the three evil realms.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"To rescue and deliver one's father and mother brings great merit."
"Because I rescued my mother, I have been free from calamities in every lifetime and have attained Buddhahood for myself.
For this reason, O bhikṣus!
Each of you should be filial and provide offerings to your parents."
6. The Discourse on the Past Deed of the Mother Kacaṇḍakālī (6). The Buddha, while traveling, arrived at the kingdom of Kukkuṭārāma and sat beneath a tree along the way.
There was an old woman named Kāṇḍarāyikā who, being bound in service to another, was drawing water at a well.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Go and fetch some water."
Ānanda, receiving the Buddha’s command, immediately went to fetch water.

At that time, hearing that the Buddha was seeking water, the old woman herself carried a basin and went there. Upon arriving at the Buddha’s location, she set the basin on the ground and went straight forward to embrace him.
Ānanda wished to stop her, but the Buddha said, "Do not stop her.
Throughout five hundred lifetimes, this old woman has been my mother; because her affection is not yet exhausted, she embraces me."
"If you had prevented me, boiling blood would have issued from my mouth and I would have died on the spot.
Having managed to embrace the Buddha, he kissed his hands and feet and stood to one side.
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Go and summon his master.
When the master arrived, he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet and stood aside.
The Buddha said to the master,
"Release this old woman so that she may leave the household life.
If she leaves the household life, she shall attain arhatship."
The master then released her immediately.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Entrust her to the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī so that she may ordain her and allow her to leave the household life."
Before long, she attained the path of Arhatship; among the bhikṣuṇīs, she was foremost in her skillful understanding of the sūtras.
The bhikṣus, filled with doubt and wonder, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"By what causes and conditions did he become dependent on others, and by what further conditions did he attain arhatship?
The Buddha said, "During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, he left the household life to study the Way; for this reason, he attained arhatship."
At that time, as the leader of a community, I reviled the noble and eminent nuns, calling them slaves. Because of this cause and condition, she now belongs to another.

For five hundred lifetimes, she has always been my mother; yet, being stingy, greedy, and jealous, she obstructed my acts of giving. By reason of these causes and conditions, she has constantly been born into poverty and low status.
"It is not only today that he has uprooted their poverty and low status.
The bhikṣus asked, "We do not know how he rescued them from poverty and low status in past lives; what were those events?"
The Buddha said:
"In a past age, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a poor household where a mother and son lived together.
The son constantly worked as a hired laborer to support his mother; with the small amount of money he earned, they barely made it from day to day."
At that time, the son said to his mother:
"I now wish to travel far with various merchants for trade.
His mother gave her consent, and so he set out.
After the son had departed, the bandits came and destroyed his home, plundering his wealth and driving his elderly mother away to sell her in another land.

When the son returned, he searched for his mother; having learned her whereabouts, he brought a great deal of money and ransomed her with difficulty. Thereupon, they lived together in their own country, and their resources became so abundant that they were twice as prosperous as before.
The mother at that time was none other than the present Kāṇḍadārikā;
the son at that time was my own self.
At that time, I already extracted my mother from her suffering.
7. The Story of the Maiden Maitrī (VII). Once, when the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"If one offers even a small amount of service to one's parents, one obtains immeasurable merit;
if one commits even a slight act of disobedience toward them, one incurs immeasurable transgression."
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What are the matters regarding the retribution of sin and merit?”
The Buddha said:

"In the distant past, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was the son of an elder named Maitrakanyaka. His father died early, and his wealth was exhausted; he sold firewood with his own labor, earning two coins a day to support his aged mother."
His schemes became increasingly successful, and he earned four coins daily to provide for his mother;
subsequently, as his condition gradually improved, he earned eight coins daily to support her;
he then became trusted and relied upon by the masses, with people from near and far flocking to him, so that his profits grew even greater until he earned sixteen coins daily to offer to his mother.
When the people saw that he was intelligent and possessed of merit, they exhorted him, saying:
"When your father was alive, he constantly entered the sea to gather treasures.
Why do you not now enter the sea as well?"
Having heard these words, he said to his mother,
"When my father was alive, what work did he constantly perform?
His mother replied:
"Your father was alive when he went to sea to fetch jewels.
He then said to his mother,
"If my father had gone to sea to gather jewels, why should I not go to sea now?"
Seeing that her son was compassionate, benevolent, and filial, the mother thought he would not be able to leave;
she spoke to him jokingly, saying, "You may go as well.
Having received these words from his mother, he took them to mean his departure was certain, and he immediately sought out companions, intending to go to sea.
When the adornments were complete, he took leave of his mother, wishing to depart.
His mother then said to him:
"I have but this one son; you must wait until my death—how could I ever let you go?"
The son replied to his mother,
"If you had not previously granted permission, I would not have dared to set my mind upon this.
Now that you have already consented to me, how could you possibly obstruct me again?"
"I hope to die establishing faith with this very body.
Since I have already given my word to another, I can no longer remain.
Seeing that her son’s resolve was firm, the mother came forward, embraced his feet, wept, and spoke these words:
"If I do not wait for my death, by what means can I depart?
The son then resolved his mind; he pulled out his own hands and feet and tore off several dozen strands of his mother's hair.
Fearing that her son might commit an offense, his mother immediately released him to depart.
Together with various merchants, he eventually entered the sea.
Upon reaching a treasure island, he gathered many precious gems; then, together with his companions, he set out on the return journey.
"At that time there were two paths: one was a water route and the other was a land route.
Everyone said, 'Go by the land route,' so he went by the land route."

At that time, according to the laws of that country, when bandits came to plunder, if they captured the caravan leader, all the goods belonging to the merchants would fall into the hands of the bandits;
however, if they failed to capture the caravan leader, even though they had seized the wealth and goods, these would all be returned to him when the caravan leader came back.
For this reason, the maiden Maitrāyaṇī always stayed apart from the camp and slept separately; the merchants would rise early in the morning to go out and fetch her.
One night there was a great wind, and the merchants rose suddenly; they forgot to go and fetch her.
Consequently, the merchant leader was later unable to find his companions and did not know the way.
Seeing a mountain, he went up to its summit and saw from afar a city of deep blue lapis lazuli; exhausted by hunger and thirst, he hurried toward it.

At that time, within the city, four jade maidens holding wish-fulfilling jewels performed music and dance as they came together to welcome him; for forty thousand years, he experienced great joy and happiness.
Thereupon, a sense of natural disenchantment arose within him, and he desired to depart.
The jade maidens said:
"The people of Jambudvīpa are utterly ungrateful; having lived together with us for forty thousand years, why do you suddenly abandon us and go?"
Disregarding their words, he continued forward.

He saw a crystal city where eight jade maidens, holding eight wish-fulfilling jewels and also performing music, came out to welcome him; for eighty thousand years, he experienced the utmost joy and pleasure.
Feeling a sense of revulsion, he again abandoned it and went far away.

Upon reaching the city of White Silver, sixteen jade maidens were there holding sixteen wish-fulfilling jewels to welcome him as before; for one hundred and sixty thousand years, he experienced great happiness, yet once more he abandoned it and departed.

Upon reaching the Golden City, thirty-two jade maidens appeared, each holding a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), coming forward to welcome him as before. For another three hundred and twenty thousand years, he experienced great bliss, yet he again desired to depart.
The various jade maidens said:

"In all your previous and subsequent dwellings, you have always occupied excellent places; from this point forward, there will be no better place than this, so it would be better for you to remain here."
Having heard these words, he thought to himself:
"These jade maidens have spoken thus only because they long for me; if I advance, there will surely be a favorable outcome."
He then departed immediately.
Seeing from afar an iron city, a sense of doubt and wonder arose in his mind, and he thought to himself:
"Though it is iron on the outside, the interior is exceedingly fine."
Gradually advancing and drawing near to the city, he still found no jade maidens coming out to welcome him, whereupon he thought again:
"The city must be a place of supreme bliss; that is why they have not come out to welcome me."
Advancing further and further, he eventually entered an iron city.
At the gate, there was a man who placed a flaming wheel upon his own head; he then removed this flaming wheel and placed it upon the girl's head, whereupon he immediately departed.
The Compassionate Maiden asked the warder,
"When may I be released from wearing this wheel?
He replied:

“There are people in the world who commit both sins and merits; just as you have done, they shall go to sea to gather treasures, travel through various cities for a long or short duration, and thereafter come to take upon themselves the retribution for your sins.”
"This iron wheel shall never fall to the ground.
The girl Maitrī asked,
"What merit have I performed?"
"What further offense did you commit?

He replied, "In the past, while in Jambudvīpa, you provided two coins daily as an offering to your mother; therefore, you obtained the city of Vaiḍūrya, the four wish-fulfilling jewels, and the four celestial maidens, where you enjoyed happiness for forty thousand years."

Because he made an offering of four coins to his mother, he obtained the city of Vaiḍūrya, eight wish-fulfilling jewels, eight jade maidens, and so forth, and for eighty thousand years, he experienced all manner of happiness.

Because he made an offering of eight coins to his mother, he obtained a city of white silver, sixteen wish-fulfilling jewels, and sixteen jade maidens; for one hundred and sixty thousand years, he experienced supreme happiness.

Because he made an offering of sixteen coins to his mother, he obtained a city of gold, thirty-two wish-fulfilling jewels, and thirty-two jade maidens; for three hundred and twenty thousand years, he experienced great happiness.
"Because you cut off your mother's hair, you must now wear this iron wheel of fire upon your head, which never falls to the ground;
only if someone takes your place may you be released.
He asked again:
"Now, within this hell, are there perhaps others who undergo retribution like me?
He replied,
"There are hundreds of thousands, immeasurable, and beyond calculation."
Having heard these words, he immediately reflected to himself:
"I shall ultimately not escape; I vow that all those who ought to suffer may have their retribution gathered entirely upon my own body."
Having formed this thought, the iron wheel immediately fell to the ground.
The girl Maitrāyaṇī said to the warder,
"According to your own teachings, this wheel has never fallen before."
"Why have you fallen now?
The hell-warden, filled with rage, struck the young girl on the head with an iron fork; she immediately passed away and was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.
"Those who wish to know who the girl Maitrī was at that time, it was none other than myself.
Monks, you should know this:
even if one commits a small unwholesome act toward one's parents, one will receive a great retribution of suffering."
"By making even small offerings, one obtains immeasurable merit.
You should train yourselves in this way: you ought to diligently and wholeheartedly serve and support your parents.
8. The Story of Lady Padumā (8) The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī and addressed the bhikṣus:

"If one gives rise to a mind of anger toward one's parents, or toward the Buddha and his disciples, this person shall fall into the Black Rope Hell, where they will undergo immeasurable suffering without end."
The bhikṣus asked the Buddha, “World-Honored One! Regarding the honoring of one’s parents:
if one does not show honor toward one’s parents and commits even a small unwholesome act, what will be the consequence of that?”
The Buddha said:

"In the distant past, immeasurable eons ago, there was a seer named Devadatta on the slopes of the Snowy Mountains. He was of the Brahmin caste; according to the Brahmin law, one who does not produce sons or daughters cannot be reborn in heaven."
This brahmin was constantly urinating upon a stone slab; his semen flowed and fell into a stone crevice.
A female deer came and licked the place where he had urinated, and she immediately became pregnant.

When the months were complete, she came down to the base of the seer’s cave and gave birth to a girl; her body was wrapped in flowers as she emerged from her mother’s womb, beautiful and most exquisite.
The rishi, knowing her to be his own daughter, took her in and raised her; as she gradually grew up, wherever her feet trod upon the ground, lotus flowers would emerge.

According to the dharma of the brahmins, one must always maintain a fire at night. Once, when the fire happened to go out for a single night and none remained, he went to another's house, wishing to beg for fire.
Seeing his footprints marked with lotus flowers, the other person said to him:
"Walk seven times around my house, and I will give you fire."
He then circumambulated it seven times, obtained fire, and returned home.

He encountered King Udayana while he was out hunting; seeing that the man’s house had seven layers of lotus flowers, the king marveled and asked him, "For what reason does your house have these lotus flowers?"
He immediately replied to the king, saying, "A Brahmin girl from the mountains came to beg for fire; this lotus flower grew beneath her foot.
He then followed the tracks of her feet until he reached the place where the seer was.
When the king saw that the girl was so upright and exquisitely beautiful, he said to the rishi,
"Give this girl to me.
He immediately gave her to him, and the rishi spoke to the king, saying:
"She shall give birth to five hundred princes.
Thereupon, she was established as the Queen, becoming the foremost among five hundred court ladies.
As the King's principal consort, she became intensely jealous of Mṛgajā and spoke these words:
"The King now holds you in such high esteem; if he were to have five hundred sons born to him, he would surely honor you all the more.
Not long thereafter, five hundred eggs were born, which were placed inside a chest.
At that time, the chief queen took five hundred pieces of dough to replace the eggs; she then sealed this casket with a lid and a seal, and cast it into the Ganges River.
The king asked the lady,
"What has been born?
She replied:
"Only pure flour noodle segments.
The King said,
"The seer speaks falsely."
He immediately demoted the queen from her position and never saw her again.
At that time, King Sāḍambava was at a lower reaches of the river, sporting with his court ladies by the riverbank.
Seeing this casket arrive, he spoke these words:
"This casket belongs to me.
The ladies-in-waiting said:
"The King should now take the casket; we shall take whatever is within it.

They sent someone to fetch the casket, and each of the five hundred queens received an egg. The eggs spontaneously opened and bloomed, and within each was a boy with handsome features. They were raised and grew up, and each possessed the strength of a great athlete, erecting the banners of the five hundred athletes.
“King Udayana constantly demanded tribute from King Sāṇḍilya; when King Sāṇḍilya heard that tribute was being demanded, he became sorrowful and unhappy.”
The sons said,
"Why are you so distressed?
The king replied:
"Now that I dwell in this world, I am being oppressed by others.
His sons asked, "By whom are you being oppressed?"
The king said,
"King Udayana constantly follows me, demanding tribute.
The sons replied:
"All the kings of Jambudvīpa desire to demand tribute; we can cause them to present tribute to Your Majesty.
For what reason, O King, do you provide tribute to others?"
The five hundred strongmen then led their troops to attack King Udayana.
King Udayana spoke in terror:
"I cannot withstand even a single strongman, let alone five hundred!"
He then recruited those within the kingdom who could repel this enemy.
Furthermore, he reflected:
"Perhaps that seer might understand how to do so."
Employing various skillful means, he went to where the seer was and said to him, "The kingdom faces a great calamity; by what means may it be dispelled?
He replied:
"There is an enemy.
The king said,
"King Sāndabhu has five hundred strongmen who have all led their troops and intend to come and attack me."
"I have now reached a point where there is no such wrestler who can oppose him.
What strategy or plan can I devise to repel this adversary?
The seer replied:
"You may go back and seek Queen Padmāvatī; she will be able to repel the enemy.
The king asked, "How can she repel them?"
The seer replied:
"These five hundred strongmen are all your sons, born of Lady Padumāvatī.
Your chief queen, harboring hatred and jealousy, cast those sons born of Padumāvatī into the river."
King Sāḍambava rescued him from beneath the river and raised him until he was grown.
Now, the King shall place Lady Padmā upon a great elephant and lead her before the military array; she will naturally submit.
Following the words of the seer, he returned to offer his apologies to Lady Padmā.
After they had both offered their apologies, he adorned the lady, dressed her in fine garments, and mounted her upon a great white elephant, placing her at the front of the military array.
The five hundred strongmen raised their bows, intending to shoot, but their arms became naturally straight and they could neither bend nor extend them;
they were struck with great alarm. A seer flew through the air and, from mid-space, spoke to the strongmen:
"Be careful not to raise your hands, and do not give rise to evil thoughts; if you give rise to evil thoughts, you will all fall into hell."
"This king and his consort are your parents.
The mother then pressed her breasts; from each breast there issued two hundred and fifty jets, all of which entered the mouths of her sons.

They immediately confessed to their parents and gave rise to a sense of shame and remorse; all of them attained the state of a pratyekabuddha. The two kings also spontaneously awakened and likewise attained the state of a pratyekabuddha.
"At that time, the seer was none other than myself.
At that time, I restrained those sons so that they would not harbor ill will toward their parents, and they attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha;
even now, I likewise praise and extol the virtue of making offerings to one's aged parents."
9. The Story of the Lady Mṛgajā (IX). The Story of the Lady Mṛgajā. The Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha and addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are two kinds of dharmas that enable a person to quickly attain the states of humans and devas, leading ultimately to the bliss of Nirvāṇa."
"There are two kinds of dharmas that can cause people to fall swiftly into the three evil realms and undergo great suffering and affliction.
"What are these two dharmas that can cause people to quickly attain the states of humans and devas, and reach the bliss of Nirvana?"
The Buddha said:
"The first is to make offerings to one's parents; the second is to make offerings to the worthy and holy ones.
[He asked: "What are the two dharmas by which one quickly falls into the three evil realms and undergoes great suffering?"
The Buddha said:
"First, one commits various unwholesome acts toward one's parents;
second, one likewise commits unwholesome acts toward the worthy and the noble."
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that good and evil are so swiftly accomplished?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, immeasurable kalpas ago, there was a kingdom named Vārāṇasī. Within that kingdom was a mountain called Ṛṣigiri."

At that time, there was a brahmin living on that mountain who always voided his excrement and urine upon the rocks. Later, some semen fell onto the ground where he had urinated; a female deer came and licked it up, and she immediately became pregnant.

When the months were complete, she came to the place of the seer and gave birth to a daughter who was exceptionally beautiful and graceful, with the exception that her feet resembled those of a deer; the brahmin took her and raised her until she had grown up.
"It is the law of the brahmins to constantly serve the fire, ensuring that it is never extinguished.
This girl, while tending the perpetual fire, was slightly inattentive and caused the fire to go out."
This woman was terrified, fearing the anger of the brahmin.
There was another brahmin living one *krośa*—in the language of Qin, five li—away from this dwelling; the woman quickly went to that brahmin to beg for fire.
The brahmin saw her footprints, which bore lotus flowers, and addressed the woman, saying:
"Walk seven times around my house and I shall give you fire.
When you depart, you must likewise walk seven times around it; do not follow your original path, but return by a different way."
He then acted according to those words, taking fire and departing.

At that time, King Brahmadatta was out on a hunting expedition when he saw that brahmin; surrounding his house were fourteen concentric circles of lotus flowers, and he further saw two rows of lotus flowers along the two paths.
Wondering at the cause of this, he asked the brahmin, saying:
"There is no pond whatsoever; how is it that there are these exquisite and beautiful lotus flowers?
He replied:
"In that hermitage there was a woman who came to me to beg for fire. The footprints this woman left were all born as lotus flowers. I then made a condition with her:
'If you wish to obtain the fire, circumambulate my dwelling seven times; when you take it away, you must likewise circumambulate it seven times.'"
"For this reason, there are these surrounding lotuses.
The king followed the traces of the flowers until he reached the place where the brahmin was; there he sought the girl and examined her.
Seeing that she was upright and beautiful, he was deeply pleased in his heart and immediately requested the girl from the brahmin.
The brahmin immediately presented her to the king, and the king appointed her as his second consort.
"This girl was raised by a seer from her youth; she is upright by nature and does not understand the wiles and charms of women."
Later, she became pregnant, and a physiognomist predicted:
"She shall give birth to a thousand sons.

Upon hearing these words, the King’s principal consort conceived feelings of jealousy and gradually devised a scheme; she used generous favors and inducements to win over the attendants and retinue of the Deer Woman, bestowing upon them abundant wealth, money, and precious jewels.
At that time, when the doe’s months were fulfilled, she gave birth to a thousand-petaled lotus.

As she was about to give birth, the chief consort covered her eyes with an object so she could not see for herself; she took a piece of stinking, rotting horse lung and placed it beneath [the doe], then took the thousand-petaled lotus, put it in a basket, and threw it into the river. Upon returning, she removed the covering from the doe’s eyes and said to her, “Look at what you have given birth to;
you will see nothing but a piece of stinking, rotting horse lung.”
The king sent someone to ask:
"What has been born?
and they replied to the king:
"Only a thing that produces stench and rot, like a horse's lung.
Then the chief queen spoke to the king, saying:
"The King has reached a state of delusion through his own joy; this beast has given birth to what is nurtured by sages—this inauspicious, foul, and filthy creature."
The Great Queen was immediately dismissed from her position as queen and was no longer permitted to enter the palace.
At that time, King Udayana, accompanied by his retinue, queens, and court ladies, went down to the lower reaches of the river to enjoy himself.
He saw a yellow cloud-canopy coming down the river, following the current; the king thought to himself:
"Beneath this cloud-canopy, there must surely be a divine being."

He sent someone to investigate, who saw beneath a yellow cloud a casket. They immediately retrieved it and opened it to look inside, finding a thousand-petaled lotus flower with a small boy upon each petal. They took them and raised them; as they gradually grew up, each possessed the strength of a great athlete.
"King Udayana regularly presented tribute to King Brahmadatta each year. Having gathered all the offerings,
he was about to dispatch his envoys when his sons asked him,
'What do you intend to do?'"
The king then replied,
"I wish to present them as tribute to the King of Brahmadatta.
Each of his sons spoke in turn:
"If even a single son could hope to subjugate the world and compel it to bring tribute, how much more so with our thousand sons—how could we offer ourselves to another?
Thereupon, the thousand sons immediately led their various armies to subdue all the kingdoms, arriving in succession at the kingdom of King Brahmadatta.
When the king heard that the army had arrived, he issued a proclamation throughout his kingdom:
"Who among you is able to repel such an enemy?
Yet, there was no one at all who could repel them.
The second lady came forward to accept the challenge, saying:
"I am able to repel them.
He asked her:
"How can they be repelled?
The lady replied, "Simply construct for me a terrace one hundred *zhang* high; seated upon it, I shall certainly be able to repel them."
When the platform had been completed, the second queen sat upon it.
At that time, when the thousand sons wished to raise their bows to shoot, their hands naturally became unable to lift them.
The lady spoke these words:
"Be careful not to raise your hand toward your parents; I am your mother.
The thousand sons asked:
"How can I know for certain that she is my mother?
He replied, "If I press my breasts, five hundred streams will emerge from each breast and enter your mouth; she shall be your mother."
"If it were not so, she would not be your mother.
Immediately, she pressed both hands upon her breasts; from each breast, five hundred channels emerged, entering the mouths of the thousand sons, while the rest of the army received nothing at all.
The thousand sons were subdued and prostrated themselves before their parents to confess their transgressions.

Thereupon, the sons reached a reconciliation, and the two kingdoms were no longer at enmity. They exhorted one another, giving five hundred sons to their biological parents and five hundred sons to their foster parents.
"At that time, the two kings divided Jambudvīpa and each raised five hundred sons.
The Buddha said,
"If you wish to know who those thousand sons were at that time, they are the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa."
The jealous lady who deceived others' eyes at that time was the dragon with overlapping scales and blind eyes.
The father at that time was King Śuddhodana.
The mother at that time was Lady Māyā.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
“By what causes and conditions was this woman born from the womb of a deer, with lotuses growing beneath her feet?
Furthermore, by what causes and conditions did she become the king’s consort?”
The Buddha said:
"In a past life, this girl was born into a poor and lowly family.
While mother and daughter were weeding grain in a field, they saw a pratyekabuddha holding an alms bowl to beg for food. The mother said to the daughter:"
"I wish to take my own portion of food from my home and give it to this noble gentleman.
The woman said,
"Take my portion as well and give it to him together."
The mother immediately returned home, took the portions of food intended for herself and her son, and brought them to give to the Pratyekabuddha.
The daughter gathered grass and plucked flowers, spreading the grass for him to sit upon and scattering the flowers over it, then invited the Pratyekabuddha to take his seat.
The daughter, wondering why her mother was so late, climbed to a high place and gazed afar at her mother. Having seen her mother from a distance, she said to her:
"Why do you not hurry?"
"The deer came galloping.
Once the mother had arrived, because he resented her for being late, he immediately spoke words of resentment:
"It would have been better for me to have been born among the deer than to have been born by my mother's side."
The mother then gave two portions of food to the pratyekabuddha, while the remainder was eaten by the mother and son together.

When the pratyekabuddha had finished eating, he cast his alms bowl into the air and immediately flew away after it. Having reached the midst of the sky, he performed the eighteen miraculous transformations.
At that time, the mother was filled with joy and immediately made this vow:
"May I, in all future lives, always give birth to a holy son such as this holy man.
By virtue of these karmic conditions, she later gave birth to five hundred sons, all of whom became Pratyekabuddhas—one being her foster mother and the others her biological mothers.
Because she spoke impulsively to her mother-deer regarding the causes and conditions [of her pregnancy], she was conceived in the deer's womb; her feet resembled the hooves of a deer.
Because she had gathered flowers to scatter over a pratyekabuddha, one hundred flowers grew within her footprints.
Because she spread the grass, she was always able to become the consort of a king.
In her subsequent life, her mother became King Brahmadatta, and her daughter’s subsequent life was as Lady Padmāvatī.
"By virtue of these karmic conditions, he will subsequently be born among the thousand sages of the Bhadrakalpa; through the power of his vows, he shall always be born as a sage or a holy one.
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
