10. The Story of the Two Inner Ministers Disputing Over Righteousness; (10) The Story of the Six-Tusked White Elephant.
Long ago, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a great householder who had a daughter born to him.
She possessed the memory of her past lives and was able to speak immediately upon birth, saying these words:
"An unwholesome deed, an act of filial impiety, an act of shamelessness, an act of malice, and an act of ingratitude.
Having spoken these words, he fell silent.
When this girl was born, she possessed great merit; they immediately bestowed a name upon her, calling her Bhadrā.
As she gradually grew up, she came to hold the *kāṣāya* robes in the utmost reverence.
On account of her reverence for the *kāṣāya*, she left the household life to become a *bhikṣuṇī*.
Without having reached the presence of the Buddha, she practiced with diligent effort and immediately attained the state of an Arhat.
Regretting that he had not gone to the Buddha's side, he went to where the Buddha was and confessed his transgression before him.
The Buddha said,
"At that time, I had already accepted your confession."
The bhikṣus, filled with doubt and wonder, asked the Buddha:
"For what reason has this virtuous bhikṣuṇī not seen the Buddha since she went forth?
What is the cause and condition for her being able to see the Buddha today and repent?"
The Buddha then explained the causal conditions for him:
"In the past, there was a six-tusked white elephant with a large following.
This white elephant had two wives: one named Bhadrā and the other named Subhadrā."
While wandering through the forest, he happened upon a lotus flower and intended to give it to Bhadra; however, Subhadra snatched it away.
Seeing his flower taken, Bhadra conceived a feeling of jealousy, thinking:
"That elephant loves Subhadra, but does not love me."
At that time, there was a Buddhist stūpa on that mountain; Bhadra would regularly gather flowers to make offerings there, and he made this vow:
"When I am born among humans, may I naturally remember my past lives, and may I also extract these white elephant tusks."
She immediately climbed to the top of a mountain and threw herself down to her death.
She was then reborn as a daughter in the house of King Videha, knowing her own past lives.
When she had grown up, she became the wife of King Brahmadatta; remembering her former enmity, she said to Brahmadatta:
"Only if you provide me with ivory to make a bed can I survive;
otherwise, I cannot live.
King Brahmadatta immediately issued a proclamation to recruit hunters:
"If anyone can obtain an elephant's tusk and bring it here, they shall be given one hundred taels of gold.
Immediately, a hunter, falsely donning a *kāṣāya* robe and carrying a bow with poisoned arrows, went to where the elephant was.
At that time, the female elephant Bhaddā, having seen the hunter, immediately said to the elephant king,
"Someone has come.
The elephant king asked:
"What clothing do you wear?
He replied,
"I wear the kāṣāya robe upon my body."
The Elephant King said,
"Within the saṃghāṭī robe there must surely be goodness and no evil.
Thereupon, the hunter was able to draw near and shot him with a poisoned arrow.
Sobhita said to her husband: "You say:
'In the saṃghāṭī robe there is good and no evil.'"
"How can this be so? He replied, "It is not the fault of the kashaya;
rather, it is the fault of the afflictions within the mind."
"Śubhavyūha immediately wished to harm that hunter, but the Elephant King comforted him with various teachings and would not allow him to be harmed.

Furthermore, fearing that the herd of five hundred elephants would surely kill this hunter, he hid him in a fork of the branches and sent the entire herd of five hundred elephants far away. He then asked the hunter:
'What did you need that you shot at me?'"
He replied, "I have no need for anything;
it is because King Brahmadatta has offered a reward for your tusks that I have come wishing to take them."
The elephant said,
"Take it quickly.
He replied:
“I do not dare take it for myself.
Such compassion has nurtured and protected me; if I were to take it with my own hands, my hands would fall off and rot.
At that moment, the white elephant went to the great tree, pulled out its tusks himself, grasped them with his trunk, and gave them away while making this vow:
"By this gift of my tusks, I vow that in the future I shall pull out the tusks of the three poisons from all sentient beings.
The hunter took the tusks and presented them to King Brahmadatta.
At that time, having obtained these tusks, the queen felt remorse and spoke these words:
"How is it that I have now taken these tusks of this noble, excellent, and pure-virtued one?"
Having cultivated great merit, he made this vow:
"I pray that when he attains Buddhahood in the future, I may leave the household life to study the Way within his Dharma and become an Arhat."
"You all should know! At that time, the white elephant was my own self.
At that time, the hunter was Devadatta."
"The worthy one at that time is this present bhikṣuṇī.
The good worthy one at that time is the bhikṣuṇī Yaśodharā. 11.

The Story of the Rabbit Who Burned Its Own Body as an Offering to the Great Seer (11) In the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was the son of an elder who had renounced the world within the Buddha’s Dharma. He constantly took pleasure in his kinsmen and relatives; he did not wish to associate with practitioners of the Way, nor did he delight in reciting the sūtras or practicing the Path.
The Buddha commanded this bhikṣu to go to a forest hermitage (āraṇya) and practice with diligence; he attained arhatship, fully endowed with the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā).
The other bhikṣus, filled with doubt and wonder, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The appearance of the World-Honored One in the world is most marvelous and extraordinary!"

"In this way, how was this son of a householder able to establish him in the forest retreat (āraṇyaka), enable him to attain the path of arhatship, and become endowed with the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā)?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is not only today that he was able to establish him; rather, in the past, he had already established him."
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
"We do not understand, World-Honored One!
What were the circumstances of that past establishment?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the past, there was a rishi dwelling among the mountain forests.
At that time, there was a great drought; the fruits, gourds, roots, stalks, branches, and leaves in the mountains were all withered and dried up."
At that time, the seer was on friendly terms with the rabbit, and he said to the rabbit:
"I now wish to enter the village to beg for food.
The rabbit said:
"Do not go! I shall give you food.
Thereupon, the hare gathered wood for himself and spoke again to the seer:
"You must accept my food; the heavens shall send down rain. Stay for three days, and when the flowers and fruits reappear, you may gather them for sustenance; do not go toward the human world."
Having spoken these words, he immediately lit a great fire and threw himself into it.
When the seer saw this, he reflected:
"This hare is compassionate and kind; he is my virtuous companion. For the sake of my food, he was able to sacrifice his own life—this is truly a difficult feat."
At that time, the seer was overcome with great anguish and immediately took and ate it.
Because the Bodhisattva was performing such difficult and painful ascetic practices, the palace of Śakra Devānām Indra shook, and he thought to himself:
"By what cause and condition has this occurred?"
The palace shook.
Observing this, he knew that the hare had been able to perform a difficult feat; moved by what it had done, he immediately sent down rain.
The rishi then remained there and returned to eating fruits and gourds.
At that time, through his practice, he attained the five supernormal powers.
"If you wish to know who the seer with the five supernormal powers was at that time, it is this bhikṣu here.
The rabbit of that time was my own self."
Since I sacrificed my own body, I enabled that rishi to dwell in an araṇya and attain the five supernormal powers;
how much more so now, could I not cause this bhikṣu to leave his kinsmen, dwell in an araṇya, attain arhatship, and acquire the six supernormal powers?
12. The Story of the Good and Evil Monkeys (12). The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One!”

Relying upon Devadatta, one constantly experiences suffering and affliction; relying upon the World-Honored Tathāgata, one attains peace and happiness in the present, is reborn in a favorable realm in the future, and attains the path to liberation.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Not only today; in the distant past, there were two monkeys, each with five hundred followers."
It happened that the Prince of Kāśī was out hunting, and his encircling troops were about to arrive.
One virtuous monkey said to an evil monkey,
"If we cross this river now, we may escape this calamity."
The wicked monkey said,
"I cannot cross.
The good monkey spoke to the other monkeys, saying:
"The branches of the *vītara* tree are extremely long.
He then pulled at the branch and ferried his five hundred followers across.
Because the followers of the wicked monkey did not cross over, they were captured by the prince.
At that time, the good monkey was I myself; the evil monkey was Devadatta.
Those who were his followers and suffered at that time are likewise those who now rely upon him.

At that time, those who rely upon me will experience happiness throughout the long night; in the present life they will receive fame and offerings, and in the future they will attain liberation among gods and humans.

At that time, those who rely upon Devadatta will experience decline and suffering throughout the long night; in the present life they will incur an evil reputation and receive no offerings from others, and in the future they will fall into the three evil realms.
Therefore, monks, you should distance yourselves from evil associates and draw near to virtuous associates.
Virtuous associates provide people with peace, security, and happiness throughout the long night.
For this reason, one should draw near to virtuous friends and distance oneself from evil friends. Why is this?
Evil friends can burn and scorch one, causing a mass of sufferings to accumulate in both this life and future lives.

13. The Story of the Buddha Extinguishing the Three Fires with the Water of Wisdom (13). There was a country named Dakṣiṇāpatha. The Buddha wished to go to that country and, while on the road, arrived at a village to stay for the night.
It happened that in that village a festive gathering was being held; the people were intoxicated with wine and, unaware of it, a fire broke out and burned the village.
The people were terrified and did not know where to turn, each saying to the others:
"We can only rely upon the Buddha to escape this calamity of fire."
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I pray that you will grant me rescue and relief.”
The Buddha said:
"All sentient beings possess three fires:
the fire of greed, the fire of anger, and the fire of delusion."
"I shall extinguish these three fires with the water of wisdom.
If these words are true, this fire shall be extinguished.
Having spoken these words, the fire was immediately extinguished.
The people rejoiced, placing their faith and deep respect in the Buddha; the Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.
The bhikṣus were filled with wonder and doubt, thinking:
"The appearance of the World-Honored One in this world is truly marvelous and extraordinary!"
"This brings great benefit to this village; the fire of the settlement is extinguished, and the defilements of the mind are likewise extinguished.
The Buddha said, "It is not only today that I have brought about such benefit; in the past as well, I once brought great benefit to those people."
The bhikṣus asked, “We do not know the details of the benefits bestowed by the World-Honored One in the past; what were those events?
The Buddha said:
"In a past age, on one side of the Snowy Mountains, there was a great bamboo grove where many birds and beasts lived.
There was a parrot named Priyamukha."

At that time, in the forest, the wind blew two bamboos together so that they rubbed against each other; fire emerged from between them and burned that bamboo grove. The birds and beasts were terrified, having no place of refuge.
At that time, the parrot gave rise to a profound sense of compassion and, pitying those birds and beasts, grasped their wings and went to the water to sprinkle it upon the fire.
Because of his compassionate and diligent efforts, he caused the palace of Śakra to tremble violently.
Śakra Devānām Indra, observing with his divine eye, wondered: "By what cause and condition are my palaces shaking?

He then saw that in the world there was a parrot who, harboring great compassion, sought to rescue [beings] from fire; yet though it exerted all its physical strength, it could not extinguish the flames.
Śakra Devānām Indra immediately went to where the parrot was and said to him:
"This forest is vast, spanning many thousands of miles; the water taken up by your wings and feathers does not exceed a few drops. How can you possibly extinguish such a great fire?"
The parrot replied, "My mind is vast and expansive;
with diligent and tireless effort, I shall surely extinguish the fire.
Even if I must exhaust this present body and fail to do so, I shall take another body in the future and vow that I will certainly extinguish it."
Śakra Devānām Indra, moved by his resolve, sent down a great rain, and the fire was immediately extinguished.
"The parrot at that time was none other than my own self."
Those birds and beasts in the forest at that time are now the people of this great settlement.
Just as I extinguished that fire for them then to bring them peace, so too do I now extinguish the fire to bring them peace.
He asked again:
"By what further conditions does one attain the path of seeing the truths?
The Buddha said:

"These people, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, observed and upheld the five precepts; by virtue of these causes and conditions, they have now attained the vision of the Truths and realized the stage of Srotāpanna."

14. The Story of the Elder’s Son from Vārāṇasī Who, Moved by a Deva, Practiced Filial Piety toward the King. Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī and addressed the bhikṣus, saying: “If there is anyone who wishes to have the Brahmādeva residing within their home, they should practice filial piety and support their parents; then the Brahmādeva will indeed reside within that home. At that time, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was the son of an elder who, together with a deva, moved the king to practice filial piety. The circumstances were as follows: In the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was the son of an elder. He was deeply devoted to his parents and always served them with utmost care. One day, while he was away on business, a deva appeared before him and said: “Your father and mother are now very old and frail; you must return home immediately to attend to them. The son replied: “I am currently occupied with affairs abroad. I shall return home as soon as I have settled my business. The deva said: “If you do not return quickly, your parents will surely pass away. Once they are gone, you will have no way to repay their kindness. You must go back at once! The son thought to himself: “This deva speaks with such sincerity; it must be true. With this in mind, he abandoned his business and returned home at once. Upon arriving, he found his parents already deceased. He wept bitterly and lamented, saying: “Alas! I have failed to fulfill my filial duty. What can I do now? At that moment, the deva appeared again and said: “Because you were moved by my words and acted with such urgency, I have granted you a boon. Your parents are now dwelling in the realm of the Thirty-three Heavens. Go there and serve them; you shall receive great merit. The son asked: “How may I reach that heavenly realm? The deva replied: “In the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there is a king named Brahmadatta. He is a righteous ruler who honors the Triple Gem and practices filial piety. If you can serve this king with devotion, you will be able to ascend to heaven and see your parents. The son followed the deva’s instructions and went to the capital of Vārāṇasī. There, he encountered the king, who was out hunting. The son approached the king and said: “I am a man of humble station who has come from afar seeking to serve Your Majesty. I wish to become your attendant. The king, seeing that the man was upright and sincere, accepted him as a servant. The son served the king with diligence and integrity, never neglecting his duties. Because of his faithful service, the king grew increasingly fond of him and eventually appointed him as a high official. Later, when the king fell ill, the son nursed him with great care and devotion. Moved by the son’s filial conduct, the king recovered. Grateful for his service, the king bestowed upon him great wealth and honor. The son then told the king of his past life and how the deva had guided him to serve the king so that he might meet his parents in heaven. The king was filled with wonder and joy, and he too resolved to practice filial piety toward his own parents. From that time forth, the son of the elder and the king of Vārāṇasī both honored their parents with the highest reverence, and because of their virtue, they were able to behold their parents in the celestial realms. Thus, through the power of filial piety, even those in the human world can attain rebirth in the heavens. (This concludes the fourteenth story: The Story of the Elder’s Son from Vārāṇasī Who, Moved by a Deva, Practiced Filial Piety toward the King.)
If one wishes for Śakra to reside within one’s home, then being able to filially support one’s parents is itself Śakra residing in the home.
If one wishes for all the celestial deities to reside within one’s home, simply by making offerings to one’s parents, one should know that all the celestial deities have already resided in the home.
If one can simply make offerings to one's parents, then the Upādhyāya is already present in one's home.
If one wishes for the Ācārya to be present in one's home, simply making offerings to one's parents is equivalent to having the Ācārya within that home.

"If you wish to make offerings to the various worthies and sages, as well as to the Buddha, or if you wish to make offerings to your parents, the various worthies and sages, as well as the Buddha, are already within your home.
The bhikṣus said, "O Tathāgata, World-Honored One!"
"It is most rare and extraordinary that you show such reverence to your parents.

The Buddha said, "It is not only today that it is most rare and extraordinary for you to revere your parents; in past lives as well, you have likewise shown rare and extraordinary reverence to your parents."
The bhikṣu asked,
“Regarding the past veneration, what were the circumstances?
The Buddha said:
"In the past, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a poor man who had only one son. Yet this son had many children of his own, and the family remained impoverished."
At that time, during a period of famine, he buried his parents alive in the ground in order to provide for and raise his son.
A neighbor asked him,
"Where are your parents?"
He replied:
"My parents have grown old and will inevitably reach death; I shall bury them.
I intend to use my parents' share of food to nourish my son, so that he may grow up."
When the second family heard this, they considered it reasonable; thus it was passed along until it spread throughout the city of Vārāṇasī, whereupon it was accepted as the law.
Furthermore, there was another elder who also had a son born to him. When this son heard of the matter, he considered it improper and thought to himself:
"By what means can I overturn this unrighteousness?"
He then said to his father, "Father, you should now go on a long journey to study so that you may become learned in the sūtras and śāstras.
His father then departed; however, having acquired only a little learning, he returned home.
As he grew old, his son dug the earth and built a fine house, placing his father inside it and providing him with excellent food and drink.
He then thought to himself:
"Who will join me in removing this unrighteousness?"
The celestial deity manifested his form and spoke to him, saying:
"I shall now be your companion.
The celestial deity wrote upon paper and questioned the king on four matters:
"If you can understand the matters set forth in this commentary, I shall provide you with protection; if you do not understand them, seven days from now, I shall split your head into seven pieces."
There are four kinds of questions:
first, what is the foremost wealth;
second, what is the supreme happiness.
Third, what is the most excellent of all flavors?
Fourth, which being has the longest lifespan?
These were posted upon the gate of the king's palace.
"Once the king had obtained it, he immediately inquired throughout the kingdom:
'Who understands this?
If there is anyone who understands it, whatever they may seek, I shall fulfill all their wishes.'"
The son of the elder took this letter and explained its meaning, saying:
"Faith is the foremost wealth; the True Dharma is the supreme joy; truthful speech is the finest flavor; and wisdom is the highest life."
Having understood this meaning, he returned and hung it at the gate of the king's palace.
When the deva saw this, his heart was filled with great joy, and the king likewise rejoiced greatly.
The king asked the son of the elder:
"Who taught you these words? He replied,
"My father taught me."
The king asked,
"Where is your father?
The son of the elder replied:
"I pray that Your Majesty grant me fearlessness!
My father was truly aged; because he violated the laws of the kingdom, I buried him beneath the ground.
I beg you to listen to what your servant has to say."
Great King!

The kindness of one's parents is profound, comparable to that of heaven and earth. They carry one in their womb for ten months, pushing away the dry to keep one moist, nourishing and raising one with breast milk, and instructing one in the affairs of human life.
The formation of this body is entirely due to one’s parents; it is through them that one beholds the sun and moon and performs the activities of daily life.

By the power of one’s parents, even if one were to carry one’s father on the left shoulder and one’s mother on the right shoulder for a hundred years, and furthermore provide them with every kind of service and offering, one would still be unable to repay the kindness of one’s parents.
Then the king asked,
"What do you seek? He replied:
"There is nothing further to be sought; we only pray that Your Majesty will abandon these evil practices.
The King agreed with their words and issued a proclamation throughout the kingdom:
"If there be anyone who is unfilial toward their parents, their crime shall be severely punished.
"If you wish to know who the elder’s son was at that time, it was my very self."

At that time, for the sake of that single kingdom, I eliminated evil practices and established the dharma of filial piety; by these causes and conditions, I attained Buddhahood for myself. Therefore, on this day as well, I again praise the dharma of filial piety.

15. The Story of the King of Kāśī, the White Elephant, Who Supported His Blind Parents and Reconciled Two Kingdoms (15). Once, when the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"There are eight kinds of persons to whom one should give with certainty, without further doubt."
"Parents [should regard] the Buddha and his disciples, those who have come from afar, those who are departing for distant places, the sick, and those who tend to the sick.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
"O Tathāgata, World-Honored One!"
"How most wonderful and extraordinary!
You always praise and show reverence toward your parents.
The Buddha said:
"I have not only today, but throughout the past as well, always honored and revered him.
The bhikṣus asked:
"In what way did you honor and praise him?"
The Buddha said:
"In the distant past, there were two kings: one was the King of Kāśī, and the other was the King of Videha."
King Videha possessed a great fragrant elephant; by the power of this fragrant elephant, he crushed and subdued the army of King Kāśī.
King Kāśī thought to himself:
"How shall I now obtain a fragrant elephant to crush and subdue the army of King Videha?"
At that time, someone said:
"I have seen a white fragrant elephant in the mountains.
Upon hearing this, the king immediately issued a proclamation:
"Whoever can capture that fragrant elephant, I shall grant them a generous reward.
Someone responded to this call, gathered a large army, and went to seize the elephant.
The elephant reflected, saying:
"If I were to go far away, my parents would be left blind and aged; it would be better for me to go tamed and compliant to the presence of the King.
At that time, the people then led the fragrant elephant toward the King.

The king was greatly delighted and had a fine house built for him, where he spread out woolen rugs and fine carpets beneath it; he provided him with various singing girls who played the lute and drummed the harp to entertain him.
When food and drink were offered to the elephant, it refused to eat them.
At that time, the elephant keeper came and reported to the king, saying,
"The elephant refuses to eat."
The king went to where the elephant was.
In ancient times, animals were all able to speak human language.
The king asked the elephant:
"Why do you not eat?
the elephant replied, "I have parents who are old and blind; there is no one to provide them with water or grass."
"If my parents do not eat, how can I eat?
The elephant said to the king, "If I wished to depart, none of Your Majesty's armies could have stopped me; it was only because my parents are blind and old that I followed Your Majesty here."
"Your Majesty, if you now grant me leave to return, I shall offer worship until the end of my years and then surely come back.
Upon hearing these words, the king was filled with great joy.
"We are humans with elephant heads, while this elephant is a human with an elephant head.
Previously, the people of Kāśī had despised their parents and lacked a heart of reverence; because of this elephant, the king immediately issued a proclamation throughout the entire kingdom:
"Whoever does not filially support and revere their parents shall be punished with a great penalty."
He immediately released the elephant and returned to his parents' place, where he served them for as long as they lived. When his parents passed away, he returned once more to the king's presence.
When the king obtained the white elephant, he was greatly delighted and immediately prepared for battle, intending to invade that country.
The elephant spoke to the king, saying:
"Do not engage in conflict; the nature of combat is such that it causes much injury."
The king said,
"He has bullied me.
The elephant said:
"Please allow me to go as an envoy, so that those enemies may not dare to insult or humiliate us.
The King said,
"If you go, it is possible you will not return."
He replied,
"There is no one capable of obstructing me so that I do not return.
Thereupon, the elephant proceeded to that kingdom.
When King Bhīmaratha heard that the elephant had arrived, he was filled with great joy; he went out in person to welcome it, and having seen the elephant, he spoke to it, saying:
"Stay in my kingdom."
The elephant said to the king:
"I may not stay here immediately; since I first took up this body, I have never violated my word or vow. Previously, I promised that king that I would return his kingdom."
"You two kings, should not you find joy in eliminating enmity and evil to bring peace to your own kingdoms?
He then spoke these verses:
"Victory increases enmity; Defeat brings only increased sorrow and suffering."
"For those who do not contend for victory or defeat, their happiness is the most supreme.
Having spoken this verse, the elephant then returned to the kingdom of Kāśī.
From that time forward, the two nations were reconciled.
At that time, the King of Kāśī was none other than the present King Prasenajit;
the King of Videha was King Ajātaśatru.
The white elephant at that time was my own body in this present life.

Because I filially supported my parents at that time, I have caused many sentient beings to likewise support their parents filially; just as I was able to bring about peace and harmony between the two kingdoms then, so it is today.

16. The Story of the Younger Brother in Vārāṇasī Who Gently Admonished His Elder Brother, Thereby Reaching the Prime Minister and Persuading the King to Transform the World (16). The younger brother in Vārāṇasī who gently admonished his elder brother, thereby reaching the prime minister and persuading the king to transform the world. Long ago, the World-Honored One said to the bhikṣus:
"You should know that in the past, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, unwholesome dharmas were prevalent in the world."
When his father was sixty years old, he gave him a pair of sandals and sent him to guard the gate.
At that time, there were two brothers; the elder brother said to the younger:
"You are to provide your father with sandals and have him guard the gate."
In the house there was only a single mat; the younger brother then cut it in half and gave one portion to his father, saying to him:
"This is for my elder brother and father; it is not what I give."
The elder brother instructed his father to have him guard the gate.
The elder brother said to his younger brother, "Why did you not give him all the mats? Why did you cut them in half before giving them to him?"
The younger brother replied, "Just now there was one piece of cloth; since you cut half of it and gave it to me, where else could I find more later?
The elder brother asked:
"Whom else do you wish to give it to?
The younger brother said,
"How could I not leave it for my elder brother?"
The elder brother said,
"Why give it to me?
The younger brother replied:
"When you grow old, your son will likewise place you at the door.
Upon hearing these words, the elder brother was struck with alarm and said,
"Will it be thus for me as well?"
The younger brother said,
"Who can take your place?
and then spoke to his elder brother, saying:
"Such evil practices ought to be abandoned together.
Thus, the brothers went together to the prime minister and spoke these words to him.
The minister replied, "It is indeed so; we too share in old age.
The minister informed the king, and the king approved these words.
He issued a proclamation throughout the realm: "Filially support your parents and sever former unlawful practices;
do not permit them to be committed again. 17. The Story of Queen Vaṃmadā’s Jealousy and the Harm Done to Her Son Dharmapāla (17) The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha and said to Devadatta:
"I have always cherished you with a heart of deep compassion, and in body, speech, and mind I have harbored no ill will toward you. Now, let us together perform repentance."
Devadatta departed with insults.
The bhikṣus said,
"How is it that while the Tathāgata’s heart of compassion is such as this, Devadatta instead responds with such foul abuse?"
The Buddha said:
"It is not only today.

In the past, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta; his queen's name was Akalyāṇī, and they had a son named Dharmapāla, who was intelligent, compassionate, and benevolent, and went to a teacher to study."
At that time, King Brahmadatta, accompanied by his court ladies, was strolling through the park, enjoying himself in peace and happiness; he gave the remains of his wine to the queen.
The lady, filled with anger, spoke these words:
"I would rather pierce Dharmapāla’s throat and drink his blood than drink this wine.
When the king heard these words, he spoke in a fit of rage:
"In the school, call Dharmapāla here.
Once Dharmapāla had arrived, [the father] intended to slit his throat.
The son said to his father:
"I am without fault or transgression; Your Majesty has but one son, so why would you kill me?
The king said, "I shall not kill you; it is my mother's wish."
"If you can confess to your mother and cause her to rejoice, she will never kill you.
The son immediately confessed to his mother, saying:
"I am your only son, and I have committed no transgression; why would you kill me?"
The mother did not accept his repentance; she then pierced her son’s throat and gave him blood to drink.
The Buddha said, “The father king at that time was Kokālika.”
The mother at that time was Devadatta;
the son at that time was I myself.
At that time, I harbored no ill will toward him, yet he would not accept my repentance; today it is the same—he will not accept my repentance.
At that time, although I was being killed, I did not harbor even a single thought of anger or resentment; how much less, on this day, could I possibly feel indignation or harbor an evil mind?
18. The Story of the Bhikṣu Tiṣya Being Slandered (18). Once there was a bhikṣu named Tiṣya, who possessed the strength of a great athlete.

Having left the household life and applied himself with diligence, he attained arhatship and was endowed with majestic virtue. He constantly attended to the affairs of the Sangha; from his five fingers there issued forth light, with which he provided the various bedding and furnishings for the assembly of monks.
For this reason, the Buddha declared that Campaka was foremost among those who manage monastic affairs.
Yet the bhikṣu Maitra, being himself of meager merit, found the food and drink at the assembly hall to be coarse and poor; he instead spoke with resentment:
"If Campaka continues to manage the affairs of the Saṅgha, I shall never obtain good food to sustain myself; I must devise a stratagem."
Pūrṇa had an elder sister who was a bhikṣuṇī; she went with him to jointly slander Cāṣa, doing so up to three times.

Cāṣa became weary of this and immediately ascended into the air, performing the eighteen transformations and entering the fire-light samādhi. In mid-air, he vanished like a flame being extinguished, leaving no corpse behind.
"Slander, greed, and envy can cause even the sages and saints to lose their lives; how much more so for ordinary people?
Therefore, the wise should be cautious regarding slander and must not speak lightly."
At that time, the bhikṣus immediately asked the Buddha:
"By what causes and conditions was the bhikṣu Trapusa slandered?
And by what causes and conditions did he obtain such great power?"
"Furthermore, by what causes and conditions did he attain arhatship?
The Buddha said,
"In a past age, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, there was a Buddha named Kāśyapa."
At that time, within the Dharma of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a young bhikṣu whose countenance was upright and whose complexion was exquisite.
Before this young bhikṣu had returned from his almsround, a certain young woman became infatuated with his physical form; she gazed at the bhikṣu, her eyes never turning away.

At that time, the bhikṣu Tāmraparṇī was serving as the supervisor of the meals. He happened to see this woman following the bhikṣu, her eyes never leaving him for even a moment, and he immediately slandered her, saying:
"This woman must have had an illicit affair with that bhikṣu."

"Because of these causes and conditions, I fell into the three evil realms and underwent immeasurable suffering; even until this day, the remaining retribution is not exhausted, and I am still subjected to slander."
Furthermore, during the time of the past Buddha Kāśyapa, he left the household life to study the Way and has now attained arhatship;

because he managed monastic affairs in the past, once carrying rice and flour on a donkey that sank into deep mud, he was able to pull it out, and by virtue of this cause, he has obtained the strength of a mighty man.
19. The Circumstances of Revata’s Slander (19). Once, in the kingdom of Kaśmīra, there was an Arhat named Revata who sat in meditation within the mountains.
There was a man who lost his ox and, pursuing its tracks, arrived directly at the place where it was.

At that time, Revata was boiling grass to dye his robes; the robes spontaneously transformed into ox hide, the dyeing liquid turned into blood, the boiled dye-herbs became beef, and the alms bowl he held turned into an ox head.
When the owner of the ox saw this, he immediately seized and bound him, taking him before the king.
The king then committed him to prison; there he remained for twelve years, constantly serving as a jailer’s attendant, feeding horses and clearing away dung.
Among the disciples of Revata, there were five hundred who had attained arhatship; they searched for their teacher but did not know his whereabouts, as his karmic conditions were about to end.
There was a disciple who, seeing that his teacher was in the prison of Kaśmīra, immediately went to inform the king:
"My teacher, Revata, is in Your Majesty's prison; I pray that you will provide a judgment in his favor."
The king immediately dispatched men to inspect the prison.

When the king’s men arrived at the prison, they saw only a man whose appearance was haggard and withered, his beard and hair extremely long, yet serving as the prison warden, feeding horses and clearing away excrement.
He returned and reported to the king, saying:
"In the prison there are no śramaṇas or practitioners of the Way; there is only the bhikṣu who is the jailer.
The disciple spoke again to the king, saying:
"I only wish that you would establish a teaching so that all bhikṣus may be permitted to leave prison.
The king immediately issued a proclamation that all practitioners of the Way were to be released from prison.

Within that prison, the Venerable Revata’s hair and beard fell away of their own accord, a kāṣāya robe appeared upon his body, and he leapt into the air, performing the eighteen miraculous transformations.

When the king saw this, he marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence; prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he said to the Venerable One, "I pray that you will accept my repentance.
Immediately, [the Venerable One] descended and accepted the king's repentance.
The king then asked:
"By what karmic conditions do you remain within this prison, suffering for so many years?
The Venerable One replied:
"In the past, I also once lost my oxen; while following their tracks through a mountain, I saw a pratyekabuddha sitting alone in meditation, and I immediately slandered him for a full day and night."

Because of these causes and conditions, they fell into the three miserable realms, suffering immeasurable agony and poison; as the remaining retribution was not yet exhausted, even upon attaining arhatship, they were still subjected to slander.

20. The Story of King Prasenajit’s Ugly Daughter Rāṣṭrā (20). Once, King Prasenajit had a daughter named Rāṣṭrā who possessed eighteen deformities; she did not resemble a human being at all, and everyone who saw her was struck with terror.

At that time, King Prasenajit issued a proclamation throughout the kingdom, seeking any sons of noble families who were impoverished, destitute, or solitary, instructing his officials to bring them before him.
At that moment, by the side of the marketplace, there was the son of a wealthy man who was alone and friendless, sustaining himself by begging.
He recruited someone to see her and bring her to the king.
Taking the man with him, the king entered the rear garden and commanded him, saying:
"I have given birth to a daughter whose appearance is hideous; she is unfit to be shown to others. I now wish to give her as a wife to you—would this be acceptable?"
Then the son of the elder addressed the king, saying:
"As for the command Your Majesty has issued, even if it were a dog, I would not yet decline; how much less could it be that I cannot do so for the king's daughter?"
The king immediately took her as his wife and built a palace for them, instructing the elder’s son:
“This woman is ugly in form; be careful not to show her to others. When she goes out, lock the gate; when she enters, close the door. Make this your constant practice.”

There were several sons of eminent householders who were close friends; they would drink, feast, and play together, and on each occasion of their gathering, the wives of those householders would all assemble there, yet this princess alone did not come.
Thereupon, the people made a mutual agreement, saying:
"Let us meet again on the following day, each bringing his wife. Whoever does not come shall be heavily fined in wealth and goods."
He then convened the assembly once more; however, the poor son of a householder still did not bring his wife as before, so the people collectively imposed a further penalty upon him.
The poor son of the elder respectfully accepted his punishment.
The others then made a collective agreement, saying:
"We shall meet again tomorrow; if you do not bring your wife, we shall impose a heavy penalty upon you once more."
"Though he was thus punished, even for the second and third time, he still did not bring [the money] to the assembly hall.
Later, the poor son of a householder returned home and said to his wife:
'I have been fined by others many times because of you.'"
The wife asked, "For what reason?
The husband replied,
"There is an agreement among the people that on the day of the drinking feast, everyone must bring their wives along to the place of assembly."
"I have been commanded by the King that you are not permitted to be shown to outsiders; therefore, I have been punished many times.
When the wife heard these words, she was deeply ashamed and felt profound self-reproach; day and night, she called upon the Buddha's name.
Thereupon, on a later day, another banquet was held; the husband went there alone once more. Inside the room, the wife felt even greater remorse and made this vow:
"The Tathāgata has appeared in the world for the great benefit of many, yet I, being now so sinful, alone do not receive his moistening grace."

The Buddha, moved by the sincerity of her heart, rose up from the earth. As soon as she saw the Buddha’s hair, she felt profound reverence and joy; her own hair immediately transformed into beautiful locks.
Next, he beheld the Buddha’s forehead; gradually, he gazed upon the eyebrows, eyes, ears, nose, body, and mouth. As he observed each part, his joy grew ever deeper.
His body immediately underwent a transformation: all ugliness vanished entirely, and his appearance became identical to that of the devas.
The sons of the elders deliberated in secret, saying:
"The reason the king's daughter has not come to the assembly must be that she is either exceptionally beautiful beyond the ordinary, or perhaps utterly ugly;
for this reason she has not come."
"We should now persuade her husband to drink wine so that he loses consciousness; then we shall take his key, open the door, and go to see her.

They immediately gave him wine until he was intoxicated, took the key, and went together to open the door and look inside. Seeing that this princess was peerlessly beautiful, they closed the door again and returned to their original place.
At that time, her husband had still not awakened; he remained with the key tied around his waist.
When the husband finally woke up, he immediately returned home. Opening the door, he saw that his wife was exceptionally beautiful and extraordinary. Surprised, he asked her:
"What goddess are you, dwelling in my house?"
The wife said, "I am your wife,
Ratī. Her husband was astonished and asked why she had spoken so abruptly.
The wife then replied:

"I had heard that you had sat upon my robe many times and was consequently punished; I felt deep shame and remorse, and with sincere devotion I called upon the Buddha. Immediately, I saw the Tathāgata emerge from the earth. Upon seeing him, I was filled with joy, and my body was transformed for the better."
The impoverished son of the elder was filled with extreme joy; he immediately went in and informed the king:
"The princess's body has naturally transformed for the better; she now requests an audience with the King."
Upon hearing this, the king was filled with joy and immediately summoned him to see him.
Having seen him, he was even more delighted, yet felt a profound sense of wonder and suspicion; he led him to the Buddha’s dwelling and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what reason was this girl born into the inner palace with such an ugly body that people were struck with wonder and alarm upon seeing her?
Furthermore, by what cause has she now suddenly become beautiful?
The Buddha said to the king:

"In the distant past, there was a Pratyekabuddha who went from door to door begging for food daily. Once, he arrived at the gate of a certain elder’s house. At that time, the elder’s daughter took some food and offered it to the Pratyekabuddha; seeing that the Pratyekabuddha’s body was coarse and unrefined, she spoke these words:
'This man is ugly and foul; his form is like fish skin, and his hair is like horse tails.'"
"The daughter of the elder at that time is now this princess.
By the causal condition of giving food, she was born into the inner palace;
yet because she reviled the pratyekabuddha, her body is ugly and deformed."
"Because they have given rise to a heart of shame, remorse, and sincere compassion, they are able to see me;
because of their joyful heart, their bodies have been transformed for the better.
At that time, the assembly, having heard what the Buddha said, paid homage with reverence and joyfully practiced it.

21. The Story of King Prasenajit’s Daughter, Kalyāṇaprabhā (Twenty-one) In the past, King Prasenajit had a daughter named Kalyāṇaprabhā. She was intelligent and beautiful; her parents doted on her, and she was beloved and respected by the entire palace.
The father said to his daughter,
"By my power, you are loved and respected by the entire palace.
The daughter replied to her father:
"I possess the power of my own karma; it is not due to my father, the King.
Thus he asked three times, and his answer remained as before.
The King, then filled with anger and resentment, thought: "Now I shall test whether you possess the power of your own karma or not."
He commanded his attendants, "Seek out within this city the most wretched and impoverished beggar.
Following the king's instructions, they immediately searched and found a man of the lowest station, whom they brought before the king.
The king then entrusted his daughter, Kalyāṇaprabhā, to the poor man.
The king said to the girl:
"If you possess your own karmic power and do not rely on mine, from this day forward, the proof shall be evident."
The woman replied as before,
"I have karmic power.
She then immediately went out together with the poor man, leading him along.
She asked her husband, saying,
"Did you previously have parents?
The poor man replied:
"My father was formerly the foremost elder in the city of Śrāvastī; his parents and household members have all died, leaving me with no one to rely upon, and thus I am destitute."
Sukhāloka asked,
"Do you know where your former residence is?
He replied:
"Know that where the walls and roof of a house have collapsed, there is subsequently an empty space.

Suvarṇaprabhāsa then took his husband and went together to the site of their former dwelling. As they walked about and inspected it, wherever they stepped, the ground sank down of its own accord, and treasures hidden beneath the earth spontaneously emerged. He then used these precious jewels to hire laborers to build a residence. In less than a month, the palace and mansions were all fully completed; palace ladies and female musicians filled them, and the number of slaves and servants was beyond calculation.
The king suddenly remembered:
"How is my daughter, Sunetra, making her living?
Someone answered him:
"The palaces and wealth have not diminished compared to those of the king.
The king said:
"The Buddha’s words are true; one creates good and evil for oneself, and one receives their retribution for oneself."
On that very day, the princess sent her husband to invite the king. The king accepted the invitation;
upon arriving at her residence, he saw that the carpets and rugs were spread out and the house was so magnificently adorned that it surpassed even the royal palace.
When the king saw this, he marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
The woman, knowing that her words were entirely true, spoke thus:
"I myself committed these deeds; I myself must undergo their retribution."
The king went to question the Buddha:
"What meritorious deeds did this girl perform in her previous lives that she was born into a royal family and possesses such bodily radiance?
The Buddha replied to the king:
"Ninety-one kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin.
At that time, there was a king named Bandhumat, who had a chief consort."
After the Buddha Vipaśyin had entered *nirvāṇa*, King Bandhumat erected a stūpa made of the seven precious gems for his relics.

The king’s first consort took the ornaments from her celestial crown and placed them upon the head of the image of Vipaśyin; she then set the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) from within the crown at its forehead. Its radiance illuminated the world, and she made this vow:
"May my future body possess radiance like that of purple-polished gold, may I be honored, majestic, and noble, and may I never fall into the three evil realms or the eight difficult conditions."
“At that time, the king’s first consort was none other than the present-day Śubhavyūha.
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, she again provided various delicacies as offerings to Kāśyapa Tathāgata and his four great śrāvakas.”
The husband tried to stop her, but the wife entreated him, saying, "Do not cut me off;
I have made this request so that she may be fully satisfied.
The husband relented and listened to his wife, and the offering was completed.
The husband at that time is today’s husband;
the wife at that time is today’s wife.
Because the husband obstructed his wife at that time, he was constantly poor; because he later allowed her [to go], it was due to his wife that he attained great wealth and honor.
When he was without his wife, he later returned to poverty and low status.
Good and evil karma pursue one; it never fails or errs.
When the King heard what the Buddha had said, he deeply understood the workings of karma; he did not boast of himself, but gave rise to profound faith and realization, and departed with joy.

22. The Story of the Two Prince Brothers Who Were Exiled from Their Country (22). Once, there were two prince brothers who were driven out of their country. Having reached the middle of a vast wilderness, their provisions were completely exhausted.
The younger brother immediately killed his wife, divided the meat, and gave it to his elder brother and sister-in-law to eat.
Upon receiving this meat, the elder brother hid it away and did not eat it; instead, he cut flesh from his own leg for the husband and wife to eat together.
When the younger brother’s wife ran out of meat, she wished to kill her sister-in-law.
The elder brother said,
“Do not kill her!”
Having hidden the meat beforehand, he gave it to his younger brother to eat.
Once they had passed through the wilderness and reached the abode of a seer, they gathered flowers and fruits to provide for their own sustenance.
Later, the younger brother fell ill and died, leaving the elder brother alone.
At that time, the prince saw a man who had been mutilated and deprived of both hands and feet; moved by compassion, he gathered fruits and sustenance to sustain that maimed man.

The prince was by nature one who had few desires; having gathered flowers and fruit, he departed, leaving his wife behind. She then consorted with a man whose feet were severed; having already formed a secret intimacy, she harbored deep jealousy toward her husband.
During the course of a single day, while gathering flowers, she followed her husband to the riverbank and said to him,
"Pick the flowers and fruits from the tops of the trees.
Her husband replied to his wife:
"Below there is a deep river; you might fall into it.
The woman said, "Tie a rope around your waist; I shall pull on the rope."
As they drew near the bank, the woman pushed her husband, causing him to fall into the river;
yet by the power of his benevolence and compassion, though he drifted away in the water, he did not drown.
Downstream from there, the king of a certain country had passed away. The state astrologers searched throughout the land to discover who was worthy to be king.
From afar, they saw a yellow cloud-canopy upon the water; having performed their divination, the astrologers declared:
"Beneath this yellow cloud-canopy, there must surely be a divine person."
He sent men into the water to go forth and receive him, establishing him as king.
The former wife of the king carried that amputated man, wandering from place to place begging for alms until she reached the kingdom of the prince.

The people of the state all said, "There is a fine woman who carries her husband, though his feet were severed; she serves him with such reverence and filial piety that her virtue has reached the ears of the King.
Upon hearing this, the King immediately dispatched messengers to summon her, and she arrived before the palace hall.
The king asked his wife,
"Is this man with severed feet truly your husband?
She replied:
"It is indeed so.
The king then said to him,
"Do you recognize me?"
He replied, "I do not know.
The king said:
"Do you recognize so-and-so or not?
When he looked toward the king and then felt ashamed,
the king, out of his compassionate heart, sent someone to provide for his livelihood.
The Buddha said:
"The king you wish to know is none other than myself.
The woman at that time was the Brahmin girl Ciñcā, who slandered me by carrying a wooden bowl."
"At that time, the one whose hands and feet were severed was Devadatta. 23.

The Story of the Wife of the Elder Sudatta Receiving a Reward for Making Offerings to the Buddha (23) Long ago, when the Buddha was in the world, the elder Sudatta eventually fell into poverty and suffering until his wealth was completely exhausted. He took up manual labor as a hired servant and obtained three *dō* of rice, which he boiled to prepare food and drink.
When the cooking was finished, it happened that Aniruddha came to beg for alms.
Sudatta’s wife immediately took his bowl, filled it with rice, and gave it to him.
Subsequently, Subhūti, Mahākāśyapa, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, and others came in succession to beg; his wife likewise took each of their bowls, filled them with rice, and offered them as alms.
Finally, when the World-Honored One came in person to beg for alms, he also gave him a full bowl.
Thereupon, as Sudatta was returning from outside, he asked his wife for food. His wife replied to her husband, saying:
"If the Venerable Aniruddha had come, would you have eaten it yourself or given it to the Venerable One?"
He replied, "I would rather not eat myself; I shall give it to the Venerable One.
[The Buddha asked: "If, moreover, Kāśyapa, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Subhūti, Śāriputra, and others—even down to the Buddha himself—were to come, what would you do?"
He replied,
"I would rather not eat myself than give it all away.
His wife said to her husband:
"In the morning, all the holy ones have come to beg for food; all the food we possess has been given away in alms.
Then the husband said to his wife, "Our transgressions are exhausted, and merit should now arise."
Immediately, the storehouses were opened, and grain, silk, and food and drink were found to be completely full; as they were used up, they would be replenished once more. 24.

The Story of the Bhikṣu Sāraṇa Being Afflicted by King Duḥśīla (XXIV) In the past, there was a prince of Ujjayinī named Sāraṇa. His heart delighted in the Buddha-dharma, so he left the household life to study the Path. Practicing the ascetic dhūta-precepts and austerities, he sat in meditation with focused mindfulness beneath trees in the mountain forests.
At that time, King Canda-Pradyota, accompanied by his court ladies, was traveling about for sightseeing when he arrived at this grove; having halted his carriage to rest, he soon fell asleep.

Because the king was asleep, the various court ladies began to play together; beneath a tree, they saw a bhikṣu sitting in meditation, contemplating with focused concentration. They went to where he was, paid their respects, and inquired after his well-being.
At that time, the bhikṣu was preaching the Dharma for her.

Later, the king suddenly became aware of her absence and went searching for his court ladies. From afar, he saw beneath a tree a bhikṣu of upright appearance and youthful beauty, with the court ladies gathered before him listening to the Dharma.
He immediately went up to him and asked, "Have you attained arhatship?"
He replied, “No.
“Can one attain the stage of Anāgāmin?”
He replied, “No.
“Then have you attained the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin?”
He replied, "I have not.
[The Buddha asked:
"Have you attained the stage of Srotāpanna?"
He replied, "I have not.
[The Buddha asked,] "Have you attained the contemplation of impurity?"
He replied, "I did not.
The king then became greatly incensed and spoke these words:
"You have attained nothing at all; how can you, a mere ordinary person caught in birth and death, sit in one place together with these court ladies?
He then seized him and beat him until his entire body was mangled and ruined.
The palace ladies said, “This bhikṣu has committed no transgression.
As they were being beaten, the king’s anger increased even further; seeing them all weeping and distressed, the king’s rage became twice as intense.
At that time, the bhikṣu thought to himself:
"The Buddhas of the past were able to attain the Unsurpassed Way because they were capable of enduring insults;
furthermore, in the past, the Seer Kṣāntivādin was able to endure even when his ears, nose, hands, and feet were severed by another."
"How much less, then, should I—who am today physically whole and sound—fail to endure this?
Thinking thus, he silently endured it.
Once the beating was finished, his entire body was in pain, which grew increasingly severe until he could no longer bear the suffering; he then thought again:

"If I had remained in the secular world, I would have been a prince of this kingdom and would have succeeded to the royal throne; my military forces and power would not have been inferior to those of that king.
Yet today, because I have left the household life and am alone, I have been subjected to such deception and beating."
Deeply distressed, he wished to abandon the path and return home; he went at once to his preceptor Kātyāyana to take leave and return to lay life.
The preceptor replied, "Your body is currently in pain from recent beating; wait until tomorrow, stay here for a while to rest, and only then depart."
Then Sālana, having received these instructions, stayed overnight.

At midnight, the Venerable Kaccāyana appeared to him in a dream, causing Sālana to see himself having left the religious life and returned home; his father king had already passed away, and he had succeeded to the throne, whereupon he assembled the fourfold army and marched against King Canda Pajjota.
Having arrived in that country, they drew up their ranks and fought together, but were defeated by the enemy; their troops were shattered and destroyed, and they themselves were taken prisoner.
When King Canda-pradyota had captured Sāṇa, he sent a man with a sword, intending to execute him.
At that time, Sāraṇa was struck with extreme terror and immediately thought to himself:
"I wish to see my preceptor; even if he were killed by another, I would harbor no resentment."
At that time, the Upādhyāya, knowing his thoughts by means of his supernormal power, took up his staff and bowl and appeared before him as he was about to go out for alms, saying to him:
"My son, I have always taught you the Dharma in various ways; yet striving for victory in dispute can never be achieved.
Since you do not follow my instructions, what else can be known?"
He replied to the Upādhyāya, saying,
"If you would now save the life of this disciple, I shall never dare [to do so] again.
At that time, Kātyāyana spoke to the king's men on behalf of Śarabha, saying:
"Please pause for a moment and listen to my petition to Your Majesty to save his life.
Having spoken these words, he went toward the king's presence.
However, the king's men were unwilling to wait and eventually led him away to be executed.
As he was about to bring the blade down, his heart was seized with terror; he let out a cry and woke up.
Upon waking, he went at once to inform the Upādhyāya of everything he had seen in his dream.
The Upādhyāya replied:
"In the battles of birth and death, there is ultimately no victor. Why is this so?

For the nature of combat is to achieve victory by harming others; through such a path of injury, one may find satisfaction for one's deluded emotions in the present, yet in future lives, one will fall into the three miserable realms and undergo immeasurable suffering."

If one does not act thus and is instead harmed by others, losing one's own life and causing calamity to extend to the masses, increasing their heavy transgressions and causing them to fall into hell; if they further slaughter one another so that enmity never ceases, wandering through the five realms of existence without end—then reflecting upon this repeatedly, what benefit would there be in such bodily wounds and the agony of torture?
If you now wish to leave behind the terrors of birth and death and the pain of being whipped and beaten, you should contemplate your own body in order to cease resentment and slander. Why is this?
This body is the root of manifold sufferings;
it is afflicted by hunger, thirst, cold, and heat, as well as by birth, old age, sickness, and death, and is harmed by mosquitoes, gadflies, venomous insects, and wild beasts.
Such enemies as these are numerous and immeasurable; you cannot repay them all—why do you wish to repay only King Aśoka?
One who wishes to extinguish enemies should extinguish the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The enemy that is affliction harms immeasurable bodies;
though worldly enemies are grave, they harm but a single body.
The enemy that is affliction harms the body of wholesome dharmas.
Although worldly enemies are cruel, they harm only this foul and impure body subject to outflows (*āsrava*).
Viewed from this perspective, the arising of enmity and injury has afflictions (*kleśa*) as its root.
If you do not now strike down the thief of afflictions, how can you hope to strike down King Aśoka?
Thus, he preached the Dharma to him in various ways.
Upon hearing these words, Sāraṇa’s mind was opened and his understanding clarified; he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
Deeply delighting in the Great Dharma, he redoubled his diligence and, before long, through the practice of the Path, attained Arhatship.

The Story of the Eunuch Who Redeemed Castrated Bulls and Regained His Masculinity (XXV) In the past, in the kingdom of Gandhāra, there was a butcher who intended to castrate five hundred young bulls. A eunuch heard of this and went to redeem the animals from him. Having obtained them, he released them all. Through the power of that merit, he subsequently regained his male organ. This is the story of how the eunuch redeemed the castrated bulls and attained masculinity. At that time, there was an inner court official who ransomed the ox with gold coins and released it to roam in a herd; by reason of this causal connection, his male organ was immediately restored upon manifesting in this body.
Returning to the royal palace, he sent someone to announce:
"So-and-so is outside.
The king said:
"This is a member of my household who acts according to his own will without ever having announced his intentions; why is he acting thus now?
The king then immediately summoned him and questioned him as to the reason.
He replied to the king, saying:
"Just now I saw a butcher leading five hundred young calves intending to slaughter them; I immediately ransomed and released them.
Because of this cause and condition, my body has become complete, and for that reason I did not dare enter."
Upon hearing this, the king was both delighted and struck with wonder; his devotion to the Buddha-dharma deepened, and he gave rise to a heart of faith and reverence.
If such is the response evoked by a mere provisional reward (*puṇyavipāka*), how much more so must its ultimate fruition (*phalavipāka*) be beyond measure?

26. The Discourse on the Dispute Between Two Inner Attendants (26). Regarding the dispute between two inner attendants: Formerly, while King Prasenajit was sleeping, he heard two inner attendants disputing over a principle.
One of them said: "I live by depending upon the King."
One man replied, "I have no one to rely upon;
I live by the power of my own karma.
When the king heard this, he felt sympathy for those who lived under his patronage and wished to reward them.
He immediately dispatched an attendant and said to the lady,
"If I send one person now, I shall give him a generous amount of money, clothing, and necklaces. Thereupon,
he sent someone who lived under the king's patronage, giving him the remainder of the wine he had drunk himself to present to the lady.
At that time, as this man was carrying the wine out of the door, blood began to flow from his nose, and he could not proceed further.
By chance, he encountered those who live by their own labor; he immediately hired them to carry the wine and go give it to the lady.
When the lady saw him, she remembered the King’s words and bestowed upon him money, clothing, and necklaces, sending him back before the King.
When the King saw this man, he was deeply struck with wonder and confusion; he immediately summoned those who lived under his patronage and asked them:
"I sent you away; why did you not go?"
He replied, "After I went outside, I suddenly suffered from a nosebleed; being unable to endure it, I immediately requested him to take the king’s leftover wine and give it to the lady."
The king then sighed and said:
"I now know that the Buddha’s words are true: one creates one's own karma and receives its own retribution; it cannot be taken away by another."
Viewed from this perspective, the retribution for good and evil is brought about by one's own karma and conduct; it is not something that can be granted by heaven or by a king.

[27] The Story of Two Brothers Who Both Left Home to Enter the Monastic Life (27) In a past age, there were two brothers whose hearts delighted in the Buddha-dharma; they left home to study the Way.
The elder brother was diligent and assiduous, gathering all manner of wholesome dharmas and practicing the conduct of an araṇya-dweller; before long, he attained the path of arhatship.

The younger brother was intelligent and possessed broad learning, having recited the Tripitaka; later, the state minister invited him to serve as his preceptor, bestowed upon him much wealth, and entrusted him with the construction of monastic quarters, stupas, and temples.

At that time, the Tripitaka Master accepted the offerings and led men across the land to construct a stupa and temple; the foundations and pavilions were majestic and dignified, while the halls and chambers were brilliant and beautiful, the craftsmanship so exquisite as to surpass the skill of any artisan.
Upon seeing this, the Prime Minister’s faith and reverence redoubled; he provided offerings and provisions so that nothing was lacking for any of his needs.
When the Tripiṭaka Bhikṣu observed the minister’s virtuous disposition, he thought to himself:
"Once the temple is completed, it must be entrusted to the Saṃgha. I shall speak with the Prime Minister and have him invite my elder brother."
Having formed this thought, he said to the minister:

"I have an elder brother who is there; having left home to enter the path, he practices with diligent and energetic resolve, cultivating the conduct of an araṇya-dweller. Patron, you should now invite him to reside at the monastery."
The minister replied,
“Regarding the instructions given by my master, I would not dare to disobey even for a mere bhikṣu, let alone for an elder brother who is an āraṇyaka.”
He immediately dispatched messengers to extend a cordial invitation.
Once the monk had arrived, the minister, observing his diligent practice, redoubled his offerings.

Later, the minister gave a fine cotton cloth worth ten million to that aranyaka bhikṣu; however, the aranyaka bhikṣu was unwilling to accept it. Only after the minister insisted and pressed him repeatedly did he finally accept it, and he thought to himself:
"My younger brother manages affairs and requires wealth," [the king] said,
and immediately gave it to him.
Later, the minister took a coarse cotton cloth and gave it to the Tripiṭaka master.
Having received it, Tripitaka felt deep resentment.
On a later day, the minister again gave a single piece of exquisite cotton cloth worth ten million coins to his elder brother, Āranya;
once he had received it, the elder brother in turn gave it to his younger brother.
When his younger brother saw this, his jealousy redoubled. He immediately took the cotton cloth and went to the residence of the minister’s daughter, whom he loved and respected, and said to her:

"Your father, the minister, formerly treated me with great kindness; however, since that bhikṣu arrived and settled here, I do not know by what illusions he has deluded him, for he now treats me with scant regard. Here, I give you this cotton cloth; you may take it before the minister and sew it into a garment."
If someone asks you this, you should answer:
"Take that which my father holds most dear and give it to me.
The minister will certainly become enraged and refuse to speak with you.
The woman said to the Tripiṭaka master:
"My father now holds that bhikṣu in such high esteem as he does his own eyes, and regards him like a bright pearl; how could he suddenly fall into such slander?"
The Tripitaka Master spoke again:
"If you do not do so, I shall sever my ties with you forever.
The woman replied once more:
"Why must you act so precipitously? You should instead consider what is appropriate.
Unable to restrain his feelings, he accepted the cotton cloth and, before his father's eyes, cut it to make a garment.
At that time, the prime minister saw the cotton cloth and immediately recognized it, thinking to himself:
"That bhikṣu is a most wicked man; having obtained my cotton cloth, instead of using it for his own needs, he has used it to deceive and delude children and women."
Thereupon, on a later day, when the āraṇyaka arrived, [the minister] no longer went out to welcome him, and his countenance had changed.
Seeing the minister thus, the bhikṣu thought to himself:
"There must be some strange person who has slandered me, causing him to act in this way."
He immediately ascended into the air and performed the eighteen miraculous transformations.

Upon seeing this, the Prime Minister felt deep reverence and submission; he and his wife prostrated at [the monk's] feet and confessed their transgressions. Their devotion was so intense that it surpassed anything they had felt before. He then immediately expelled the Tripitaka Master and his own daughter, ordering them both to leave the country.
The Buddha said, "At that time, the Tripitaka Master was my own self.
Because I slandered another, I underwent great suffering and affliction for immeasurable kalpas; even until today, I am slandered by Sunakṣatra."
At that time, because this woman had slandered the noble ones, she was immediately expelled and reduced to a state of destitution, surviving by begging.
Therefore, in all matters, people of the world should investigate thoroughly; do not engage in frivolous slander, lest you invite retribution and punishment.

28. The Story of Kokālika’s Slander of Śāriputra and Others (28) In the past, the Venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were traveling through various villages when they arrived at the abode of a potter. Encountering heavy rain, they stayed there for the night.
It so happened that at that time, there was a cowherd girl within the depths of the kiln;
however, because those who hear the voice (śrāvakas) are no different from ordinary people when they have not entered meditative concentration, they did not know or see her.
When that cowherd girl saw that Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were so handsome in appearance, her heart became infatuated with them, and she involuntarily discharged her impurity.
The Venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana then emerged from the tile kiln.

Kokālika was skilled in physiognomy and could discern people’s facial expressions; he knew when someone was manifesting signs of desire and when they were not. Seeing a cowherd girl pass behind him, he observed that her facial expression bore the marks of lust. Not knowing that she had spontaneously become infatuated and emitted impurity, he immediately slandered them, saying:
"The Venerable Sāriputta and Moggallāna have committed adultery with a cowherd girl."
He related this matter in detail to the bhikṣus.
Then the bhikṣus immediately admonished him three times:
"Do not slander the Venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana."
At that time, Kokālika’s mind gave rise to anger and envy, and his resentment became even more intense.

There was an elder named Bhaga; when the Venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana taught him the essentials of the Dharma, he attained the stage of Anāgāmin. Upon the end of his life, he was reborn in the Brahma Heaven, where he was immediately given the name Bhagavān.
At that time, the Blessed One, perceiving from afar in the heavens that Kokālika was slandering the Venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, immediately descended and arrived at Kokālika’s dwelling.
Kokālika asked, "Who are you? He replied:
"I am Bhagavān. "For what purpose have you come?
Brahmā said:
"I have heard with my divine ear that you slandered the Venerable Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana; do not say that these Venerables are capable of such things.
Thus he admonished him three times.
When his admonitions were not heeded, he instead spoke these words: "O Bhagavan!
You say you have attained the state of an Anāgāmin; one who is an Anāgāmin is called 'one who does not return. Why, then, have you come to my side?"
"If that were so, the Buddha's words would also be false.
The Brahmā said:
"One who does not return means one who does not return to take birth in the desire realm."
At that time, a malignant eruption broke out on Kauṇḍinya’s body, from head to foot, with spots as large as beans.
He went to where the Buddha was and said to him:
"How is it that Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana committed sexual misconduct with the cowherd girl?"
The Buddha admonished him again, saying:
"Do not speak such words regarding Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana.
Upon hearing these words of the Buddha, his anger redoubled; at that moment, his malignant boils grew even larger, as big as *nāḍa* fruits.
A second time, he reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha again admonished him, saying:
"Do not speak of this matter.
The pustule grew even larger, as big as a fist.

If they do not cease at the third stage, their blisters grow as large as gourds and their bodies become intensely feverish; they enter a pool of cold water, which causes that icy pool to boil and seethe violently, until all the blisters burst open and they immediately die, falling into the Mahāraurava Hell.
At that time, a bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions?"
"Venerable Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the others— have they been falsely slandered by others?
The Buddha said, "In a past kalpa, Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the others were once ordinary worldlings."
He saw a Pratyekabuddha emerging from a potter’s kiln, followed by a cowherd girl who came out after him;
he immediately slandered them, saying, "That bhikṣu must have been having illicit relations with this woman."
"Due to these karmic conditions, he fell into the three evil realms and underwent immeasurable suffering;
although he has now attained sainthood, the prior conditions are not yet exhausted, and he is still subjected to slander."
You should know that śrāvakas cannot act as great spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) for sentient beings. Why is this?
If Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana had manifested even a small degree of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) for Kokālika, Kokālika would certainly have been spared from hell.
"It was not for the sake of the present that I caused Kokālika to fall into hell; such was the matter.
The Buddha spoke thus:
"Regarding this bodhisattva person: in the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a seer named Dīpaṃkara who lived with five hundred seers in a grass hut within a mountain forest."

At that time, there was a woman who happened to be passing by when she encountered a rainstorm; as the wind and cold were most intense and she had no place to take shelter from the rain, she went to the hermit Dingguang to stay for one night.
The next day, when he went out, the various seers saw him and immediately slandered him, saying:
"This Seer Dīpaṃkara must have engaged in impure conduct with that woman."

At that time, Dīpaṃkara, knowing his thoughts and fearing that he might fall into hell due to slander, immediately ascended into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees and performed the eighteen miraculous transformations.
When the various seers saw this, they said:
"If one can rise four finger-widths above the ground and be free from lustful desire,
how much more so for Dīpaṃkara, who ascends into the midst of the sky and possesses such great supernormal transformations— how could he have any sexual desire?"
"How could we have slandered such a pure person?
At that time, the five hundred rishis prostrated themselves, touching their five limbs to the ground, and bowed deeply in repentance.
"For this reason, you have been spared from grave offenses.
You should know that the Bodhisattva possesses great skillful means and is truly a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) to sentient beings.
The Buddha said:
“The seer Dīpaṃkara at that time was none other than Maitreya now.
The five hundred seers at that time were these five hundred bhikṣus, the elders, now.”
29. The Story of the Dragon King’s Verses (29). While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, Devadatta went to where the Buddha was and reviled him with harsh words.
Having heard this, Ānanda became extremely incensed; he drove Devadatta out and said to him:
"If you come here again, I shall cause you to suffer great torment."
When the bhikṣus saw this, they said to the Buddha:
"It is rare, World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata constantly gives rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion toward Devadatta, yet Devadatta always harbors an evil mind toward the Tathāgata."
Ānanda became angry and immediately drove him away.
