The Buddha said, "Not only today; in a past life as well, it was just like this."

Long ago, in the kingdom of Kāśī, there were two dragon kings who were brothers: the first was named Mahāda and the second was named Upamada. They constantly sent down sweet rain, causing the grasses and trees within their realm to flourish and the five grains to ripen. The livestock that drank this water all became fat and strong, and the cattle and sheep multiplied in great numbers.
At that time, the king of that country slaughtered many oxen and sheep and went to the dragon's abode to offer them as a sacrifice.
The dragon immediately manifested its form and said to the king:
"Since I do not eat these, why do you kill living beings to sacrifice to me?"

Even after these repeated words, he did not change his mind. The brothers took one another by the hand and eventually sought refuge elsewhere, arriving at the dwelling of another minor dragon named Tundubhi.
This dragon, Tundubhi, was filled with rage day and night, reviling them with foul language and insults.
Dadara said: "Do not be angry!
Return to your place."
Upadada became extremely enraged and said to him:
"You are but a minor dragon who constantly eats frogs;
if I were to exhale my breath and blow upon your kin, I would cause them all to be utterly destroyed."
The Great Attainer said to his younger brother, "Do not give way to anger!
We should now return to our original place; the King of Kāśi yearns for us."
The King of Kāśī spoke these words:
"If the two nāgas come, I shall provide them with whatever they require for their ritual offerings—milk and curd—and shall no longer kill living beings."
Upon hearing this, the Dragon King immediately returned to his original abode.
Then, the Great Sage spoke these verses:
“Listen all together with a harmonious and sincere mind To the most excellent and pure mental factors.”
The events recounted in the *Bodhisattvapūrvapraṇidhāna* were manifested by the Buddha today through these ancient verses.
When the Tathāgata was in the world, the bhikṣus among the devas of gods—the Sambuddhas—uttered further evil words to revile and disparage one another;
the Great Compassionate One saw and heard such speech as this.
He assembled the community of bhikṣus and spoke thus:
"Unlawful matters should not be performed; you each have uttered coarse words, mutually slandering one another and bringing harm upon yourselves."
You have cultivated and accumulated the difficult practices of loving-kindness and patience; if you wish to rely upon the Buddha-dharma, you should practice the six points of harmonious respect.
Desiring to benefit and bring peace to all sentient beings, do not cause harm to anyone at all.
If one practices the path and hears [this teaching], one should distance oneself from evil,
just as ice and water emerge from fire. If one wishes to accord with the Dharma of renunciation,
one should sever anger and strife and practice in accordance with the Way.
There were two brothers living together; the elder brother was named Mahāda and the second was named Upada.
Both abstained from taking life and maintained the pure precepts;
possessing great majesty and virtue, they grew weary of their naga forms and constantly sought rebirth as humans in the auspicious realms.
If one sees śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who maintain pure precepts and possess great learning,
one should transform oneself to make offerings and constantly attend upon them. On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the month,
one should observe the eightfold precepts and restrain the mind, leaving one’s own dwelling to travel to other regions.

There was a nāga named Tuṇḍila; seeing that we two nāgas possessed such great majesty and virtue, he realized he was not our equal and gave rise to jealousy and malice, constantly reviling us with harsh speech.
The cheeks swell and the mouth emits coarse breath; with a mind full of rage, the body becomes bloated and large.
Uttering such evil sounds, they slander others; deluded by illusion and deceitful falsehood, they are subjected to invasion and oppression.
Hearing these insults from the lowly and wicked dragon, Upada became exceedingly enraged and addressed his elder brother, Mahāda, saying:
"Having been reviled with such evil words, you who constantly eat frogs and dwell by the water's edge— how dare such a base creature insult me?"
Whether in the water, you disturb the nature of the waters; Or on dry land, you harass and harm human beings.
Hearing such evil, one’s desire for patience becomes difficult to sustain; Now we shall eliminate you and your retinue, Destroying you all so that you return to your original place.
Upon hearing his brother’s words, the Great Power Dragon King spoke these sublime verses praised by the wise:
"Having received but little support, one sleeps in peace; one should not harbor evil thoughts toward such a person.
To know gratitude and repay kindness is praised by the Sages."
One who does not destroy the branches, leaves, flowers, or fruits, yet commits even slight evils against those who are kind and close—
such a person shall never find happiness from beginning to end.
This person, ignorant of gratitude and practicing evil, will see no good fruit arise and shall instead meet with destruction.
Just as a forest, though scorched and withered by fire, Grows back again to its former state;

So it is for one who betrays kindness—no goodness arises in them. Even if one nurtures such an evil person with a hundred kinds of offerings, They will never remember the kindness and will surely repay it with enmity.
The child was born dead, yet the immortal nurtured him to life; once grown, he became wild and reckless and killed the immortal.
He trampled the trees, the wooden house, and the dwellings to ruin; such is the ingratitude of an evil person.
The mind is flighty and restless, never pausing for a moment; it is like a tree in a swirling eddy.
Failing to cultivate friendship, there is no returning to it, just as white cotton cloth is dyed by the *jintu* plant.
If you wish to repay an enmity, you should respond with goodness; you should not destroy or harm with evil.
The wise repay enmity entirely through compassion. To carry the heavens and earth, as well as the mountains and seas, is a burden lighter than that of betraying one's kindness.
This is the foremost and most supreme happiness—like crossing a river at a ford and passing safely to the other side;
the two kinds of happiness, such as loving-kindness, are likewise so.
To not harm friends and kin is happiness, and to eliminate arrogance is also happiness.
Lacking virtue within while being arrogant and dissipated without,
truly ignorant yet giving rise to pride, delighting in contentiousness and associating with evil friends,
their reputation diminishes and they incur an ill repute.
Those who have newly lost their wealth and status, the weak and inferior, the destitute and penniless who have lost their sovereign,
the solitary ones suffering in distress with no one to rely upon— toward those variously afflicted as described above,
he who does not give rise to compassion cannot be called benevolent.
If one travels to another land without kinsmen, it is a joy to endure the many insults of others; for this can restrain all evils and cause strife to cease.
It is better to be in a foreign land where people do not know you than to be in one's own country where one is held in contempt.
If one receives honor in a foreign land, all will come to associate with one affectionately, free from anger and contention.
These are one's own kinsmen and relatives;

their decline and extinction bring forth manifold suffering and distress. If one sees that sentient beings are all falling away and losing [their status], being constrained by forces beyond their own control, one remains silent and at ease.
When the enemy’s power prevails and one is weak oneself, when one has few kinsmen and no one to rely upon— observing things thus, one finds joy in silence.
Toward those who delight in unrighteousness, who are greedy and stingy, who lack faith, are shameless,
and do not accept counsel— one finds joy in silence toward such evil ones.
One should find joy in remaining silent toward those who are full of anger, who commit great harm and evil, and who delight in inflicting bitter suffering upon sentient beings;
one should find joy in remaining silent toward those who are faithless, arrogant, and fond of self-exaltation, and toward those who are perverse,
sycophantic, deceitful, fraudulent, and delusive.
Those who break the precepts, being fierce, cruel, and lacking forbearance; who constantly act contrary to the Dharma and behave without faith—it is a joy to remain silent toward such people.
Those who speak falsely without shame, who delight in double-tongued speech, hold wrong views, use harsh words, or engage in frivolous chatter;
those who are arrogant, self-exalting, and deeply attached to the notion of "I"; and those who are exceedingly stingy, greedy, and full of envy—[it is a joy to remain silent toward them].
One should delight in remaining silent in the presence of such a person;
if one does not know oneself in another place, nor possesses the discernment of lineage or conduct, one should not exalt oneself or give rise to arrogance.
When one arrives and stays in another country, relying on others for food and clothing and lacking independence,
one should endure all insults and abuse.
When dwelling as a guest in another realm and depending on others for sustenance, if one desires to establish a foundation for happiness, one should likewise cultivate patience as described above.
If one dwells in another realm dependent on food and clothing, or even if those who are lowly and base come to treat oneself with contempt,
all such things the wise should endure.
When dwelling in another realm among evil companions, or living together with the foolish and the lowly, the wise person conceals themselves like a fire covered by ashes.
Just as a blazing fire fanned by a fierce wind burns up forests and wilds, so does anger burn oneself and others like fire; this is called the most evil form of harm.
Those who possess wisdom should eliminate anger and desire; if one cultivates loving-kindness and the like, anger will gradually be extinguished.
To become intimate with someone immediately upon meeting, while constantly associating with the wicked—such a person is a fool.
To fail to examine their faults and then suddenly abandon them—one who acts in such ways is not a wise person.
If there were no fools, the wisdom of the small-minded would not be manifest; just as a bird with broken wings cannot fly, so it is for the wise without fools.
Because there are many fools and the small-minded, and because they lack wisdom, the power of the wise is able to bring about awakening.

The one of vast knowledge and great learning attains a joyful dwelling; the wise person, upon gaining profit, does not become elated, nor do they become dejected when losing it, for they are free from delusion.
Whatever they say is intended to ward off evil; they speak with eloquence only for the sake of peace, happiness, and benefit.
To ensure that others certainly understand these words,
one contemplates and deliberates upon their true meaning; having clearly realized their principle before acting,
this is called benefiting oneself as well as others.
Committing evil deeds and irrational acts, they do not violate the True Dharma for the sake of pleasure or pain;
they never abandon right practice for their own sake.
They do not harbor malice or succumb to folly; even when danger is imminent, they feel no terror.
One never slanders or instigates others for the sake of profit;
one is neither fierce nor timid,
nor is one base, but dwells in the middle way— such are the characteristics of the wise.
The majestic and fierce provoke resentment, while the weak and timid are held in contempt; therefore, one should avoid these two extremes and dwell in the Middle Way.
At times, one remains silent like a mute; at times, one teaches with words like a sovereign.
At times, one acts with coldness like falling snow; at times, one manifests heat like a blazing fire.
Sometimes appearing as lofty as Mount Sumeru, sometimes appearing as lowly as prostrate grass;
sometimes manifesting with the ferocity of a king, sometimes appearing in the tranquility of liberation.
At times they are able to endure the suffering of hunger and thirst; at times they can withstand both painful and pleasant circumstances.
Regarding all wealth and treasures as mere excrement and filth, they possess the mastery to subdue all forms of anger.
At times he is at ease, indulging in music and song; at times he is terrified like a deer;
at times he is as fierce as a tiger or a wolf; observing the proper and improper times, as well as strength and weakness.
One who can contemplate both prosperity and its decline, Who endures what is unbearable—this is true endurance;
The one who practices what should be endured possesses constant endurance, And should likewise practice endurance toward those who are weak.
When wealthy, noble, and powerful, one should always be humble and patient; to endure what is unbearable is called patience.
One does not harbor resentment toward those who resent; amidst those who are angry, one’s mind remains ever pure.
Seeing others do evil but not doing it oneself is called "fearful patience" (bhayakṣānti), when one endures those superior to oneself;
enduring those equal to oneself is out of fear of conflict; enduring those inferior to oneself is called "excellent patience" (uttamakṣānti).
The foolish cannot endure harsh abuse and slander; it is as if two stones were pressed into their eyes.
The wise, however, can endure severe abuse and heavy slander, remaining as patient as an elephant under a rain of flowers.
If one encounters harsh abuse or severe slander, the wise who possess the eye of insight can endure it;
just as when rain falls upon a great rock, the rock is neither damaged nor destroyed,
so too the wise can endure evil words, kind speech, suffering, and pleasure, remaining steadfast like a stone.
If one is reviled with words that correspond to reality, there is no reason for anger toward such truthful speech;
if one is reviled with words that are false, they are merely self-deception like the ravings of a madman—
the wise understand both cases and remain free from anger.
If one endures suffering, pleasure, abuse, and slander for the sake of wealth, treasures, or various benefits, yet remains unable to do so when it is not for the sake of wealth or profit—
even if one were to obtain hundreds of thousands of precious jewels— one should nevertheless swiftly distance oneself from such evil persons.
When a tree branch has been cut, it should not be pulled out; when a person’s heart has turned away, they should not be befriended.
One should depart by a different path and avoid them from afar; those who are worthy of friendship fill the world.
Having first shown respect and later becoming arrogant and contemptuous, or likewise lacking reverence and failing to offer praise—
like a white crane that lightly flies away, the wise should swiftly distance themselves from the foolish.
Delighting in strife and harboring deceit, they take pleasure in seeing the faults of others and engage in divisive speech;

they utter falsehoods, harsh words, and frivolous chatter. They treat all sentient beings with contempt and humiliation, further uttering agonizing words that pierce to the very marrow of their bones;
they fail to guard their physical actions, nor their speech or mind.
The wise person distances themselves and goes to another land.
Seeing the profit, happiness, and fame of others, their heart gives rise to burning affliction and great poisonous suffering;
though their speech is gentle, their mind is extremely evil. Only through wisdom can one distance oneself and go to another land.
People delight in evil desires and greed for gain; they are sycophantic and crooked, seeking only to take while lacking shame or remorse.
Being impure within, they are likewise so without; the wise quickly distance themselves and depart for other lands.
If a person lacks a heart of reverence and is possessed by arrogance, devoid of the teachings of the Dharma, they consider themselves wise though they are truly foolish;
the wise will distance themselves from them and go to other lands.
Having obtained food, drink, bedding, and seats, as well as various garments and coverlets, which serve as one's livelihood,
one should protect them and mind their kindness, just as a compassionate mother protects her only child.
Craving can give rise to and grow all suffering; one should first sever craving and abandon hatred, for both can lead people to the evil realms.
One should likewise relinquish self-exaltation and arrogance.
When wealth and status depart, friends and kin leave one behind; such friends should be swiftly distanced.

If for the sake of a family one must abandon an individual, if for the sake of a village one must abandon a family, if for the sake of a nation one must abandon a village, and if for the sake of one’s own person one must abandon the whole world.
If for the sake of the True Dharma one sacrifices one’s own body;
if for the sake of a single finger one sacrifices present wealth; if for the sake of life and limb one sacrifices the four limbs; then for the sake of the True Dharma one should sacrifice everything.
The True Dharma is like a parasol that can shield one from the rain; those who practice the Dharma are protected by the Dharma.
By the power of practicing the Dharma, one cuts off the evil realms, just as one finds cool shade when the spring heat is intense.

The practitioner of the Dharma is likewise so: Accompanying the wise and virtuous on their path, He does not rejoice when gaining great wealth and profit, Nor does he grieve when losing precious treasures;
Without constantly toiling in the pursuit of begging, Such a person is called a steadfast and true Great Man.
Giving wealth and treasures to others with great joy, swiftly abandoning the evils of the world,
and establishing oneself as deep as the ocean— such a person is called a heroic and superior man.
"If one understands the principles of meaning and is skillful in all matters,
being gentle toward others and finding joy in shared practice, people will praise him as a virtuous man. Thus spoke Upatissa.
"I now have redoubled my faith and reverence for you, my brother; even if I should encounter suffering or extreme distress, I shall never again commit any evil deeds.
Whether I live or die, whether I gain wealth or lose it, I shall not create evil."
Brother, you should now know that I serve [the Dharma]; I wish to meet death through the observance of precepts, rather than meeting life through the violation of them.
For what reason should one, for the sake of a single lifetime, be heedless and commit evil deeds?

Do not be heedless amidst birth and death; I have committed unwholesome deeds within birth and death, encountering evil friends and performing what is contrary to the Dharma, but having met with virtuous friends, I shall sever these [tendencies].
The Buddha, having entered into the knowledge of past lives and understood them, spoke these original verses to the bhikṣus:
"At that time, Mahāda was my own body; Upada was Ānanda.
You should know that at that time, Tuṇḍila was none other than the body of Devadatta."
"Monks, you should know that you must train yourselves thus; this is called the summary teaching on the collection of the Dharma.
You should practice it extensively and with care, and act with reverence; let the community of monks cultivate this Dharma."
30. The Circumstances of Devadatta’s Attempt to Harm the Buddha (30) The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha and said to Devadatta:
"Do not harbor thoughts of malice toward the Tathāgata; do not bring about your own ruin, encounter misfortune, or suffer for yourself."
The bhikṣus said:
"How extraordinary it is, World-Honored One!
Devadatta constantly harbors evil intentions toward the Tathāgata."
"For a long night, the World-Honored One has spoken with a compassionate heart, with pity and kindness, and with gentle words.
The Buddha said:

"Not only today, but in the distant past, in the kingdom of Kāśī, at the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a great Nāga King named Campaka. He constantly sent down seasonal rains to bring the crops to maturity; on the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the month, he would transform into human form, observe the five precepts, practice giving, and listen to the Dharma."
At that time, a master of incantations came from the kingdom of South India; he erected arrows and performed a spell to capture the Dragon King Campaka.
Then a celestial deity said to the King of Kāśī:
"A master of incantations is taking the Dragon King Campaka away to the kingdom of Kāśī."
The king immediately dispatched his army to pursue him; however, that brahmin then cast a spell, rendering the king’s entire host unable to move at all.
The king spent a great amount of wealth to ransom the dragon king.

Then the brahmin came for a second time to summon the dragon king with incantations; the dragon’s retinue raised clouds and sent down rain, with thunder and lightning crashing, intending to kill the brahmin.
The Dragon King spoke with a compassionate heart to the assembly of dragons:
"Do not harm his life; comfort him well and let him depart.
When he came for a third time, the dragons were about to kill him.
The Dragon King shielded him and would not permit his killing, immediately releasing him to depart.
The Dragon King of that time was none other than my current self.
The mantra-practitioner of that time was Devadatta.
"When I was a dragon, I was still able to act with a compassionate heart and rescue others repeatedly; how much more so today, that I should not be compassionate?
31. The Story of the Jīvamjīvaka Bird (31). While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, the bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!"
“Devadatta was the younger brother of the Tathāgata; why does he always seek to harm the Buddha?
The Buddha said, “Not only today;
long ago, in the Snowy Mountains, there was a bird called Saṃjīva, which had one body and two heads.”
One head constantly ate fine fruits, desiring for its own body to attain peace and security; the other head then gave rise to a mind of jealousy and spoke these words:
"How is it that he always eats such excellent, delicious fruits, while I have never obtained any?"
He immediately took the poisonous fruit and ate it, causing both heads to die.
If you wish to know who was the one eating the sweet fruit at that time, it was my own self.
The one who ate the poisonous fruit at that time was Devadatta.
"In the past, when we shared one body, he still conceived evil thoughts toward me; now that he is my younger brother, it is exactly the same.

32. The Story of the White Goose King (32). The Story of the White Goose King. While the Buddha was in Rājagṛha, Devadatta pushed down a mountain to crush the Buddha, released the elephant Dhanapāla intending to trample him, and his evil reputation spread abroad.
Devadatta, in the presence of the multitude, prostrated himself before the Buddha and repented at the Tathāgata’s feet;
yet when no one was present, he reviled the Buddha with foul language among the bhikṣus.
Everyone said:
"Devadatta has repented before the Buddha, and his mind is now perfectly disciplined and compliant; it is without cause that this evil reputation has spread."
The bhikṣus said, "It is rare, World-Honored One!
Devadatta is exceedingly crafty and hypocritical; before the multitude, he behaves with such humility toward the Buddha."
"In a secluded place, he reviled the Buddha with an evil mind.
The Buddha said, "Not only today;
in the distant past, there was a lotus pond where many water birds lived."
At that time, there was a crane in the pond; as it walked slowly with measured steps, all the other birds said, "This bird is well-behaved;
its deportment is dignified and orderly, and it does not disturb the aquatic creatures."
At that time, there was a white goose who spoke in verse:
"Stalking with slow steps, With a voice exceedingly soft,
Deceiving the world— Who does not know this craftiness?"
The stork replied, "Why do you speak such words?
Come, let us be friends."
The white goose replied, "I know your deceit and guile; I shall never be intimate with you.
You wish to know who the king of geese was at that time—it was none other than myself.
"At that time, the crane was Devadatta. 33.

The Story of the Great Tortoise (33) The Great Tortoise Story: When the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, Devadatta, whose mind was constantly harboring evil, desired to harm the World-Honored One. He therefore hired five hundred Brahmins skilled in archery, commanding them to take up bows and arrows and go to where the World-Honored One was, drawing their bows to shoot at the Buddha.
The arrows he had shot transformed into *kubjaka* flowers, *puṇḍarīka* flowers, *padma* flowers, and *utpala* flowers.

When the five hundred brahmins witnessed this miraculous manifestation, they were all struck with great terror; they immediately cast away their bows and arrows, prostrated before the Buddha to repent, and sat down to one side.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they all attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
They then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We pray that you will grant us permission to leave the household life and study the Way."
The Buddha said, “Welcome, Bhikṣu!
His beard and hair fell off naturally, and the dharma robes clung to his body. The Buddha preached the Dharma to him again, and he attained the path of Arhatship.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The supernatural power of the World-Honored One is truly rare!
Although Devadatta constantly sought to harm the Buddha, the Buddha always gave rise to great compassion toward him."
The Buddha said, "Not only today;
in the past, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a merchant leader named Ajñātakarman who, together with five hundred traders, entered the sea to gather treasures."
Having obtained the treasures, they returned and reached the place of the Revolving Abyss, where they encountered a water-rākṣasa who seized their ship, preventing them from moving forward.
The merchants were struck with extreme terror and all cried out together:
"O gods of heaven and earth, O deities of the sun and moon! Who can show us compassion and deliver us from this calamity?"
There was a great tortoise, its shell one *li* in breadth; moved by compassion, it came toward the ship and carried all the people upon its back, whereby they were immediately able to cross the sea.
At that time, while the tortoise was taking a short nap, the one who did not recognize his kindness intended to kill it by striking its head with a large rock.
The merchants said, "We have been saved from calamity and our lives preserved thanks to this tortoise; to kill it would be inauspicious and a failure to acknowledge its kindness."
Not recognizing the kindness, he said, "I am suffering from urgent hunger; who asks about your kindness?
He then immediately killed the tortoise and ate its flesh.
That very night, a great herd of elephants trampled and killed many people.
At that time, the large tortoise was my own self.
Those who did not recognize his kindness were Devadatta.
The five hundred merchants were none other than these five hundred brahmins who left the household life, studied, and attained the Way.
In the past, I rescued them from their perils; now, I have again delivered them from the affliction of birth and death.

34. The Story of the Two Ministers’ Deceitful Conspiracy (34). While the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, Devadatta employed various means and causes in an attempt to kill the Buddha, yet he was unable to do so.
At that time, a brahmin from the kingdom of South India arrived; he was skilled in incantations and the compounding of poisonous drugs.
Devadatta, at the brahmin's place, immediately compounded a poison and scattered it over the Buddha.
The wind blew this medicine back onto his own head, whereupon he immediately fell into a stupor and collapsed to the ground as if dead; the physician was unable to treat him.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One!”
Devadatta has been poisoned and is on the verge of death.
Out of compassion, the Buddha spoke these truthful words for him:

"Since I attained Buddhahood from my time as a Bodhisattva, I have always maintained loving-kindness and compassion toward Devadatta and harbored no ill will; therefore, Devadatta, the poison shall naturally be extinguished."
After these words were spoken, the poison was immediately extinguished.
The bhikṣus said,
“It is marvelous, World-Honored One!”
“Devadatta constantly gives rise to evil thoughts toward the Tathāgata; why does the Tathāgata still allow him to live?
The Buddha said, “Not only today has he harbored evil thoughts toward me; it was likewise so in the past.”
At that time, he asked the Buddha,
"What constitutes having an evil mind toward the Buddha?
The Buddha said:
“In a past age, in the kingdom of Kāśī, there was the city of Vārāṇasī.
There were two chief ministers: one named Sena and the other named Duṣṭamati.”
Sena always followed the practice of the Dharma, whereas Evil Mind constantly committed evil deeds and delighted in sowing discord;
he then said to the king, "Sena intends to commit an act of rebellion."
The king immediately had him arrested and imprisoned.
Thereupon, various devas and benevolent deities, from within the void, raised their voices and said:
"This worthy man is truly without fault or transgression; why is he being detained?"
At that time, the nāgas spoke these words, and the ministers and the people also spoke these words; the king then released him.
His second evil intention was to plunder the royal treasury and deposit it in the house of Sna.
The king also did not believe him, and said to him:
"Out of hatred and envy for him, you have committed this act unjustly.
Thus spoke the king.
"Seize this evil-minded one and hand him over to Senaka; I entrust you with the task of executing him.
Senaka then instructed the evil-minded man to confess his transgressions to the king.

Realizing he was guilty, the evil-minded man fled to the King of Videha. He fashioned a precious casket, placed two venomous snakes within it that were fully endowed with poison, and sent a messenger to deliver it to the king of that country as well as to Senaka.
"Let us both look together; do not show it to anyone else.
When the king saw the precious casket, which was most exquisitely adorned, his heart was filled with great joy, and he immediately summoned Senaka, wishing to open and examine it together.
Sena replied:
"One must not look at things brought from afar; one must not eat fruits and food brought from afar immediately. Why is this?"
"There may be wicked people there who might come to see me and cause me harm.
The King said,
"I must certainly go to see it."
After he had earnestly admonished him three times, the king would not heed his words.
He spoke to the king again, saying:
"If you will not follow the words of your minister, let Your Majesty examine it yourself; I am unable to do so."
The king immediately opened them to look, but his two eyes were blind and dark, unable to see any object.

Sona was filled with grief and suffering; so distressed and withered that he was on the verge of death, he sent men out in all directions to travel through various kingdoms and seek a potent medicine from afar.
Having obtained the excellent medicine, he treated the king’s eyes, and they were restored to their former state.
The king at that time was Śāriputra; Sna at that time was my own self.
"At that time, the one with evil intent was Devadatta.

35. The Story of the King of the Mountain Pheasants (35): The Story of the King of the Mountain Pheasants. The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha. Devadatta went to where the Buddha was and spoke these words:
"The Tathāgata should now dwell in quiet seclusion; please entrust this great assembly to me."
The Buddha said, "You foolish man who eats spittle!
I would not even entrust the great assembly to Śāriputra or Maudgalyāyana; how then could I ever entrust it to you?"
Devadatta departed, reviling them in anger.
The bhikṣus said,
“World-Honored One!”
Devadatta desired to inflict various sufferings upon the Buddha and repeatedly employed skillful means to deceive the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said:
"Not only today; in a past life, by the side of the Snowy Mountains, there was a king of mountain fowl who led a great multitude of fowl as his followers."
The cock’s comb was extremely red and its body was very white; it spoke to the other chickens, saying:
"All of you, stay far away from cities and villages so that you will not be eaten by people. We have many enemies and those who envy us; be careful to protect yourselves."
At that time, there was a kitten in the village who, hearing that there was a rooster there, went toward it.
Standing beneath a tree, walking slowly and looking down, she spoke to the rooster, saying:

"I shall be your wife and you shall be my husband. Your form is upright and lovely; with a red crest upon your head and a body entirely white, I shall serve you, and we shall dwell in peace and happiness."
The hen spoke in verse:
"A yellow-eyed cat, a foolish and insignificant creature, Harbors malice toward all things and desires to devour them.
I have never seen a woman such as this one Who can enjoy long life and peace."
"At that time, the cock was my own self;
at that time, the cat was Devadatta.
In the past, he sought to seduce and deceive me, and today he again seeks to seduce and deceive me."
36. The Story of the Śikhaṇḍin Bird (36). The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, Devadatta thought to himself:

"The Buddha has five hundred blue-clad yakṣas who constantly attend and protect him; he possesses the ten powers and a hundred thousand Nārāyaṇa-strengths which none can equal. I shall not be able to harm him now."
“I shall return to serve him, observe his vital channels, and strike him there; only then can he be killed.
He then confessed before the great assembly of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, addressing the Buddha with these thoughts:
“If you accept my confession, I may employ this expedient; if you do not accept my confession, it will suffice to cause the Tathāgata’s ill repute to spread abroad.”
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Accept my repentance; I wish to cultivate my resolve in a secluded and quiet place.”
The Buddha said:
"In the Dharma there is no flattery or deception; as for those who practice flattery and deception, they possess no Dharma.
The six heterodox teachers all said:
“Devadatta wishes to confess his transgressions before the Buddha, but the Buddha does not accept his confession.
The bhikṣus said,
“Devadatta approaches the Buddha with deceit and crookedness.”
The Buddha said:
"Not only today; in the distant past, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta who established a decree prohibiting killing."
At that time, there was a hunter who wore the robes of a seer; he killed various deer and birds, yet no one recognized him for what he was.
A bird named Kṣemaka spoke to the people, saying:
"This great evildoer, though wearing the robes of a seer, is in fact a hunter who constantly commits acts of killing, yet people do not know it."
"The multitude all believed the auspicious bird, for it was indeed as he had said.
At that time, the auspicious bird was none other than myself.
At that time, the hunter was Devadatta."
"The king at that time was Śāriputra. 37.
The Story of the Old Seer (37). The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru daily sent five hundred pots of rice for Devadatta, and he received great offerings and support.
All the bhikṣus said to the World-Honored One:
"King Ajātaśatru daily sends five hundred pots of rice for Devadatta."
The Buddha said,
“Monk! Do not envy Devadatta for his acquisition of gain and offerings.”
He then spoke in verse:
“The plantain tree withers when it bears fruit; so too it is with the reed, the bamboo, and the bulrush.
The mule dies when it conceives; the hinny and the kyang do likewise.”
"The fool, greedy for gain and honor, brings harm upon himself and is ridiculed by the wise.
Having spoken this verse, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Devadatta was not only harmed by gain and honor and slandered me today; it was also thus in the past."
The bhikṣu asked the Buddha,
"What is the meaning of past events?
The Buddha said:
"In the past, in the land of Vārāṇasī, amidst the Mountains of the Sages, there were two rishis:
one was old and had attained the five supernormal powers;
the other was young and had attained nothing at all."
At that time, the aged seer, by means of his supernormal powers, went to Uttarakuru and took back ripe non-glutinous rice, which they ate together;
he then went to the Jambu tree and took back jambu fruits, which they also ate together;
finally, he went to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and took back the divine *sudhā* nectar, which they ate together.
Having seen this, the young seer felt a sense of longing and respect in his heart, and said to the old man:
"I pray that you will instruct me in the cultivation of the five supernormal powers.
The old seer replied:
"If one possesses a virtuous mind, one will attain the five supernatural powers and surely derive benefit;
if one lacks a virtuous mind, it will conversely lead to evil harm.
Thus he earnestly entreated him:
"Please teach me," he requested.
Thereupon, the aged seer taught him the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), which he attained immediately.

Having acquired the five supernormal powers, he manifested various miraculous feats before the multitude; thereafter, he gained great renown and offerings. Consequently, he conceived a heart of envy toward his elder and began slandering him everywhere, whereupon he immediately fell away from his supernormal powers.
Having heard this, the people said:
"The elder seer is long-established and virtuous;
it is this young seer who has slandered him groundlessly."
They all became enraged at him, blocked him at the city gate, and would not allow him to enter; thus, he lost his offerings.
If you wish to know who that old seer was at that time, it was I myself.
"The powerful seer of that time was Devadatta. 38.
The Story of the Two Merchants (38). The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.

At that time, those bhikṣus who followed the Buddha’s words all attained the path of nirvāṇa and the realms of devas and humans; whereas those who followed Devadatta’s words all fell into hell and underwent great suffering and affliction.
The Buddha said,
"It is not only today that those who follow my teachings obtain great benefit,
while those who act upon Devadatta's words incur great suffering."
It was likewise in the past.
In a former age, there were two merchants who, each leading five hundred traders, arrived in the midst of a wilderness.
There was a yakṣa who transformed himself into a youth, wearing fine garments and a flower garland upon his head; playing the lute as he walked, he spoke to the merchants, saying:
"You are not exhausted; carrying this water and grass, what use will they be in the end?
Nearby ahead there is excellent water and grass. Follow me back and forth, and I shall show you the way."
One merchant leader immediately followed his advice, saying,
"Let us now discard the water and grass we are carrying.
They then set out with lightened loads and proceeded ahead.
One merchant said:
"We do not see water or grass now; be careful not to throw anything away.
Those who had previously discarded water and grass all died of thirst and exhaustion.
He who did not discard them reached his destination.
At that time, the one who did not discard the water and grass was my own self;
the one who discarded the water and grass was Devadatta.

39. The Account of the Eight Devas Asking About the Dharma in Succession (39). Once, when the Buddha was in the world, during the middle of the night, eight devas suddenly arrived one after another and came to where the World-Honored One was.

The first to arrive was of upright and handsome appearance, with a radiance that illuminated one *li*. Ten celestial maidens served as her retinue; they approached the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated themselves with sincere hearts, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha told the deva:
"By cultivating merit, you have obtained this celestial body; you delight yourself with the five desires and have swiftly attained peace and happiness.
Thereupon, the deva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Although I have been born in the heavens, my mind is constantly filled with sorrow and suffering. Why is this? Because...”

When I practiced in my previous lives, although I was loyal and filial toward my parents and teachers, and felt reverence for śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, I was nevertheless unable to show them diligent respect by bowing, welcoming them, or seeing them off.
"Due to these karmic conditions, the retribution is truly meager and does not compare to that of other devas. Because it is inferior, I reproach myself for being unable to fulfill my practice.

Then another deva, whose physical appearance, radiance, and retinue were ten times superior to the former, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha said to the deva,
"Having been born in the heavens, you have quickly attained peace and happiness.
The deva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Although I have been born in the heavens, I am constantly beset by sorrow and suffering. Why is this? Because—”

In my previous lives when I was practicing the path, although I gave rise to loyalty and filial piety toward my parents, teachers, and elders, as well as toward śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and paid them respectful homage, I was nevertheless unable to provide them with gifts such as beds, seats, warm bedding, or mats.

"By virtue of these karmic conditions, I have now obtained this retribution; yet it does not compare to that of other devas. Because it is inferior, I reproach myself for being unable to fulfill the cultivation of the causes.

Then another deva, whose physical form, radiance, and retinue were ten times superior to the former, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha said to the deva,
"Having received this celestial body, you have swiftly attained peace and happiness.
The deva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Although I have been born in a celestial palace, I am constantly filled with sorrow and distress. Why is this?

It is because in my previous life, although I was filial and respectful toward my parents, teachers, elders, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—offering them sincere devotion, paying homage, and providing them with beds and mats—I was unable to extensively prepare various delicacies and food and drink to offer as sustenance to them."

Due to these karmic conditions, he now receives this retribution which is inferior to that of other devas; because it is inferior, his mind feels self-reproach for not having fully cultivated the causes, and for this reason he is distressed.

Furthermore, another deva, whose countenance and radiance, along with his retinue, were ten times superior to those before, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha said to the deva,
"Having received this celestial body, you have quickly attained peace and happiness.
The deva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Although I have been born in the heavens, my mind is constantly filled with sorrow and distress. Why is this?

Because in the past, although I was loyal, filial, respectful, and offered prostrations to my parents, teachers, elders, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, and provided them with bedding, seats, food, and drink, I did not listen to the Dharma."

For this reason, the retribution he now receives is not equal to that of other devas; because it is inferior, he constantly reproaches himself for his failure to fulfill the cultivation of causes, and thus he suffers from grief and affliction.

Next, another deva, whose bodily color and radiance—and those of his retinue—were ten times superior to the former, came to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha told the deva:
"Having received this celestial body, you have quickly attained peace and happiness.
The deva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Although I have been born in heaven, my mind is constantly filled with sorrow and distress. Why is this?

It is because in my previous life, although I was able to be loyal, filial, respectful, and reverent toward my sovereign, parents, teachers, elders, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—providing them with bedding, food, and drink, and listening to the Dharma—I did not understand its meaning."

Because they did not understand, they now receive this karmic retribution, which is inferior to that of other devas; because it is inferior, their minds are constantly filled with regret and self-reproach for having failed to fulfill the cultivation of causes, and for this reason they suffer from anxiety and distress.

Next, there was a deva whose bodily color and radiance, along with his retinue, were ten times superior to those before; he came to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha said to the deva,
"Having received this celestial body, you have quickly attained peace and happiness.
The deva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Although I have been born in heaven, my mind is constantly filled with anxiety and distress. Why is this?

Because in my previous lives, when I practiced the path, although I was able to be loyal, filial, respectful, and reverent toward my sovereign, parents, teachers, elders, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas—providing them with bedding, food and drink, listening to the Dharma, and understanding its meaning—I was nevertheless unable to practice according to those teachings."

Due to these karmic conditions, they now receive this retribution; being inferior to other devas, and because of this inferiority, they deeply reproach themselves for the incompleteness of their cultivation of causes, and thus they suffer from grief and distress.

Next, there was a deva whose physical appearance and radiance, along with his retinue, were ten times superior to those before; he came to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha said to the deva,
"Having received this celestial body, you have quickly attained peace and happiness.
The deva addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Today I have been born in a celestial palace, where I enjoy myself with the five desires; whatever I require arrives as soon as it is thought of, and there is true happiness, free from all sorrow and affliction."

Why is this? It is because when I cultivated the causes in previous lives, I was loyal, filial, respectful, and reverent toward my parents, teachers, elders, śramaṇas, and brahmins; I provided them with bedding, food, and drink; I listened to the Dharma and was able to understand its meaning; and I practiced according to what was taught.

By these causes and conditions, they receive celestial retribution: their physical forms are upright and handsome, their radiance is exceptionally sublime, and their retinues are numerous, surpassing those of all other devas.
By practicing this conduct, one attains the fulfillment of the fruits;
by virtue of that fulfillment, one attains the most supreme retribution;
because of that supreme retribution, among all the devas, there is none who can equal him.
"Because there is nothing that can surpass it, the mind attains happiness.
*Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra*, Volume Three;
*Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra*, Volume Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Jikaya from the Western Regions together with Tanyao during the Northern Wei Dynasty:
The Circumstances of a Poor Man Receiving Immediate Retribution for Offering a Ball of Flour;
The Circumstances of a Poor Woman Receiving Immediate Retribution for Offering Two Coins; The Story of the Painter Jinadatta of the Kingdom of Gandhāra.
The causal conditions for receiving retribution through eating; the causal conditions for the couple Kairava selling themselves to provide a feast and receiving immediate retribution;

the causal conditions for a śrāmaṇera rescuing ants from a water disaster and obtaining the retribution of longevity; the causal conditions for the King of Gandhāra repairing an old stūpa and temple and thereby extending his life;

the causal conditions for a bhikṣu patching holes in a temple wall and obtaining the retribution of extended life; and the causal conditions for the son of an elder seeing the Buddha and requesting longevity.

The story of the merchant’s son Mṛgāra who, by providing a feast for hire, obtained a reward in his present life; the story of Purna who, by offering a bowl of food to the Buddha, obtained a reward in his present life;
the story of Mahaprajapati who, by offering a gold-woven robe to the Buddha along with a pearl-embroiderer;

and (40) the story of forty poor people who, by offering balls of parched grain, obtained a reward in their present lives; (41) the story of a poor man who, by offering a ball of flour, [obtained a reward].
An instance of obtaining retribution for past conditions: Long ago, there was a man who lived in poverty.
He worked as a laborer for others and obtained six *sheng* of parched grain flour, which he carried home to support his wife and children.
While on the road, he encountered a practitioner who held an alms bowl and carried a mendicant's staff, walking about to seek alms. He immediately thought to himself:
"That śramaṇa has a dignified appearance and a composed, orderly demeanor; he is truly worthy of respect. Would it not be a joy to offer him a single meal?"
At that time, the practitioner, knowing the man's thoughts, followed the poor man to the side of a body of water. The poor man then said to the practitioner:
"I now have some parched grain; I wish to offer it to you. Would you be able to eat it?"
The practitioner replied,
"I have indeed attained it.
He then spread out his robes by the water's edge for the practitioner to sit upon, mixed one *sheng* of parched grain into a single lump, and gave it to him, thinking to himself:
"If this practitioner of the Way is one who has attained the Way by purely maintaining the precepts, let me now become a minor king.
Having received the flour, the practitioner said to the poor man,
"Why is it so very little?"
"Why is it so small?
This man thought that this practitioner was eating too much, so he mixed another one *sheng* [of flour] and formed it into a single lump, which he gave to him while making this aspiration:
"If this practitioner is a person who maintains pure precepts and has attained the Way, may I become the king of two small kingdoms."
The practitioner spoke again:
"Why is it so extremely few?
Why is it so extremely small?"
The poor man thought to himself:

"Only this practitioner of the Way seems to eat excessively; even when given this much parched grain flour, he still complains that it is too little. Nevertheless, since I have already invited him, I must provide for his needs."
He then mixed two sheng of flour, formed it into a single lump, and gave it to him, further making this thought:
"If this practitioner of the Way is one who has attained the Way by purely maintaining the precepts, may I immediately come to rule over four minor kings."
The practitioner spoke again:
"Why is it so extremely few?
Why is it so extremely small?"
There were two *śēṅ* remaining; he mixed them all together to form a ball and gave it to the practitioner, making this vow:
"If this practitioner is one who is pure and maintains the precepts, may I become the King of Vārāṇasī, ruling over four minor kingdoms, and attain the Path of Seeing the Truths."
When the practitioner received the flour, he expressed dissatisfaction because it was so little.
The poor man said to him, "I only pray that you will eat it for now; if it is not enough, I shall take off my clothes and trade them for food and drink to provide for you together."
The practitioner then ate, consuming only one *śoṇa*; the remainder was returned to its owner.
The poor man asked, "Venerable sir, previously you complained that the flour was far too little; why do you not finish eating it now?"
The practitioner replied, "When you first gave me a single lump of flour, it was precisely because you sought to become a minor king; for this reason, I said:
'Your aspiration is small.'"
"The second ball of flour was intended for the wish to become two minor kings;
therefore, I said: 'Your wish is small.
The third ball of flour was intended for the wish to become four minor kings; therefore, I said:"
"Your aspiration is small.

Regarding the fourth portion of flour, you were specifically seeking to become the King of Vārāṇasī, ruling over four minor kingdoms, so that you might later attain the fruit of the Path of Seeing; therefore, I said:
"Your aspiration is very small."
"Do not be dissatisfied or feel it is too little because of its smallness.
At that time, the poor man conceived this thought within himself:
"For me to actually obtain the five kingdoms from the king is no small matter; I fear it may not be real."
He further reflected:
"Since he can know my mind, he must surely be a sage and a great field of merit; I ought not to deceive him.
Having understood this, the man of the Way immediately cast his alms-bowl into the midst of space and flew away after it. He then manifested a massive body that filled the void.
He further manifested himself as small, like a mote of dust.

With a single body he became infinite bodies, and with infinite bodies he merged into a single body. Water issued from his upper body and fire from his lower body; he walked upon water as if on land and walked upon land as if on water.
Having performed these eighteen transformations, he said to the poor man, "Make a great vow; do not harbor any doubt."
He then vanished from sight.
At that time, as the poor man was heading toward the city of Vārāṇasī, he encountered a high minister along the way.
Upon seeing him, the minister scrutinized his physical appearance and said to him:
"Are you not the son of so-and-so? He replied, "I am."
He asked, "Why are you so ragged, even to this extent?
He replied:
"Having lost my parents at a young age, my family home has been utterly destroyed, and there is no one to look after me; for this reason, I am in such distress and am dressed in rags like this.
The minister then addressed the King of Vārāṇasī:
"The son of a person close to Your Majesty, so-and-so, is currently outside the gate, appearing extremely impoverished and worn."
The king immediately issued an edict:
"Let a messenger lead him forward.
He questioned him in detail; knowing him to be a close relative, the king then spoke to him:
“Be good friends with me; take care not to distance yourself.
Seven days later, the king fell ill and passed away. The ministers deliberated, saying, “The king has no heir.
This impoverished son alone was the king’s close confidant; we should collectively elect him to be the King of Vārāṇasī.”
After ruling over the four kingdoms, he became tyrannical and violent.
Before him, a certain practitioner appeared in mid-air in front of the royal palace, sat cross-legged, and said to him:
"In the past, you made a vow to seek and attain the vision of the Truth."
"Why have you committed such manifold evils today, acting so contrary to your original nature?
He then preached various Dharmas to the king.

Having heard the Dharma, the king repented for his previous misdeeds; he reformed his ways with a sense of shame and remorse, applied himself single-mindedly to the practice of the Way, and attained the stage of Srotāpanna.

41. The Story of the Poor Woman Who Received Rebirth as a Reward for Giving Two Coins (41) The Story of the Poor Woman Who Received Rebirth as a Reward for Giving Two Coins: Long ago, in Mount Zhuan'an, there were many holy sages and monks living in seclusion.
In various regions and lands, having heard the name of that mountain, many people made offerings.
There was an elder who, together with his kinsmen and retinue, went there to present offerings.
There was a poor woman who begged for alms, and she thought to herself:
"Now that these elders are sending offerings to the mountain, they must intend to hold a great assembly; I shall go there to beg."
He then proceeded into the mountains.
Having arrived at the mountain, he saw the aforementioned elder preparing various kinds of food to provide for the assembly of monks;

he thought to himself, "That man cultivated merit in his previous lives and is now wealthy and noble; now that he again performs such meritorious deeds, his future rewards will surely be even greater."
"I did not perform [meritorious deeds] in my past lives, and thus I suffer poverty and hardship in this life; if I do not act now, it will become even more severe in the future.
Having reflected thus, he wept in distress and thought to himself:

"Once, while scavenging through refuse, I found two coins. I have always cherished them as treasures, intending to use them to purchase food and drink for my own survival when my begging fails to yield results."
"I shall now take these to give as alms to the Sangha; even if they were deprived of food and drink for one or two days, they would ultimately not die.
Waiting until the monks had finished their meal, he took these two coins and immediately offered them as a gift.

According to the monastic custom of that mountain monastery, whenever someone made an offering, the *karmadāna* would stand before the assembly of monks to recite the prayer of blessing (*svastyayana*).
At such times, the senior monk (*sthavira*) would not allow the *karmadāna* to recite the blessing, but would instead recite it himself.
The junior monks and others felt deep resentment and thought to themselves:

"Having obtained two small coins from that beggar girl, the Elder treats them with such contempt as to offer a blessing for them as if they were common coins; why does he not do so for [other] coins?"
The Elder immediately set aside half of his own food and gave it to this woman.
Seeing that the Elder had given so much, everyone else also gave generously.
At that time, the woman received a heavy load of food and drink and was filled with extreme joy:
"I have just performed an act of giving and have now received its reward.
He then carried the food and drink back out of the mountain; arriving beneath a tree, he lay down to rest.

It happened that seven days had passed since the King’s chief consort had died; the King dispatched a messenger to traverse the borders of the kingdom to see who possessed such merit and virtue as to be worthy of becoming the consort.
The physiognomist divined, "Beneath this yellow cloud-canopy, there must surely be a worthy person.
They then went together to that tree.

Seeing the woman there, her complexion was radiant and moist, possessing the marks of merit and virtue; the tree bent its branches to shade her, and the light and shadow remained fixed. The physiognomist said:
"This woman possesses such merit that she is worthy to be a consort.

He immediately bathed her with fragrant water and provided her with the garments of a consort; they were neither too large nor too small, fitting her body perfectly. With a retinue of thousands of chariots and tens of thousands of horsemen leading and following on both sides, he brought her to the palace.
The king, seeing this, was filled with joy and conceived a heart of deep respect. After some time had passed, he thought to himself:
"The reason I have obtained these conditions of wealth and fortune is because of my gift of money."
"Now those monks have bestowed upon me a most profound and heavy kindness.
He then addressed the king, saying:
"I was formerly a lowly person, yet the King has drawn me forth and elevated me to the status of a human being; please allow me to repay the kindness of those monks."
The king said, "As you wish.
Thereupon, the lady immediately loaded food, drink, and precious jewels onto a carriage and went to that mountain; having finished offering the food to the Sangha, she gave the jewels as alms.
The Elder did not rise, but sent the *karmadāna* to offer a prayer of blessing instead of blessing her himself.
The Queen said, "In the past, when I had only two coins, you offered a prayer for me; [why do you not do so now?]"
"Now, when this chariot carrying precious jewels passes by, why do you not offer a blessing for me?

The young bhikṣus all felt resentment toward the elder; they thought, "Previously, when that poor woman gave two coins as an offering, he offered a blessing for her. Now, when the King’s consort has a chariot laden with precious jewels, he does not offer a blessing—is it because he is senile and decrepit?"
At that time, the Elder spoke these words of the True Dharma for the sake of the King’s consort:
“O Consort! Your mind harbors resentment toward me.”
"When you previously gave me two coins, you offered a blessing for my sake; now that I am laden with a cart of precious jewels, you do not offer a blessing.
In my Buddha-dharma, we do not value precious jewels; we value only the virtuous mind."

"O Lady! When you first gave two coins, your virtuous mind was most excellent; but when you later gave precious jewels, you were arrogant with self-importance. For this reason, I do not now offer a blessing."
"Young practitioners!
Do not resent me; you must deeply understand the mind of renunciation.
The young practitioners each felt ashamed and remorseful, and all attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
The King’s consort listened to the Dharma; filled with shame and joy, she also attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.
Having finished listening to the Dharma, she paid her respects and departed. 42.

The Story of the Painter Kṛṣṇa from the Kingdom of Gandhāra Who Received a Reward for Providing a Meal (42) Long ago, in the kingdom of Gandhāra, there was a painter named Kṛṣṇa. After working as a laborer for three years, he obtained thirty *tolas* of gold and intended to return home. On his way, he saw others performing a *pañcavārṣika* festival and asked the *karmadāna*: "What is this?"
"How much will be required for a single day's assembly?
The *karmadāna* replied,
"Thirty taels of gold will suffice for a one-day assembly."
He then thought to himself:

"Because I failed to plant seeds of merit in my previous lives, I have received this retribution and must support myself by manual labor. Now that I have encountered a field of merit, why should I not cultivate it?"
He then said to the *karmadāna*:
"Please strike the gavel to assemble the Sangha for my disciple; I wish to hold a ritual assembly.
When the assembly had concluded, he was filled with exuberant joy and immediately returned home.
Having arrived home, his wife asked him,
"Where are the coins from three years of labor?
Her husband replied:
"The wealth I have acquired has now been placed within a secure storehouse.
His wife then asked,
"Where is this secure storehouse located now?"
The husband replied, "He was right there among the monks.
At that time, the wife felt resentful and reproached him; she immediately gathered her relatives, bound her husband, and went before the magistrate, saying these words:

"My mother and I have suffered in poverty and hardship, lacking both clothing and food, yet my husband takes the surplus of his wealth for his own use and does not bring it back; please inquire into the reason for this."
At that time, the judge asked her husband,
"Why is this so? He replied:
"My body is like a flash of lightning that does not shine for long, and it is also like morning dew that perishes in an instant. Out of fear of this, I reflect deeply within myself:
'Because I did not perform meritorious deeds in my previous lives, I now encounter poverty and suffering, lacking even food and clothing.'"

"Therefore, upon seeing the Pañcavārṣika assembly being held in the city of Pukara, where the community of monks was pure, joy arose in his heart and a sense of reverent faith emerged within him. He immediately asked the karmadāna:
'How much wealth has been obtained to provide for one day's meal?'"
The karmadāna replied,
"With thirty measures of gold, one can provide for one day's meal.
During my three years of labor, whatever I earned, I immediately gave to the karmadāna to have him prepare a day's food for the community of monks.

When the judges heard these words, their hearts were filled with joy; out of compassion for the man, they removed their own garments, necklaces, saddles, horses, and all their riding equipment, bestowing them entirely upon Keṇa, and immediately divided a village to grant him as a fief.
If the immediate retribution is such as this, the ultimate fruit will follow later. 43.

The Story of the Couple Kṣemila Who Sold Themselves to Host a Feast and Received Immediate Retribution (43). The Story of the Couple Kṣemila Who Sold Themselves to Host a Feast and Received Immediate Retribution: Long ago there was a man named Kṣemila; he and his wife were so utterly destitute that they had no means of support and lived by taking up employment as laborers.

Seeing that other elders all went to the monastery to hold great assemblies of giving, yet upon returning home they slept with their wives, with their heads resting on their wives' arms, he reflected to himself:
"It is because I failed to perform meritorious deeds in my previous lives that I am poor today."
"Just as that householder performed meritorious deeds in his previous life and continues to do so now, whereas I currently possess no merit;
in future lives, my suffering will only increase in intensity."
Having had this thought, he wept and was unhappy, his tears falling upon his wife's arm.
The wife asked her husband,
"Why are you shedding tears?"
He replied, "I see others cultivating merit and always obtaining happiness, yet I despise my own poverty and low status, having no means to cultivate merit; for this reason, I shed tears.
His wife said:
"What is the use of weeping?
I can sell my own body to another person to obtain wealth for making merit.
The husband said:
"If we were to sell each other, how could my body possibly survive?
The wife said,
"If you fear that you will not survive and cannot see me leave, I shall now sell myself along with you so that we may together cultivate merit."
Thereupon, the husband and wife took one another with them to a wealthy household and said to them:
"Now we, this couple, offer these humble bodies of ours to purchase gold coins."
The host asked,
"How much money do you wish to receive?
He replied:
"I wish to obtain ten gold coins.
The host said, "I will give you the money now; however, if you do not repay me after seven days, you and your wife shall become my slaves."
Having established their agreement, they took money and went to that stupa-temple to arrange a religious assembly.
The husband and wife together pounded the rice, encouraging one another, saying:
"Today we have been able to exert our own strength to create meritorious karma; once we belong to another family, how could we act according to our own will?"

Thereupon, day and night, he diligently prepared the requisites for the assembly. On the sixth day, as the assembly was about to commence, it so happened that the ruler of that country also wished to hold an assembly and came to contest the date.
The monks all said, "Since we have already received those who were destitute, we shall by no means move [the date]."
Upon hearing this, the ruler of the land spoke thus:
"What kind of petty person dares to contend with me regarding the day of the assembly?
He immediately dispatched a messenger to say to Keli:
"You must avoid my light," Keli replied,
"I truly do not avoid it."
Thus he repeated this three times, yet the man persisted in his refusal as before.
The King, wondering at the reason for this, went in person to the monastery and said to the man:
"Why do you not work on the following day instead, so that we may contend over the date?"
He replied, "Only for one day was I independent; thereafter I fell under the control of another family and could no longer act as I pleased.
The king then asked:
"Why can you not? the one selling himself replied:
"I reflect that in my previous lives I did not perform meritorious deeds, and so today I am in such poverty and suffering; if I do not do so now, I fear I shall suffer even more in the future."
Reflecting upon this matter, he thought only of selling his own body to obtain money for making meritorious offerings, desiring thereby to sever this suffering.
When seven days had passed and he still possessed no wealth to repay his debt to others, he immediately became a slave.
"Now that six days have passed and tomorrow will mark their completion, for this reason, we shall divide the days of our death-struggle.
When the king heard these words, he felt deep compassion and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence:

"You truly understand the suffering of poverty; you are able to exchange this non-enduring body for an enduring body, this non-enduring wealth for enduring wealth, and this non-enduring life for an enduring life."

The King immediately granted permission for the assembly to be held; he then removed his own robes and jewelry, as well as those of his consort, and gave them to Kila and his wife, and he ceded ten villages to them as a meritorious fief.
If those who can cultivate merit with a sincere heart obtain such a "flower-reward" (immediate result) in this very life, how much more so will they obtain the ultimate fruit-reward in the future?
Viewed from this perspective, all people in the world who wish to escape suffering should diligently cultivate merit; why should they indulge their passions, being indolent and negligent?

44. The Story of the Śrāmaṇera Who Saved Ants from a Flood and Received the Reward of Longevity (44) In the past, there was an arhat practitioner who kept a śrāmaṇera as his attendant. Knowing that this śrāmaṇera would surely reach the end of his life in seven days, he granted him leave to return home. When the seventh day arrived, the arhat commanded him to return.

The śrāmaṇera took his leave of his teacher and departed. Along the way, he saw a swarm of ants being swept away by the current, their lives on the verge of ending. Moved by compassion, he removed his own kāṣāya robe, filled it with earth to dam the water, and gathered the ants, placing them in a high and dry spot; thus, they all survived.
When the seventh day arrived, he returned to his teacher.

The teacher was greatly surprised by this and immediately entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Using his divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), he observed that the man possessed no further merit to account for such a thing; rather, it was due to the causal conditions of having saved some ants that he did not die on the seventh day and had obtained an extension of his life.

45. The Story of the King of Gandhāra Extending His Life by Repairing an Old Stūpa and Temple (45) In the past, in the kingdom of Gandhāra, there was a sovereign. A skilled physiognomist divined for the king that in seven days, he would surely meet his end.

While out on a hunting excursion, he saw an old stupa that was ruined and collapsed; he immediately ordered his ministers to repair it together. Once the repairs were completed, he returned to the palace in joy, remaining in peace and security for seven days.
After seven days had passed, the physiognomist marveled at what was occurring and asked the king,
"What meritorious deed have you performed?
The king replied:
"There is nothing further to be done; there is only one damaged stūpa that must be repaired with mud.
Because of repairing the stūpa, such is the merit. 46.

The Story of the Bhikṣu Who Repaired a Hole in the Temple Wall and Received the Reward of Extended Life (46). Once, there was a bhikṣu whose time of death was approaching. A non-Buddhist brahmin happened to see him and, by examining his physical signs, knew that he would certainly pass away seven days later.
At that time, this bhikṣu, upon entering the monastery, saw a hole in the wall and immediately kneaded mud to patch it over.
By virtue of this merit, his lifespan was increased, allowing him to survive for more than seven days.
The brahmin saw this and, wondering at its cause, asked him:
"What merit have you cultivated?
The bhikṣu replied:
“I have practiced nothing; I merely entered the monks’ quarters yesterday and saw a hole in the wall, which I simply repaired.
The brahmin sighed in admiration and said, “This Sangha is a field of merit most profound and weighty, for it can cause a monk who was destined to die to prolong his life and extend his years.”
47. The Story of the Elder’s Son Who Sought Longevity upon Seeing the Buddha (47). Once, when the Buddha was in the world, there was a son of an elder who was five or six years of age.
An astrologer divined his marks and found that while his merit and virtue were complete, he alone possessed a short lifespan.
He went to the six heterodox teachers in hopes of seeking long life, but he found that those six teachers were entirely unable to provide him with the dharma for longevity.
Upon arriving at the Buddha’s dwelling, he addressed the Buddha, saying, “This child has a short lifespan;
I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant him long life.
The Buddha said:
"There is no such dharma that can grant long life.
He addressed the Buddha again, saying,
"I pray that you will show us the skillful means."
The Buddha then instructed him, saying:
"When you reach the city gate, bow to anyone coming out, and likewise bow to anyone entering.
At that time, there was a spirit who transformed himself into the body of a Brahmin and intended to enter the city; when the boy bowed toward him, the spirit offered this blessing:
"May you live long.

This ghost was a spirit that killed infants; however, according to the laws of ghosts and spirits, one may not speak more than two words. Having granted him longevity, he was no longer permitted to kill.
Because he possessed such humility, patience, and reverence, he was able to prolong his lifespan. 48.

The Story of the Elder’s Son Who Received Immediate Retribution for Hosting a Feast While Working as a Laborer (48). Once, when the Buddha was in the world, there was the son of an elder who had lost both parents at an early age. Destitute and solitary, he made his living by working as a hired laborer.

Having heard someone say that the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is exceedingly joyful, and having also heard it said that by making offerings to the Buddha and the Saṅgha one will certainly attain rebirth there, he immediately asked him:
"How much wealth is required to be able to make offerings to the Buddha and the assembly of monks?"
The people of the time said,
"For thirty taels of gold, one may hold a feast.
He then went to the marketplace and sought a place for hire.
Near the city lived a very wealthy elder who hired him as a laborer.
The elder asked him, "What work can you do now? He replied:
“I am capable of all these tasks.
“If you work as a hired laborer for three years, how much will you ask for?
He replied:
"I require thirty taels of gold.
When the elder heard that he was capable of performing all these tasks, he immediately hired him to work.
Being upright and honest, he gained double his usual profit from every kind of shop dealing in gold, silver, copper, and iron.
When the months were complete, he requested the payment from that elder.
The elder asked,
"Now that you have received the gold, what will you do with it?"
He replied,
"I wish to make offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha.
The elder said to him:
"I shall now assist you; with various vessels, rice, and flour, I will prepare food for you. You need only invite the Buddha and the Sangha.
He then went at once to the monastic quarters and invited the Buddha and the monks.
The Buddha directed the assembly of monks to accept his invitation; the Buddha himself remained in his own quarters, while the monks all accepted the invitation of that elder’s son.
It happened to be a festival day, so many people brought various kinds of food and drink to offer to the monks.
When the assembly of monks had finished eating, they went to the house of the elder.
At that time, the elder’s son was personally serving the food with his own hands.
The senior monk said, "Put less on."
In succession, everyone said they had eaten only a little, until it came to the last row.
At that time, the son of the elder wept in distress, saying: "I have labored for three years to prepare this food and drink, hoping the Sangha would eat;
since the Sangha will not eat, my hope to be reborn in heaven will surely not be fulfilled."
He went to the Buddha’s side and said to him,
“The Sangha will not eat my offering, and thus my wish shall certainly not be fulfilled.
The Buddha said:
"Did you eat little?
They replied,
"We all ate very little."
The Buddha said, “If even by not eating your vow would certainly be fulfilled, how much more so when you eat only a little? Why should it not be fulfilled?
The youth was filled with joy and returned to eat and drink.
At that time, the assembly of monks finished their meal and immediately returned.
Then there were five hundred merchants who, having returned from the sea, entered the city seeking food and drink.
At that time, the world was suffering from famine, and there was no one to give them anything.
Someone said to him, "That son of a householder is hosting a gathering today; there will surely be food and drink.
When the son of the householder heard that there were merchants, he joyfully gave them food. The five hundred merchants all received their fill, and all his attendants were likewise satiated.
To the lowest merchant, he gave one pearl to take, which was worth ten thousand taels of gold;
to the highest-ranking merchant, he gave one pearl to take, which was worth one hundred thousand taels of gold.
Five hundred merchants each gave him a pearl and a copper helmet, yet the son of the elder did not dare to accept them.
He went to the Buddha to inquire about this, and the Buddha said:
"These are merely the karmic fruits of past flowers; you may take them without concern. Afterward, you will surely be reborn in heaven, so there is no need for fear."
The householder, the master of the household, having no other sons, gave his only daughter to the youth.
Consequently, their family business flourished greatly until it became the foremost in the city of Śrāvastī.
When the elder passed away, King Prasenajit, having heard of his wisdom and insight, bestowed all of his family estate upon him.
Such was the immediate retribution; its ultimate fruition shall follow later.

49.
