The Story of Pūrṇa Receiving Immediate Retribution for Offering a Bowl of Food to the Buddha (49) The story of Pūrṇa receiving immediate retribution for offering a bowl of food to the Buddha: Long ago, when the Buddha was in the world, there were five brothers who were brahmins; the first was named Yaśas.
The second was named Vimala, the third Kātyāyana, and the fourth Sudinna;
these four elder brothers entered the mountains to study the Way and attained the five supernatural powers.
His youngest brother was named Pūrṇa. Seeing the Buddha begging for alms, he filled his bowl with fine, pure white rice and offered it to the Buddha.
At that time, Pūrṇa’s constant occupation was farming; having finished his plowing and sowing, he was returning home.

Later, on one day, he went out into the fields and saw that the crops growing there had transformed into golden grain, all several feet in height; though they were harvested until nothing remained, they grew back again as before.
When the king heard of this, he also came to harvest it, but he could not finish it; likewise, all those who came to take it were unable to exhaust it.
The elder brothers thought to themselves, "Is our younger brother Purna living in prosperity, or is he in poverty?
They immediately went together to see him; seeing that his meritorious karma surpassed even that of the king, they spoke to their brother, saying:
"You were previously poor; how did you suddenly become wealthy?
He replied, "I saw Gautama and offered him a bowl of rice; I have obtained such a reward as this."
Upon hearing this, the four elder brothers were filled with joy and leaped for gladness.

They then said to their younger brother, "Now, for our sake, prepare some *modaka* cakes. We four shall each take one cake to offer to Gautama. We pray to be reborn in heaven; we will not listen to his Dharma, nor will we seek liberation."
Thereupon, each of them took a ball of joy-food and went to where the Buddha was. The eldest brother took one ball and placed it in the Buddha’s bowl. The Buddha said:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent."
A second time, he again placed a ball of joy-food into the Buddha’s bowl, and the Buddha spoke these words:
“This is a phenomenon subject to arising and ceasing.
A third time, he again placed a ball of joy-food into the Buddha’s bowl, and the Buddha spoke these words:
"When birth and death have ceased," he said.
On the fourth day, he again placed a ball of joy into the Buddha’s alms bowl, and the Buddha spoke these words:
"Cessation is bliss."
They immediately returned home and, having gone to a secluded place, asked one another:
"What words did you hear?
The eldest brother said:
"The first hears, 'All conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
The second further hears that they are subject to arising and ceasing. The third hears that once arising and ceasing have ceased, the fourth hears that tranquility is bliss."
The four brothers each contemplated this verse and attained the stage of Anāgāmin; they all came to the Buddha’s presence, requested ordination, and attained the path of Arhatship.

50. The Story of Mahāprajāpatī Offering a Gold-Thread Woven Robe and the Pearl-Stringer (50). In the past, when the Buddha was in the world, Mahāprajāpatī had a robe woven from gold threads for the Buddha. She brought it to offer to the Buddha, and the Buddha said to her:
"Give this to the community of monks."
Mahāprajāpatī said:
"I nourished and raised the World-Honored One with my own milk; I have made this robe myself and have come to offer it to the Buddha, truly hoping that the Tathāgata will accept it from me."
"How can you speak dialectically with the Saṃgha?
The Buddha said,
"I wish to enable my maternal aunt to attain great merit."
Why is this? The Sangha is a field of merit, vast and boundless; therefore, I exhort you.
If you follow my words, you will have already made offerings to the Buddha.
Then Mahāprajāpatī took this robe and went into the midst of the Saṃgha, passing it down from the senior monk; yet no one dared to take it.
When it came next to Maitreya, Maitreya accepted the robe, put it on, and entered the city to beg for alms.

Maitreya’s body was endowed with the thirty-two marks and possessed the color of purple-polished gold; once he had entered the city, the multitude vied with one another to gaze upon him, yet no one offered him food.
There was a pearl-stringer who, seeing that the people offered him no food, immediately stepped forward on his knees to invite him, led him to his home, and gave Maitreya food.
When Maitreya had finished eating, the pearl-stringer spread out a small seat before him and requested to hear the Dharma.
Possessing the power of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), Maitreya immediately expounded for him various sublime teachings.
At that time, the pearl-driller listened with eager delight, never feeling weary or satisfied.
Previously, there was an elder who, wishing to marry off his daughter, hired the pearl-driller to bore a single precious gem for a fee of one hundred thousand coins.
At that time, the family of the bride sent someone to request the pearls.
The pearl-piercer, being deeply absorbed in listening to the Dharma, had no leisure to pierce them and replied to him:
"Please wait for a brief moment."
He came again to demand it, and even after three such visits, he still did not receive it.
The householder became angry and, gathering his pearls and coins together, went back to seize them.
The wife of the pearl-driller, enraged at her husband, said:
"There is no further business; in a mere moment I can string pearls and obtain a profit of one hundred thousand. Why would I listen to this practitioner’s flowery rhetoric?
Having heard this, her husband felt deep resentment in his heart.
At that time, Maitreya, knowing his resentment, asked him:
"Would you be able to follow me to the monastery?
He replied:
"I can," he replied,
and immediately followed Maitreya to the monastery. There he asked the elder,
"If someone were to obtain a hundred thousand catties of gold, how would that compare to joyfully listening to a person preach the Dharma?"
Kauṇḍinya said:

"Suppose there were someone who obtained a hundred thousand pieces of gold; this would not equal the merit of someone who gives a single bowl of food to one who upholds the precepts. How much more so for one who, with a faithful heart, listens to the Dharma for even a brief moment—this surpasses the former by hundreds of thousands of millions of times."
Thereupon, he asked the second elder, who replied:

"Even if someone were to obtain a hundred thousand pieces of gold from wagons, it would not equal the merit of giving a single bowl of food to one who observes the precepts; how much more so for one who listens to the Dharma with joy over the course of time."
Again, he questioned the third elder, who replied:

"If someone were to obtain a hundred thousand pieces of gold, it would not equal the merit of giving a single bowl of food to one who upholds the precepts, let alone the merit of listening to the Dharma."
He then questioned the fourth elder, who replied:

"Even if one were to obtain the gold of a hundred thousand kingdoms, it would not equal the merit of giving a single bowl of food to one who maintains the precepts; how much more so for listening to the Dharma, which is hundreds of thousands of millions of times greater."
In this manner, he questioned them in succession until he reached Aniruddha.

Aniruddha said, "If someone were to obtain gold filling the four continents of the world, it would still not be equal to giving a single bowl of food to one who observes the precepts; how much more so for one who listens to the Dharma?"
Maitreya replied:
"Venerable sir, you have said that giving a single bowl of food to a bhikṣu is even more excellent than obtaining gold filling the four continents; how is this so?"
The Venerable replied:

“Taking myself as witness, I recall that ninety billion eons ago there was an elder who had two sons, one named Liṭha and the other named Ariṭha. He would constantly tell them: ‘That which is high shall fall;
that which is constant shall perish. For all that is born there is death; all that meets must part.’”
When the elder fell ill, as his life was drawing to a close, he instructed his sons:
"Be careful not to divide the estate.
For example, a single strand of thread cannot bind an elephant, yet when many strands are gathered together, an elephant cannot break them."
"The brothers standing side by side are also like many strands of thread.
At that time, after the elder had finished instructing his sons, he drew his last breath and passed away.
Because of their father's command, the brothers lived together, treating one another with the utmost respect and affection.
Later, he took a wife for his younger brother. Not long after they had begun their life together, the brother’s wife said to her husband:
"You are just like that slave. Why is this so?"
"Regarding the expenditure of wealth and the reception of guests, all such matters depend upon your elder brother; you now receive only food and clothing. Are you not a slave?
He spoke these words many times.
At that time, the husband and wife felt a change in their hearts and requested to live separately from their elder brother.
The elder brother said to his younger brother,
"Do you not remember the words your father spoke at the time of his death?"
Still not reforming himself, he repeatedly requested a separate residence.
Seeing his brother’s intent, the elder brother granted him a separate dwelling, and all their possessions were divided equally between them.
The younger brother’s wife and husband were young and dissolute, living in extravagant luxury; before long, they became impoverished and destitute, and came to beg from their elder brother.
At that time, his elder brother gave him one hundred thousand coins; not long after he had departed, he spent them all and returned to ask for more.
This happened six times in succession, and each time the brother gave him one hundred thousand.
Upon reaching the seventh time, the elder brother rebuked him, saying:
"You did not heed my father’s final words and sought to divide the estate; you were unable to live with a sincere heart, yet you have repeatedly come to demand goods.
Now I give you another hundred thousand coins. From this day forward, if you do not manage your livelihood well and come again to demand more, I shall give you nothing further."
Having received this harsh speech, the husband and wife applied themselves diligently to their livelihood and gradually attained wealth.
The elder brother, having lost his money and property, gradually fell into poverty; he came to beg from his younger brother, but the younger brother would not even spare his own food for him, saying:
"I thought you were always wealthy; have you too become poor?"
"In the past, when I followed you and asked for something, you rebuked me with harsh words; why do you come to ask of me today?
Upon hearing this, the elder brother was overcome with extreme distress and thought to himself:
"If even brothers born of the same womb are like this, how much more so will it be toward strangers?"

"Disgusted with birth and death, he consequently did not return home, but entered the mountains to study the Way. Through diligent and arduous ascetic practice, he attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha.
Later, his younger brother also gradually fell into poverty; encountering a time of famine, he sold firewood to sustain himself."
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha entered the city to beg for food, but returned with an empty bowl, having obtained nothing at all.

When the wood-seller saw the Pratyekabuddha leaving the city with an empty bowl, he took the coarse millet porridge he had received from selling his wood and wished to give it to him, saying to the Pratyekabuddha:
"Venerable One, can you eat such coarse and poor food?"
He replied, "I do not inquire whether it is good or bad; I simply take what is enough to sustain my body.
Thereupon, the wood-seller immediately gave it to him.
The Pratyekabuddha accepted and ate it. After he had finished eating, he soared into the void and performed the eighteen transformations, then returned to his dwelling place.

Later, when the wood-seller went out again to gather firewood, he saw a rabbit on the path; as he prodded it with his staff, it turned into a dead man who suddenly rose up and threw his arms around the wood-seller’s neck. The wood-seller tried every possible means to push him away, but could not free himself.

He stripped off his clothes and hired others to pull the corpse off, yet they could not dislodge it. As night fell, he carried it back toward his home. Once he arrived at his house, the dead man untied himself and fell to the ground, becoming a man of pure gold.

At that time, the wood-seller immediately cut off the golden man’s head, but the head grew back instantly; he then cut off its hands and feet, but the hands and feet grew back as well. In a mere moment, golden heads and golden hands filled his house, piling up into a great heap.
A neighbor informed the authorities:
"In this poor man's house, there is naturally this heap of gold.
Upon hearing this, the King dispatched an envoy to go and investigate it further.
Upon entering the house, he saw nothing but the head of a rotting, stinking dead man.
The man himself took hold of the golden head and presented it to the King; it was indeed pure gold.
The King was greatly delighted and said,
"This is a person of merit.
He immediately granted him a village as a fief.

From this point, at the end of his life, he was reborn in the second heaven as Śakra, Lord of the Devas; subsequently descending to be born among humans, he became a Wheel-Turning Sage King. For ninety-one kalpas, he never ceased to be either a celestial king or a human king.
Now, in his final incarnation, he was born into the Śākya clan; on the day of his birth, within a radius of forty li, hidden treasures and precious jewels spontaneously surged forth from the earth.

Later, as they gradually grew up, his elder brother was named Śākyamāna; his parents doted on him exclusively. At that time, Anuruddha’s mother, wishing to test her sons, sent word to them that there was no food.
Aniruddha said, "Just carry it back without food.
He immediately gave him an empty vessel; at that moment, the hundred-flavored foods naturally filled the empty vessel to the brim.
Even if one were to use the gold of the four continents as sustenance for nursing, it would not suffice for a single kalpa, let alone for ninety-one kalpas of constant enjoyment of happiness.

Thus, that I have now obtained this spontaneous food is precisely due to having given this single bowl of food in a previous life; having now received this retribution, from the Buddhas above down to Brahmā below, those who purely maintain the precepts are all called "upholders of the precepts."
At that time, having heard these words, the pearl-worker was filled with great joy.

Circumstance 51: The Story of How a Goddess Formerly Offered a Flower Garland to the Stūpa of Kāśyapa Buddha (51).
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, attained the stage of Srotāpanna. He immediately returned to the heavens and assembled the hosts of devas.
They praised the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

At that time, there was a goddess wearing a floral garland; the radiance of the garland was exceedingly brilliant and resplendent. Together with the host of devas, she came and assembled in the Sudharmā Hall.
The assembly of devas, seeing this goddess, gave rise to a sense of wonder.
Śakra-devānām-indra then spoke a verse, asking the goddess:
"What meritorious deeds have you performed, That your body is like refined, pure gold?"
Your radiant complexion is like a lotus flower, and you possess great majestic power;
from your body issues forth wondrous light, and your face is like a blossoming flower. With a golden hue shining brilliantly, by what karmic actions was this attained?
“I pray that you will explain this to me.
At that time, the goddess replied with a verse:
“In the past, I offered a flower garland To the stupa of Kāśyapa Buddha.”
Having attained these supreme merits, one is born among the devas,
receiving as karmic retribution a body of golden hue.
Śakra Devānām Indra spoke again in verse, praising him, saying:
"How marvelous is this field of merit! Having weeded away all impurities and evils, such a small seed yields a supreme celestial fruit; who would not offer worship to it?"
Who would not make offerings to the Buddha, that mass of true gold, the supreme field of merit,
whose eyes are exceedingly long and wide, like blue lotus flowers?
"You have been able to offer worship to the Unsurpassed, Supreme Honored One; by performing even a small deed of merit, you have obtained such an appearance as this.
At that time, the goddess immediately descended from the heavens, holding a flower parasol, and came to where the Buddha was;
the Buddha preached the Dharma for her, and she attained the stage of Srotāpanna before returning to the heavens.
The bhikṣus, wondering at the reason for this, immediately asked the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
What merit did this goddess cultivate to obtain this celestial body, so exceptionally beautiful and distinguished?"
The Buddha said, "In times past, she offered various flower garlands as an offering to the stūpa of Kāśyapa Buddha; by this causal condition, she has now obtained this fruit."

52. The Story of the Goddess Who Formerly Offered a Lotus to the Stūpa of Kāśyapa Buddha (52). At that time, there was another goddess whose head-garland of flowers radiated brilliant light; she came together with a multitude of devas to assemble in the Sudharmā Hall.
At that time, the assembly of devas, seeing this heavenly maiden, gave rise to a sense of wonder.
Then Śakra, Lord of Devas, asked her in verse:
"What merit did you perform in the past, That your body is like a mass of pure gold?"
Your complexion is like a lotus flower, and you possess great majestic power;
from your body issues forth subtle and wondrous light, and your face is like a blossoming flower.
This radiance is exceedingly brilliant—by what karmic conduct was this attained?
"I only pray that you will speak for me.
The goddess then immediately replied with a verse:
"In the past, I offered a lotus flower To the stupa of Kāśyapa."
"Today I have encountered the World-Honored One and obtained these supreme merits;
born and dwelling in the heavens, I have received this retribution of golden hue.
Śakra Devānām Indra then praised him again with a verse:
"How marvelous is this field of merit, which eradicates all defilements and evils!
Those who plant the seeds therein are few, yet they obtain the most excellent retribution.
Who would not delight in making offerings to it, honoring this mass of pure gold?"
Who would not make offerings to the Buddha, the supreme and most excellent field of merit,
whose eyes are wide and long, resembling blue lotuses?
You were able in the past to offer worship to the foremost and most sublime Honored One.
"By performing wondrous deeds of merit, one obtains such a retribution.
At that time, the goddess immediately descended from heaven, carrying a flower parasol, and came to where the Buddha was;
having heard the Buddha preach the Dharma, she attained the purity of the Dharma-eye and returned to the heavens.
At that time, the bhikṣus asked the Buddha,
"What karmic actions did this woman perform in the past to receive such a retribution?
The Buddha said:
"In the past, by offering a magnificent lotus flower to the stupa of Kāśyapa Buddha, she obtained this supreme fruit and now beholds the traces of the Path.

53. The Story of the Heavenly Maiden Who Was Born in Heaven by Observing the Eight Precepts (LIII). The Story of the Heavenly Maiden Who Was Born in Heaven by Observing the Eight Precepts: At that time, there was another heavenly maiden who, having observed the eight precepts, was born in the heavens. She received the retribution of exquisite beauty; her radiant countenance and majestic appearance were far superior to those of the other hosts.
At that time, he was together with the devas, assembled in the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā). When the devas saw him, they were struck with wonder.
Śakra Devānām Indra questioned him with a verse:
"What karma did you perform in the past, That your body is like a mountain of pure gold?"
Your radiant countenance is most brilliant, And your complexion is like a pure lotus flower.
Having attained such supreme majesty and virtue, With what karmic conduct did you obtain this great and wondrous light emanating from your body?
“I pray that you will explain this to me.
At that time, the goddess answered with these verses:
“In the past, under Kāśyapa Buddha, I observed the eightfold precepts of the fast.”
Now I have been born among the gods, And obtained this reward of such exquisite beauty.
Śakra Devānām Indra further praised him with these verses:
“How marvelous is the field of merit! It is able to produce such supreme and wondrous retribution.”
In the past, by cultivating even slight causes, one was able to be born in the heavens.
Who would not offer worship to such a mass of supreme merit?
Who would not show reverence to one who is most supreme?
"Those who hear this should feel great joy;
those who wish to seek rebirth in heaven should maintain the pure precepts.
At that time, this deity, holding a beautiful flower parasol, came to where the Buddha was.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the Path of Seeing the Truths (*darśanamārga*).
At that time, the bhikṣus asked the Buddha:
"What meritorious deeds did this deva perform in the past to be born among the gods and yet attain the fruit of the noble ones?"
The Buddha said:
"In the past, when he was a human being, he observed the eight precepts under Kāśyapa Buddha. By virtue of this wholesome conduct, he was reborn in the heavens and attained the traces of the Path."

54. The Story of the Goddess’s Past Life Offering a Lamp to Dīpaṃkara Buddha (54) At that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, King Bimbisāra had attained the Path within the Buddha-dharma and acquired indestructible faith; he constantly made offerings of bright lamps to the Buddha.

Later, Devadatta became an evil associate of King Ajātaśatru and sought to harm the Buddha-dharma; consequently, the kingdom was filled with fear, and people no longer offered lamps as an act of worship.
There was a woman who, out of habit, lit a lamp as an offering at the head of the path where the Buddha walked during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony of the Saṃgha.

King Ajātaśatru, hearing of this, became extremely enraged and immediately slew her by cutting through her waist with a sword-wheel. At the end of her life, she was reborn in the Maṇi-jvālā palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; riding upon that palace, she proceeded to the Sudharmā Hall.
Śakra asked in verse:
"What karma did you perform in the past, that your body is like a mass of pure gold,
possessing such great majesty and virtue, and your countenance is so exceedingly radiant?"
The goddess immediately replied with a verse:
“The true savior of the three realms, The great lamp of the three existences—
With the eye of ultimate reality, I behold the Buddha, His body adorned with the marks and signs.”
The most supreme among all dharmas is to kindle the bright lamp;
as the lamp burns away the darkness, the Buddha-lamp extinguishes all evils.
Seeing this lamp like the light of the sun, one gives rise to true faith.
Beholding the lamp blazing with brilliance, he joyfully paid homage to the Buddha.
Having spoken this verse, he came to where the Buddha was; the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, immediately returning to the heavens.
A bhikṣu asked the Buddha,
"By what causes and conditions is one born in a celestial palace?
The Buddha said:

"In a former life when he was among humans, on the day of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony for the Saṃgha, he lit a lamp as an offering at the head of the path where the Buddha was walking; King Ajātaśatru then cut his waist and killed him."

By virtue of these wholesome causes, after his life ended, he was reborn among the devas; there, hearing the Dharma from me once again, he attained faith and understanding, and realized the stage of Srotāpanna.

55. The Story of the Girl Who Joyfully Yielded the Road upon Seeing the Buddha while Riding in a Carriage (55). At that time, the Buddha was in Śrāvastī. As he entered the city to beg for alms, there was a young girl riding in a carriage for recreation, intending to go toward a park. When she encountered the Tathāgata on the road, she turned her carriage to yield the way and gave rise to a heart of joy.
Thereafter, when his life ended, he was reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three and went to assemble in the Hall of Good Dharma.
Śakra Devānām-indra questioned him with a verse, saying:
"What deeds did you perform in the past, that your body’s color is like pure gold?"
Your radiant countenance is most brilliant, Like a blue utpala lotus;
having attained such supreme majesty, Why have you been born among the gods?
I pray that you will now explain to me: By what means was this obtained?
The goddess immediately replied with a verse:
"When I saw the Buddha enter the city, I turned my chariot to make way for him;
Filled with joy and born of reverent faith, At the end of my life, I was reborn in heaven."
Having spoken this verse, he went to where the Buddha was;
the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and having attained the stage of Srotāpanna, he immediately returned to his celestial palace.
A bhikṣu asked:
“By what karmic conditions was he born into this heavenly realm?

The Buddha said, “Formerly, while in the human world, he turned his chariot to avoid me; now he has attained birth in heaven. Out of great respect for me, he heard the Dharma and received it with faith, thereby realizing the fruit of Srotāpanna.”

56. The Story of the Goddess Who Offered Flowers to the Buddha, Which Transformed into a Canopy (56) At that time, in the city of Śrāvastī, there was a woman who, during a festival, gathered Aśoka flowers and was returning to the city when she encountered the Buddha as he went out. She immediately scattered these flowers over the Buddha, whereupon they transformed into a floral canopy. Overjoyed and leaping for happiness, she conceived a heart of reverence and faith.
Thereupon, his life came to an end, and he was reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three. Immediately mounting a celestial palace, he proceeded to the Sudharmā Hall.
Śakra, Lord of Devas, questioned him with a verse:
"What karma did you perform in the past, that you have attained birth among the gods?"
Your body is like the color of pure gold, and your majestic virtue is most radiant;
by what course of action was this obtained?
I pray that you will explain it to me.
The goddess then replied with a verse:
"In the past, in Jambudvīpa, I gathered Aśoka flowers;
returning, I encountered the Tathāgata and immediately made an offering to the Buddha."
Filled with joy and giving rise to profound respect, he was reborn in heaven at the end of his life.
Having spoken this verse, he came to where the Buddha was;
the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and having attained the stage of Srotāpanna, he returned to the heavens.
The bhikṣu asked:
"By what causes and conditions did this heavenly maiden obtain this celestial body?
The Buddha said:
"In the past, while among humans, he went out of the city to gather *aśoka* flowers; on his way back, he encountered me and immediately offered those flowers to me, giving rise to a heart of joy."
"By virtue of this wholesome karma, at the end of his life he was reborn in heaven; there, out of deep respect for me, he heard the Dharma and attained awakening, realizing the stage of Srotāpanna.

57. The Story of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana Making Offerings to a Stūpa (57) King Bimbisāra, having already realized the Truths, frequently went to the Buddha’s presence to pay homage and inquire after his well-being.

At that time, the women of the palace were unable to come to the Buddha's side every day; therefore, the king used the Buddha’s hair to erect a stūpa within the palace, which the people of the palace constantly made offerings to.
When King Bimbisāra passed away, Devadatta and King Ajātaśatru became close allies; harboring a mind of slander, they prohibited the offerings made within the palace to this stūpa.
There was a palace lady named Śāriputramātṛ who, on the day of the Saṃgha’s *pravāraṇā*, recalled her former practices and immediately made offerings of incense and flowers to this stūpa.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru, resentful of his offerings to the Buddha’s stūpa, used a drill to bore him to death.
Upon the end of his life, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where he ascended a celestial palace and gathered at the Sudharmā Hall.
Śakra questioned him with a verse:
"What merit did you perform in the past, That you have been born among the gods,
With such majestic power and great radiance, Resplendent like the color of pure gold?"
"What kind of karmic actions must one perform to obtain this? Please explain it to me.
The goddess replied to him in verse:
"In the past, when I was among humans, with a heart of joy and reverence,
I made offerings of various fine incenses and flowers to the Buddha’s stūpa;
yet for the sake of Ajātaśatru, they used a drill to bore into and kill me."
"At the end of his life, he was reborn in heaven, where he experienced this supreme bliss.
Having spoken this verse, he went to where the Buddha was;
the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of Srotāpanna, immediately returning to his celestial palace.
The bhikṣu asked,
"By what causes and conditions was this heaven born?
The Buddha said:
"Based on her human existence, she once offered flowers and incense to a Buddhist stūpa.
By virtue of this wholesome karma, she has now attained a celestial body; having again heard the Dharma from me, she has awakened and realized the stage of Srotāpanna."

58. The Story of the Elder and His Wife Building a Stūpa and Rebirth in Heaven (58). In the city of Śrāvastī, there was an elder who constructed a stūpa and a monastery. The elder fell ill and, upon his death, was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

The wife, remembering her husband, was filled with sorrow, anxiety, and distress; because of these memories, she maintained the stupa and the monastic quarters just as she had when her husband was alive.
While her husband was in the heavens, he observed and said:
"By what cause have I been born here in this heaven?"
He realized that it was by virtue of the merit of constructing stūpas and temples that he had come to this place.

Seeing for himself that he was indeed a celestial being, his heart was filled with joy; he constantly kept the stūpas and temples in mind and, observing them with his divine eye, wondered: "Who is now maintaining these stūpas and temples that were built?"
He then saw his wife, who day and night remembered her husband and was filled with sorrow and distress; for the sake of her husband, she was repairing a stupa and temple.
The husband thought to himself:
"My wife has performed great meritorious deeds for my sake; I should now go to where she is to inquire after her and comfort her."
He vanished from the heavens and appeared immediately by the woman's side, saying to her,
"You are greatly distressed and thinking of me.
The woman replied:
"Who are you that exhorts and admonishes me?
He replied:

"I am your husband. Because of the causes and conditions of constructing monasteries and stūpas, I have been reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three. Seeing that you are diligently repairing the stūpa and monastery, I have come to your side."
The wife said,
"Come forward and have intercourse with me.
The husband said:

“The human body is foul and impure; it can no longer be approached. If you wish to be my wife, simply diligently make offerings to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus. After your life ends, you will be reborn in my celestial palace, and I shall take you as my wife.”
The wife followed her husband’s words, making offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha, performing various meritorious deeds, and vowing to be reborn in heaven.
Subsequently, when her life ended, she was immediately reborn in that celestial palace. The husband and wife went together to the presence of the Buddha;
the Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
The bhikṣus, marveling at the reason for this, asked:
"By what karmic causes and conditions was birth in this heaven attained?
The Buddha said:
"In the past, while among humans, I built Buddhist monasteries and provided offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha. By virtue of this merit, I have now attained birth in heaven.

(59) The Story of the Elder and His Wife Who Attained Birth in Heaven through Faithful Reverence for the Buddha. In the city of Rājagṛha, there was an elder who went daily to the presence of the Buddha.
His wife became suspicious and thought to herself,
"He must be having an illicit affair with another woman, for he goes away every single day.
She then questioned her husband, saying:
"Where do you go and from where do you return every single day?
The husband replied to his wife,
"I go to and come from the presence of the Buddha."
He asked, "Is the Buddha superior to you in beauty or ugliness?
Yet you always go to his side."
The husband then spoke to his wife, extolling the various merits of the Buddha.
At that time, having heard of the Buddha’s merits, the wife felt great joy in her heart and immediately set out by carriage.

Having arrived at the place where the Buddha was, there were at that time various kings and great ministers surrounding him on all sides, so crowded that they could not advance; they paid homage to the Buddha from afar and then returned to the city.
Thereafter, when his lifespan ended, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, whereupon he thought to himself:
"The Buddha’s grace is profound; by the merit of a single prostration, I have been made to be born in heaven."
He immediately descended from heaven and went to the Buddha’s side; the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.
A bhikṣu asked:
“By what causes and conditions were you born into this heaven?”
The Buddha said: "In a former life among humans, she paid me homage. By the merit of that single prostration, at the end of her life, she was reborn in heaven. 60.

The Story of the Non-Buddhist Brahmin Woman Who Became a Disciple of the Buddha, Performed a Feast Offering, and Was Reborn in Heaven (60). The Story of the Non-Buddhist Brahmin Woman Who Became a Disciple of the Buddha, Performed a Feast Offering, and Was Reborn in Heaven. At that time in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there were various disciples of the Buddha; a woman organized a village assembly and went frequently to the presence of the Buddha.
Among the companions was a Brahmin woman who held heterodox views and lacked faith; she had never observed the fasts or maintained the precepts.
Seeing the women gathered together for a meal, she asked, "What auspicious assembly are you holding now?"
"You are close and intimate with us, yet you do not invite me.
The women replied,
"We are performing a ritual fast (upavāsa)."
The Brahmin woman said, "Today is neither the sixth nor the twelfth day of the lunar month; for whose sake is this fast being observed?
The women replied:
"I am performing a Buddhist feast.
The Brahmin woman asked,
"By performing this Buddhist feast, what merit do you obtain?"
He replied,
"One attains rebirth in heaven and liberation.
Because the Brahmin woman was greedy for food and drink, she accepted water to serve as a meal offering and later gave her excellent, delicious beverages.

The fasting method of the Brahmins consists of neither drinking nor eating; however, the fasting method of the Buddha involves eating fine food and drinking delicious beverages. This fast is very easy, giving rise to faith, joy, and gladness.
Later, when his life came to an end, he was reborn in the heavens. He came before the Buddha, who preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.
A bhikṣu asked:
"By what causes and conditions were you born among the devas?"
The Buddha said:

"In the past, while among humans, you saw various women gathering to perform a *śrāddha* feast; you rejoiced in their performance of the feast. By virtue of this wholesome karma, you have been reborn in heaven."
61. The Story of the Poor Woman Who Gave a Piece of Cotton Cloth to Sudatta and Was Reborn in Heaven (61) At that time, the householder Sudatta had this thought:
"Those born into my family do not fall into the evil realms after their lives end. Why is this?"

Because I have taught them exclusively the pure dharmas, they have fallen into poverty and hardship, whether they have faith or lack it; I shall now likewise teach them the wholesome dharmas so that they may make offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha.
Thereupon, he reported all these matters in detail to King Prasenajit. The king immediately had the drums beaten and the bells rung.
Seven days later, the Elder Sudatta intended to solicit offerings for the Triple Gem; all the people rejoiced accordingly and each gave as much as they could.
When the seventh day arrived, the elder Sudatta went among the people to solicit alms for their conversion.

There was a poor woman who, having worked with great hardship to earn a price, had obtained only a single piece of cotton cloth to cover her body; seeing Sudatta begging, she immediately gave it to him as an offering.
Having received [the gift], Sudatta marveled at her capability and provided her with whatever she desired—money, grain, silk, clothing, and food—to her heart's content.

Later, when the poor woman’s lifespan ended and her life was over, she was reborn in the heavens. She came before the Buddha, who preached the Dharma for her, and she attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.
The bhikṣu asked,
“By what causes and conditions has this celestial maiden been born in the heavens?
The Buddha said:

"In the past, while among human beings, he encountered the elder Sudatta teaching those who begged for alms; his heart was filled with joy, and he immediately offered the white cotton cloth he was wearing as a gift to Sudatta."
"By virtue of these wholesome karmas, she was reborn in the heavens; there, having heard the Dharma from me once more, she attained faith and understanding, and realized the fruit of Srotāpanna. 62.

The Story of the Elder’s Daughter Who Did Not Believe in the Triple Gem, but Was Hired with Gold Coins by Her Father to Uphold the Five Precepts and Be Reborn in Heaven (62). At that time, in the city of Śrāvastī, there was an elder named Puṣya who had two daughters. One of them left the household life; through diligent practice, she attained Arhatship.
The other held wrong views, slandering and disbelieving the teachings.
Her father then said to this woman who lacked faith:

"If you now take refuge in the Buddha, I shall pay you a thousand gold coins; even if you go on to take refuge in the Dharma and the Sangha and receive and uphold the five precepts, I shall give you eight thousand gold coins."
Thereupon, he received the five precepts.
Before long, his life came to an end and he was reborn in heaven. He then came to where the Buddha was; the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
The bhikṣu asked:
"By what karmic actions did this goddess attain birth in the heavens?
The Buddha said:
"Originally a human being, he coveted his father's wealth; having turned toward the Triple Gem, he received and upheld the five precepts.
By these causes and conditions, he has now attained birth in heaven; out of deep respect for me, he heard the Dharma and realized the Path."

63. The Story of the Girl Who Attained Rebirth in Heaven through Joy upon Seeing the Buddha while Sweeping the Ground (63). According to the custom of South India, whenever there was a young girl in a household, she was invariably made to rise early and sweep the courtyard clean, as well as the areas to the left and right of the gate.

There was the daughter of an elder who rose early to sweep the ground. She happened to encounter the Tathāgata as he passed by her door; seeing him, she felt great joy and gazed at the Buddha with focused attention.
Her lifespan being short, she immediately passed away and was reborn in heaven.
Now, those born in the heavens possess three reflections by law; they reflect to themselves, saying:
"What was my original body?
and they know for themselves that it was a human body.
"Where have you been reborn in this life?
"I know for certain that it is in the heavens.
"What karma did you perform in the past to be born here?"
He realized that this retribution was obtained through the wholesome karma of seeing the Buddha with joy.
Moved by the Buddha’s profound kindness, he came to make offerings to the Buddha; the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
The bhikṣus asked:
"By what causes and conditions did this woman attain rebirth in heaven and realize the Way?
The Buddha said:
"In a former life among humans, she rose early to sweep the ground. When she encountered the Buddha passing her door, she felt a heart of joy.
By virtue of this wholesome karma, she was reborn in the heavens; furthermore, in my presence, she heard the Dharma and realized the Path."

64. The Story of the Elder Who Built a House, Invited the Buddha for Offerings, and Was Reborn in Heaven by Giving the House (64). In the city of Rājagṛha, there was a great elder who had newly constructed a house. He invited the Buddha to offer him hospitality and, having made the offering, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"From this day forward, whenever you enter the city, after washing your hands and bowl, always come here.

Later, when his life came to an end, he was reborn in the heavens; riding upon a celestial palace, he came to the place where the Buddha was, and as the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
The bhikṣu said:
"By what causes and conditions is one reborn in the heavens?
The Buddha said:
"In the past, while among humans, he built a new dwelling and invited the Buddha to receive its offering.
By virtue of this wholesome karma, he was reborn in a celestial palace; subsequently, in my presence, he heard the Dharma and attained the Way."

65. The Story of the Wife Who Offered Sugarcane to an Arhat and Was Reborn in Heaven (65) In the past, in the city of Śrāvastī, there was an arhat bhikṣu who entered the city to beg for alms and came upon the house of a sugarcane presser.
The daughter-in-law of that household placed a large, coarse stalk of sugarcane into the bhikṣu’s alms bowl.

When her mother-in-law saw this, she became angry and seized a staff to beat her; it struck the vital channel at her waist, and she died instantly, being reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven with a female body, dwelling in a palace made entirely of sugarcane.
When the assembly of devas gathered in the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā), those celestial maidens also assembled in this hall. Śakra questioned them with a verse:
"What karma did you perform in the past, That you have obtained such a wondrous body?
Your radiant form is peerless, Like a mass of molten gold."
The goddess replied with a verse:
"In the past, when I was among humans, I gave a small amount of sugarcane as an offering;
now I have obtained this great fruit and reward, dwelling amidst the hosts of devas."
The radiance was exceedingly brilliant and dazzling.

(66) The Story of a Woman Who Was Reborn in Heaven for Anointing the Buddha’s Feet with Incense. Long ago, in the city of Śrāvastī, there was a woman who sat on the ground grinding incense. She encountered the Buddha as he entered the city; upon seeing the Buddha’s body, she felt a heart of joy and took the incense she had been grinding and anointed the Buddha’s feet.
Thereafter, when his life ended, he was reborn in the heavens; the fragrance of his body wafted afar, reaching four thousand li, as he proceeded to assemble in the Hall of True Dharma.
Śakra, the Lord of Devas, questioned him with a verse:
"What merit did you perform in the past, That your body emits such subtle and wondrous fragrance?"
“Having been born among the gods, why is your radiance like molten gold?
The goddess then replied in verse:
“With the most excellent incense, I made offerings to the Most Victorious Honored One.”
Attaining peerless majesty and virtue, they are born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and experience great bliss.
Their fragrance is heard for a hundred yojanas; all who smell it, [are transformed].
"Everyone has obtained great benefit.
At that moment, the goddess approached the World-Honored One; the Buddha preached the Dharma for her, and she attained the stage of Srotāpanna before returning to the heavens.
The bhikṣus asked,
"What merit did you perform in the past to be born among the devas with a body as fragrant as this?
The Buddha said:
"Because this goddess, while formerly in the human realm, anointed my feet with perfume, by this causal condition, she passed away and was reborn in heaven to receive this karmic retribution."

67. The Story of the Maidservant of the Elder Sudatta Taking Refuge in the Triple Gem and Rebirth in Heaven (67). At that time, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, the Elder Sudatta hired people with one hundred thousand *niṣkas* of gold to take refuge in the Buddha.
At that time, there was a maidservant who, upon hearing the householder’s words, immediately took refuge in the Buddha.
After her life ended, she was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, whereupon she went to assemble in the Sudharmā Hall.
Śakra asked in verse:
"What merit did you possess in your past life, that you have been born among the devas with such subtle and wondrous radiance?"
"Now, please explain this to me.
The goddess replied with a verse:
"The most steadfast and supreme within the three realms, capable of uprooting the suffering of birth and death,"
The true deliverance from the three realms, Severing the bonds of the three defilements—
In the past, I took refuge in the Buddha, As well as in the Dharma and the Saṅgha;
By reason of these causes and conditions, I have obtained this karmic fruition.
Having spoken this verse, he came to where the Buddha was. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
A bhikṣu asked:
"By what karmic conditions did he receive this retribution?"

The Buddha said, "In the past, among human beings, because he took refuge in the Buddha, he has now attained birth in the heavens; having encountered my preaching of the Dharma, he has attained the stage of Srotāpanna."

68. The Story of the Poor Woman Who Begged Food from the Buddha and Was Reborn in Heaven (68). Once, in the city of Śrāvastī, there was a woman who was impoverished and distressed; she constantly lived by begging at the roadside.
As time passed, no one among the people would look upon her.

When the Buddha encountered her walking along, he went to her side; seeing that the poor woman was so destitute and starving she was on the verge of death, he felt compassion for her and immediately instructed Ānanda to give her food.
At that time, this poor woman, having received the food, was filled with joy; she subsequently passed away and was reborn in the heavens.
Moved by the Buddha’s past kindness, she came to make offerings to the Buddha. The Buddha preached the Dharma for her, and she attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
The bhikṣus asked the Buddha,
"By what causes and conditions has this heavenly maiden been born in the heavens?
The Buddha said:

"This goddess, in her former life as a human being, was on the verge of death from hunger and starvation; the Buddha sent Ānanda to give her food, and once she had received it, joy arose in her heart."
"By virtue of these roots of goodness, at the end of his life he was reborn in this celestial palace; out of deep respect for me, he heard the Dharma and attained the Way.

69. The Story of the Elder’s Maid Who, While Delivering Food for Her Master, Encountered the Buddha, Made an Offering, and Received the Reward of Rebirth in Heaven (69). In the city of Śrāvastī, there was the son of an elder who was playing in a garden together with other sons of elders.
When he was about to depart, he said to his family members,
"Send me food. Later, the family sent a maidservant to deliver the food.
When the maidservant reached the gate, she encountered the Buddha and immediately offered her food to the Tathāgata.
She returned home, took more food, and went to offer it again; yet on the way, she met Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others, and gave it to them as well.
For the third time, he took food and gave it to the elder’s son.
When the elder’s son had finished eating, he returned home on his own and said to his wife,
"Why was the food sent today so extremely late?"
The wife replied to him, "Today I have passed by three times to bring you food; for what reason have you been so late?
She then called her maidservant and questioned her:
"Whom did you give the food to when you went out three times this morning?
The maidservant then replied,
"The first time I sent the food, I encountered the Buddha and gave it to him as an offering."
When she sent food for the second time, she saw Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others, and gave it to them as well;
when she took the food for the third time, she finally gave it to her mistress.
Upon hearing this, the mistress became extremely enraged and struck her with a staff; she died instantly and was reborn in the heavens.
When first born in the heavens, one forms three thoughts: first, one thinks to oneself, "Where have I now been born?
and realizes for oneself that one has been born in the heavens;
second, one thinks to oneself, "From where did I pass away?"
Having been reborn in the heavens, he knows that he was born in the celestial realm from the human realm.
Third, he reflects to himself: "By what karmic conditions have I attained birth in the heavens?"

Realizing that he had obtained this karmic fruit through the gift of food, he came to the Buddha’s presence to make offerings and pay his respects. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
A bhikṣu then asked the Buddha:
“By what causes and conditions was this heavenly maiden born in the heavens?
The Buddha said:

“In her previous life among humans, she was the servant of an elder. While delivering food for the elder’s son, she encountered the Tathāgata Buddha and immediately offered it to him. Her mistress became enraged and beat her to death with a staff.”
"By virtue of these karmic conditions, at the end of his life he was reborn in heaven, and furthermore, in my presence, he heard the Dharma and realized the Path.

70. The Story of the Elder Who Built a Lecture Hall for the Buddha and Received the Reward of Rebirth in Heaven. At that time, in the city of Rājagṛha, King Bimbisāra built a stūpa and monastic quarters for the Buddha.

There was an elder who also wished to build a fine dwelling for the Buddha, but being unable to obtain land, he instead constructed a lecture hall at the place where the Tathāgata used to walk; the hall had four gates opening upon it.

Later, when his life came to an end, he was reborn in the heavens; riding upon a celestial palace, he came to make offerings to the Buddha. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
The bhikṣu asked,
"By what karmic conditions has this devaputra been born in the celestial palace?
The Buddha said:
"Originally, while among humans, he constructed a lecture hall for the Buddha; by virtue of this wholesome cause, at the end of his life he was reborn in heaven.
Having come to my place, he expressed his gratitude and made offerings, and upon hearing the Dharma again, he attained the stage of Srotāpanna."

71. The Story of the Elder Who, Seeing the King Build a Stūpa, Also Built a Stūpa and Received the Reward of Rebirth in Heaven (71). At that time, in South India, on the south side of Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, there was an elder who saw that King Bimbisāra had built a fine stūpa and monastery for the Buddha. He also invited the Tathāgata and, for his sake, constructed a stūpa and a dwelling place consisting of monastic cells.

Subsequently, when his life ended, he was reborn in the heavens. He came to where the Buddha was to offer a meal in gratitude for the Buddha's kindness. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.
A bhikṣu asked:
"By what causes and conditions did this devaputra attain birth in the celestial palace in days past?"
The Buddha said:
"Formerly, when he was among humans, he saw a king erecting a stupa; his heart gave rise to sympathetic joy, and he immediately invited the Tathāgata to construct a pagoda."
"By virtue of this wholesome karma, he was reborn in the heavens; furthermore, having heard the Dharma from me, he attained faith and realization, becoming a Srotāpanna. 72.

The Story of the Merchant Who Built a Hall for the Buddha and Received the Reward of Rebirth in Heaven (72). The Story of the Merchant Who Built a Hall for the Buddha and Received the Reward of Rebirth in Heaven: At that time, there was a merchant in Śrāvastī who traveled far away on business and died without returning.
The mother raised her son, and when he had grown up, he wished to travel far away.
His grandmother said to him:
"Your father went far away and died without returning; do not go far away yourself, but stay near here and sit in a shop in the marketplace."
He immediately followed his instructions and set up a merchant’s stall in the marketplace, thinking to himself:
"The people of this city have all invited the Buddha; now that I have newly constructed my house, I too shall invite the Tathāgata."
He then went to invite the Buddha.
Once the Buddha had arrived, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I offer this house to the Tathāgata; from this day forward, whenever you enter the city, please always come to my house to wash your hands and your bowl."
Subsequently, when his life came to an end, he was reborn in the heavens. He came to where the Buddha was, and the Buddha preached the Dharma for him; he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
A bhikṣu asked:
"By what karmic causes and conditions did this deva attain rebirth in the heavens in his previous life?"
The Buddha said, "In a former life as a human, he newly constructed a dwelling and invited the Buddha to stay within it.
By virtue of this wholesome karma, he has now been reborn among the devas; furthermore, having heard the Dharma from me, he has obtained this retribution."
*Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka Sūtra*, Scroll Five;
*Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka Sūtra*, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Ki-carya of the Western Regions under the Yuan Wei dynasty, together with Tanyao.
The Circumstances of Śakra’s Questions (73) Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Magadha, south of Rājagṛha, in a brahmin village named Āmrapālīvana.
To the north of this village, within a stone cave on Mount Vaidehaka, [the Buddha resided].
At that time, Śakra, hearing that the Buddha was there, addressed the Gandharva prince Pañcaśikha, saying:

"In the kingdom of Magadha, there is a brahmin village named Āmrapālīvana. To the north of this village is Mount Vaidehaka, where the World-Honored One resides. You should now go there together with us."
The Gandharva prince Pañcaśikha replied,
"Indeed, this is most excellent.
Rejoicing and eager to hear [the teaching], he immediately took up his lapis lazuli lute and followed Śakra to the place where the Buddha was.

At that time, when the various devas heard that Śakra, together with the Gandharva princes and others, intended to go to the Buddha’s dwelling, they each adorned themselves and followed Śakra; vanishing from the heavens, they immediately arrived at Mount Vaideha.
At that time, the mountain was illuminated by a brilliant light; those sages nearby all thought it was the glow of a fire.
Śakra then addressed the Gandharva prince, saying:

"This place is pure and far removed from all evils. It is a forest retreat (*āraṇyaka*) where one may sit in meditation in peace. Now, near the Buddha, there are many noble and eminent devas, crowding his presence and filling his surroundings."
"How may we now have the fortune to behold the World-Honored One?
Śakra then addressed the Gandharva prince:
"You should go to the Buddha's dwelling on my behalf to convey our intention, that we wish to come and pay our respects and inquire after him."

The Gandharva prince, having received these instructions, went forth immediately; neither too far nor too near, he gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance, took up his lute and played it so that the Buddha might hear, and recited this verse:
"Desire gives rise to attachment, Like an elephant sinking into the mud, Or like an elephant intoxicated with madness— It cannot be restrained by a hook."
Just as an Arhat yearns for the sublime Dharma, and as I,
craving beauty, reverently prostrate before my father;
because he was born of noble and exalted lineage, my heart feels a twofold increase of love and joy.
"You greatly increase my love, like cool breezes meeting hot sweat,
or like one who is parched with thirst finding a cold drink. Your physical form is most delightful,
like an Arhat rejoicing in the Dharma, or like a sick person obtaining excellent medicine."
Like one who is hungry obtaining fine food, may this quickly extinguish my fever with its coolness;
though my greed now still wishes to rush away, it is as if it seizes my heart so that I cannot go.
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, Pañcaśikha!"
"Now that this sound has been made, with the strings and pipes in harmony, you should compose songs and hymns from near and far.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the past, I encountered a virtuous woman named Śūlipāñcālī, who was the daughter of the Gandharva King Bhīmāratha."

The Mātarali devaputra named Śikhaṇḍin previously sought that maiden; at that time, being filled with affection for her, I spoke these verses in her presence. Now, before the Buddha, I shall once again recite those original verses.
Śakra thought to himself:
"The Buddha has arisen from his meditative absorption and is now conversing with Pañcaśikha.
Śakra then spoke again to Pañcaśikha:
"You should now utter my name, prostrate at the Buddha's feet, and inquire after the World-Honored One:
'Are you free from illness and affliction? Are your daily activities light and easy? Is your diet harmonious? Are your physical strength and well-being secure? And are you free from all evils?'"
"Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?
He then replied with these words.
Having received Śakra’s instruction, he went again to the place where the Buddha was, announced Śakra’s name, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and conveyed Śakra’s greetings to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said,
"Śakra and all the devas, are they all at peace and well?
He addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Śakra and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven wish to see the Buddha; may they be permitted to come and see him?
The Buddha said:
"Now is precisely the right time.

Having heard the Buddha's instruction, Śakra and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Where should I sit?
The Buddha said,
"Sit upon this seat."
He addressed the Buddha, saying, “This cave is extremely small, yet the assembly of devas is extremely large.
Having spoken these words, he saw that through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, the stone cave had become vast and spacious, capable of accommodating many.
Śakra immediately prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat before him, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Throughout the long night, I have constantly desired to see the Buddha and to hear the Dharma.”

In the past, when the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, he entered the fire-light samādhi. At that time, there was a female attendant of Vaiśravaṇa named Puṣpavatī. Puṣpavatī joined her palms toward the Buddha, and I then said to that female attendant of Vaiśravaṇa:
"The Buddha is now in meditative concentration; I do not dare disturb him. For my sake, prostrate at the feet of the World-Honored One and convey my greetings."
The goddess, following the words of Śakra, paid homage and inquired after his well-being.
The Buddha said to Śakra:
"At that time, upon hearing your voices, I arose from meditative concentration before long."
Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the past, I heard from those of long standing that when a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world, the hosts of devas increase and the hosts of asuras decrease."
"Today I have personally been born among the devas; the hosts of devas increase while the asuras decrease.

Now that I see the disciples of the Buddha who have attained birth in the heavens, they surpass the other devas in three respects: their lifespan is superior, their radiance and complexion are superior, and their renown is superior."
At that time, the Jewel Woman Viśeṣamati was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; having previously been a disciple of the Buddha, she became a son of Śakra, named the Devaputra Ghoṣadatta.

Furthermore, there were three bhikṣus who practiced the holy life (brahmacarya) before the Buddha; though their minds were not yet free from desire, at the dissolution of the body after death, they were reborn into the family of gandharvas, serving as messengers for the devas three times every day.
Perhaps a certain deva, seeing these three men acting as servants, will say:

"My heart finds this neither pleasing nor endurable. In the past, when I was formerly among humans, those three men would constantly come to my home and receive my offerings; yet today they serve as attendants to the various devas."
I cannot bear to see this.

These three gods were originally śrāvaka disciples of the Buddha; when I was formerly a human being, they received my respectful offerings of food, drink, clothing, and robes. Today, having fallen into such lowly and base states, how is it that you—having heard the Dharma from the Buddha’s own mouth and being liberated by him—have been reborn in such a vulgar and despicable place?

"In the past, I served and made offerings to you; however, I followed the Buddha, heard the Dharma, and practiced generosity. Because I have faith in causes and conditions, I am now a son of Śakra, possessing great majesty and power, with sovereign authority, and all the devas call me Kauśika."
"You have attained the supreme Dharma of the Buddha; why then could you not practice with diligent mind, yet instead take birth in such a lowly place?
I cannot now bear to witness this evil matter; I do not rejoice at seeing such a thing."
"How is it that within this same Dharma, one is born into such a lowly station?
This is a place where a disciple of the Buddha should not have been born.
When Kuho (Kauśika) the Devaputra spoke these words of censure, these three individuals were deeply ashamed and felt a sense of revulsion; they joined their palms and said to Kuho:
"As the Devaputra has said, this is truly my fault; I shall now sever such evil desires.
He then applied himself with diligent effort, cultivating meditative concentration and wisdom.

The three men, reflecting upon the Dharma of Gautama and seeing the faults and perils of desire, immediately severed the fetters of lust; just as a great elephant breaks free from its tether, so too did they sever their greed and desire.

Śakra, along with the god Sunirmita and the rest of the celestial hosts, as well as the Four World-Protecting Kings, all came to this seat; these three who had severed desire then soared into the midst of the sky before all the gods.
Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what dharma have these three men attained such power that they are able to perform these various miraculous transformations?
They have come to see the World-Honored One, wishing to inquire about what they have attained."
The Buddha said,
“These three persons, having abandoned that place, have attained rebirth in the Brahma world.
[They replied,] “We only pray, World-Honored One!”
"Explain to me the method for being born in the Brahma-heaven.
"Excellent, O worthy Śakra!
You have asked about your doubt with discernment."
At that time, the Buddha thought to himself:
"Śakra is free from flattery and deceit; he asks about his doubts with sincerity. He does not seek to trouble or disturb me. As for what you ask, I shall explain it in detail."
Śakra asked the Buddha:
"What are these fetters that are able to bind humans, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, and mahoragas?"
The Buddha then replied:
“The two fetters of greed and envy bind humans, devas, asuras, gandharvas, and all other classes of beings; they are all bound by themselves through greed and envy.”
"It is indeed so, O God among Gods!
The causes and conditions of greed and envy can bind all beings. Having now heard this meaning from the Buddha, the net of my doubts has been removed."
Deeply filled with joy, he further inquired about other matters:
"From what cause does greed and envy arise?
By what cause and by what condition are greed and envy produced?"
“By what causes and conditions does it arise?
By what causes and conditions does it cease? “Kauśika!

“Greed and envy arise from hatred and attachment; hatred and attachment act as their conditions. Where there is hatred and attachment, greed and envy necessarily exist; where there is no hatred and attachment, greed and envy are extinguished.
“It is truly so, O God among Gods!”
"Now that I have heard this meaning from the Buddha, the net of my doubts has been removed.
Feeling profound joy, he asked further about another matter:
"By what causes and conditions do love and hatred arise?"
"By what causes and conditions are they extinguished? He replied:
"Love and hatred arise from desire; when there is no desire, they are extinguished."
“It is truly so, O God among Gods!
Having heard this meaning from the Buddha, my faith and understanding have arisen, and the net of doubt has been removed.
Feeling profound joy, he further asked about another point of doctrine:
"From what cause does desire arise?
By what condition does it increase?
How is it extinguished?"
The Buddha said:

"Desire arises because of applied thought (*vitarka*); it increases conditioned by sustained thought (*vicāra*). Where there is applied and sustained thought, there is desire; where there is no applied and sustained thought, desire ceases."
"It is truly so, O God among Gods!
Having now heard this meaning from the Buddha and understood it, the net of my doubts has been removed.
Deeply filled with joy, he further asked about another matter:
“From what cause do vitarka and vicāra arise?
By what condition do they increase?
How are they extinguished?”
“Initial and sustained application of thought arise from frivolity; they increase by taking frivolity as their condition. When frivolity is absent, initial and sustained application of thought cease.
“It is so, O God among Gods!”
"Having now heard this meaning from the Buddha, my net of doubts has been removed.
Feeling profound joy, he further asked about another matter:
"By what causes does frivolous play arise and grow?"
"How does one extinguish frivolous chatter?
The Buddha told Kauśika:

"To extinguish frivolous chatter, one should cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path: right view, right action, right speech, right livelihood, right effort, right thought, right mindfulness, and right concentration."
Having heard this, Śakra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is truly so, O God among Gods!
That frivolity is indeed extinguished by means of the Eightfold Noble Path. Having now heard this meaning from the Buddha, the net of my doubts has been removed."
Śakra rejoiced and further asked about another matter:
“One who wishes to extinguish frivolous play can cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path. By what further dharma, O Bhikṣu, does this Eightfold Noble Path increase?”
The Buddha said:
"Furthermore, there are three dharmas:
first, aspiration; second, right diligence; and third, frequent practice of mental concentration."
Śakra said: “It is truly so, O God among Gods!
Having heard this teaching, the net of our doubts has been removed.”
“A bhikṣu who is able to practice the factors of the right path truly increases by means of these three things.
Having heard this, he was filled with joy. Śakra then asked again:
“If a bhikṣu wishes to extinguish frivolity, how many dharmas should he study?”
The Buddha said:
"You should train in three dharmas.
You should train in increasing the mind of ethical discipline, you should train in increasing the mind of concentration, and you should train in increasing the mind of wisdom."
Having heard this, Śakra said:
"It is truly so, O God among Gods!
Having heard this teaching, the net of my doubts has been removed."
Leaping for joy, he asked further regarding another meaning:
"To extinguish frivolity, how many meanings should I understand when I hear [the teaching]?
The Buddha said:

"One should understand six meanings: first, eye-consciousness cognizes forms; second, ear-consciousness cognizes sounds; third, nose-consciousness cognizes odors; fourth, tongue-consciousness cognizes tastes; fifth, body-consciousness cognizes tactile sensations; and sixth, mind-consciousness cognizes all phenomena."
Having heard this, Śakra said:
"It is truly so, O God among Gods!
Having heard this meaning, the net of my doubts has been removed."
Filled with joy and exultation, he further asked about another matter:
"Do all sentient beings share the same greed, the same desire, the same inclination, and the same destination?
The Buddha said:

"Śakra! All sentient beings do not have a single greed, a single desire, a single direction, or a single destination. Sentient beings are immeasurable and worlds are immeasurable; their inclinations and aspirations differ and are not the same, as each clings to their own views."
Having heard this, Śakra said:
“It is truly so, O God among Gods!
Having heard this teaching, the net of my doubts has been removed.”
Filled with joy and exultation, he asked further about other matters:
"Have all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas attained ultimate perfection?
Have they attained the one stainless state?"
"Can one attain the ultimate, final Brahma-faring?
The Buddha said,
"None of the śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas can fully attain that which is ultimately one and stainless, nor can they attain the ultimate, final Brahma-faring."

If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who have attained the unsurpassed liberation through the eradication of the fetters of craving, and have attained perfect liberation, they have fully realized the one ultimate goal, the one stainless state, and the one ultimate holy life.

“As the Buddha has taught, for one who has attained liberation through the supreme severance of the fetters of craving and has achieved right liberation, this constitutes the attainment of the single ultimate end, the single stainless state, and the single ultimate holy life.”

Having now heard this from the Buddha, I have immediately understood its meaning; having attained this Dharma, I have crossed to the further shore beyond doubt, have extracted the poisonous arrows of all views, and having already eliminated the view of self, my mind shall never regress.
When this sutra was being spoken, Śakra and eighty-four thousand devas were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
The Buddha said: “Kauśika!
“Have you ever asked this question of any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas?
“World-Honored One!
I recall that in the past, while gathered with various devas in the Sudharmā Hall, I once asked those devas whether a Buddha had appeared in the world.”
The various devas each said, "No Buddha has yet appeared.
Hearing that no Buddha had emerged in the world, they each dispersed; those devas of great majesty and virtue reached the end of their lives as their merit was exhausted.
At that time, being terrified, I saw a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa in a secluded place; I went to him, and that śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa asked me, "Who are you?"
I said, "This is Śakra.
I did not bow to him, but he bowed to me in return.
I have not yet questioned him, but he has questioned me.
Knowing him to be without wisdom, I therefore do not take refuge in him.
I now go from here to take refuge in the Buddha as his disciple.
He then spoke these verses:
"I have long harbored doubts, My thoughts remained unsatisfied.
Through the long night I sought a wise one To resolve such doubts as these."
Seeking out the Tathāgata, he saw various ascetics and brahmins in secluded places;
thinking they were the World-Honored One,
he went immediately to their locations, paid his respects, and inquired after their well-being.
I asked this question: "How does one cultivate the true path?
Those śramaṇas do not understand what is the path and what is not the path."
Now that I behold the World-Honored One, the net of my doubts is entirely severed.
Today there is indeed a Buddha, a great teacher of the world,
who destroys and subdues the enemy Māra and has utterly exhausted all afflictions.
The World-Honored One has appeared in the world;
rare and peerless, among all the hosts of devas and Brahmās, there is none who is like the Buddha.
“World-Honored One!”
"I have attained the stage of Srotāpanna,
Blessed One! I have attained the stage of Srotāpanna!"
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent, excellent, Kauśika!"
"If you are not negligent, you shall attain the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin.
The Buddha said to Śakra:
"In what place did you obtain this indestructible faith?"
Śakra addressed him, saying:
"I obtained this from the World-Honored One; I have now further attained this divine life-span. I only pray that you will awaken to and remember this matter."
Śakra said: “World-Honored One!
I have now had this thought:”
"One shall be born among humans in a place of noble and wealthy status, with all necessities fully provided.
Within that state, one shall renounce worldly life to leave the household and advance toward the Noble Path; if one attains Nirvana, it is most excellent;
if not, one will be reborn in the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven."
At that time, Śakra gathered the assembly of devas and immediately addressed them, saying:
"I have made offerings to Brahmā at the three times of day; from this day forward, I shall cease doing so and instead offer worship to the World-Honored One at the three times."
At that time, Śakra addressed the gandharva son Pañcaśikha, saying:
"Your kindness toward me is now exceedingly great; because you were able to awaken the Buddha, the World-Honored One, you have enabled me to see and hear the profound Dharma."
"When I return to the heavens, I shall take the maiden Bhānuvatī, daughter of Viśvāvasu, to be your wife; furthermore, I shall cause you to succeed her father and become the King of the Gandharvas."

At that time, Śakra, leading the host of devas, circumambulated the Buddha three times, then withdrew and departed. Reaching a secluded place, they all thrice uttered the words, "Namo Buddhāya," and returned to the heavens.
Not long after Śakra had departed, the Brahmā King thought to himself:
"Śakra has already gone; I shall now go to where the Buddha is.

In the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, he arrived at the Buddha's location. Having prostrated at the Buddha's feet, he sat to one side; the radiance of the Brahmā Heaven then shone everywhere across Mount Vaideha.
At that time, Brahmā spoke these verses:
"Of great benefit is the manifestation of this meaning.
In that land of Śacī, Magadha, All around are the virtuous, Who are able to pose challenging questions. Śā...
"Śakra. Having repeated what Śakra had asked, he immediately returned to the heavens.
At dawn, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“Brahmā Sahāmpati came to my dwelling yesterday; after reciting the aforementioned verse, he immediately returned to the heavens.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the bhikṣus rejoiced and, having paid homage at the Buddha’s feet, departed.

74. The Account of the Past Causes and Conditions of Ājñātakauṇḍinya and Others (74). The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha. While he was preaching the Dharma, he brought Ājñātakauṇḍinya, Śakra Devānām Indra, and King Bimbisāra across; each led eighty-four thousand followers, and all attained the Way.
The bhikṣus were filled with doubt and wonder, [asking], "How is it that each of you has rescued so many people from the three evil realms?
The Buddha said, "Not only today; in the past as well, I have likewise delivered them."
The bhikṣus asked:
"Regarding his deliverance in the past, what was that event?
The Buddha said:

"In a past age, there were several merchants who went to sea to gather treasures. On their way back, they encountered a python in a vast wilderness; its body was six *krośas* high, and it coiled itself around the merchants on all four sides, leaving no way for them to enter or exit."
At that time, the merchants were filled with extreme terror, and each cried out:
"O gods of heaven and gods of earth, you who possess compassion, deliver us!"
At that time, there was a white elephant who had become a companion to the lion. The lion leaped forward and crushed the brain of the python, enabling the merchants to escape a great peril.
Thereupon, the python released its venomous breath from its mouth, killing both the lion and the white elephant, though their lives were not yet severed.
The merchant said, "You have rescued me; what wish do you seek?
He replied:
"I seek only to become a Buddha in order to deliver all people.
The merchants said,
"If you attain Buddhahood, we pray that our kind may be among the very first in your initial assembly, hearing the Dharma and attaining the Way."
The lion and the white elephant then passed away; the merchants cremated them and erected a stupa for their bones.
The Buddha said, "If you wish to know who that lion was at that time, it was I myself."
At that time, the white elephant was Śāriputra.
At that time, the caravan leader was Kauṇḍinya, Śakra, and King Bimbisāra.
"The caravan leaders at that time were none other than these gods and humans who have now attained the Way. 75.

The Story of the Śākya Son Kṣema, Who Suffered from Eye Disease, Took Refuge in the Triple Gem, and Attained Pure Vision (75). The Story of the Śākya Son Kṣema, Who Suffered from Eye Disease, Took Refuge in the Triple Gem, and Attained Pure Vision. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying in the Śākya Garden.
At that time, in the city of Cātumā, there was a member of the Śākya clan named Kṣema, who possessed pure faith in the Buddha, pure faith in the Dharma, and pure faith in the Saṅgha;
he had taken refuge in the Buddha, taken refuge in the Dharma, and taken refuge in the Saṅgha;
