he was single-mindedly devoted to the Buddha, single-mindedly devoted to the Dharma, and single-mindedly devoted to the Saṅgha.
He has no doubt regarding the Buddha, no doubt regarding the Dharma, and no doubt regarding the Saṅgha;
he has no doubt regarding the Truth of Suffering, no doubt regarding the Truth of the Origin, no doubt regarding the Truth of Cessation, and no doubt regarding the Truth of the Path.

Having attained the vision of the Truths and realized the fruit of the Path, like a Srotāpanna, he possesses complete knowledge and vision of all that is to be known and seen; regarding the three types of enlightenment, he will certainly attain them without exceeding the allotted time limit.
Because of his eye ailment, the Śākya son Kṣema was unable to see various forms.
The Śākya son Kṣema then thought of the World-Honored One:
"Homage to the Giver of Eyes! Homage to the Giver of Light! Homage to the Dispeller of Darkness! Homage to the Holder of the Torch! Homage to the Bhagavān! Homage to the Sugata!"
With his pure divine ear, which surpasses that of humans, the Buddha heard those sounds and said to Ānanda:

"Go now; with these verses, protect Kṣemā the Śākya woman, acting as her savior, her guardian, and her shepherd. Eradicate her misfortunes and provide benefit, profit, and peaceful dwelling for the fourfold assembly."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke the Sūtra of the Pure Eye for the Śākya Kṣema:
"Tathā śiri miri kiri hī hī tathā."
By means of this *Vimalanetra* mantra, may the eyes of the Śākya Kṣema become pure and the cataracts be removed.

Whether it be a cataract caused by wind, heat, cold, or a combination of these [humors], let there be no burning, no boiling, no swelling, no pain, no itching, and no tearing. May the precepts be real; asceticism be real; the ṛṣis be real; the devas be real; medicine be real; the words of the mantra be real; causes and conditions be real; suffering be real; accumulation be real; cessation be real; the path be real; the Arhats be real; the Pratyekabuddhas be real; and the Bodhisattvas be real.

In this way, just as he was addressed by the name Khema, others were likewise addressed by their names; they thereby attained the purity of vision, and having attained the purity of vision, darkness was dispelled and the film was removed.

Whether it be a wind-induced cataract, a heat-induced cataract, a cold-induced cataract, or a cataract caused by a combination of these factors, may there be no burning, no boiling, no swelling, no pain, no itching, and no tearing.

Ānanda! These words and phrases have been spoken thus by these six Buddhas, World-Honored Ones; I, the seventh, now likewise speak them. The Four Heavenly Kings also speak this mantra, as does Śakra; the Brahmā King and the assembly of Brahmās likewise rejoice in accordance with it.

“Ānanda! Among gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, the assembly of śramaṇas, or the assembly of brāhmaṇas—among humans or gods—I do not see anyone who, having recited these phrases three times, could cause an obscuration, darkness, a film, a swelling, or a bluish tint in the eye; nor could they cause a flaw to emerge in the eye, whether by the work of a deva, a nāga, a yakṣa, an asura, a kumbhāṇḍa, or a preta; or by the work of a piśāca, or poison, or an evil incantation, or sorcery, or a vaitālīya spell, or an evil star, or any of the lunar mansions.”
Ānanda went immediately and recited this mantra three times for the Śākya woman Kṣemā; her eyes became pure as they were before, and she was able to see all forms.

By reciting this mantra while calling out a person’s name—just as he did for the Śākya woman Kṣemā—all [afflictions] such as darkness, cataracts, wind-disorders, heat-disorders, cold-disorders, and those of balanced humors are eliminated. May there be no burning, no boiling, no swelling, no pain, no itching, and no tearing of the eyes.
Homage to the Bhagavān, homage to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. By means of these mantra-words, all Bodhisattvas shall attain auspicious success; may all Brahmās rejoice; svāhā!

76. Seven Causes and Conditions for Giving (76). Regarding the seven kinds of giving taught by the Buddha, which do not deplete one's wealth yet yield great rewards: there are seven causes and conditions for giving. The Buddha has declared that there are seven types of giving that do not diminish material resources and yet obtain a great karmic fruit.

The first is called the gift of the eyes: constantly regarding one's parents, teachers, elders, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas with kind eyes, and never with malicious eyes—this is called the gift of the eyes.
When one casts off this body and receives another, one obtains the pure eye;
when one attains Buddhahood in the future, one obtains the divine eye and the Buddha-eye—this is called the first karmic retribution.

Second, as for giving with a gentle countenance and a joyful expression toward parents, teachers, elders, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, without frowning or showing a foul expression: when one casts off this body and receives another, one obtains a handsome and upright appearance.
Upon attaining Buddhahood in the future, one will obtain a body of true golden color; this is called the second karmic reward.
Third is the gift of pleasant speech: toward parents, teachers, elders, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, one utters gentle words rather than harsh or evil speech.
When casting off this body and receiving another, one attains eloquence in speech such that whatever one says is believed and accepted by others;
in the future, upon attaining Buddhahood, one will possess the four types of analytical eloquence—this is called the third retribution.
The fourth is the gift of the body (*kāyadāna*). To rise to greet, prostrate before, and pay homage to one's parents, teachers, elders, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas is called the gift of the body.
By relinquishing this body and receiving another, one obtains an upright body, a tall body, a body respected by others;
and in the future, upon attaining Buddhahood, one’s body will be like a nyagrodha tree, such that its crown cannot be seen—this is called the fourth fruit of retribution.
The fifth is called giving with the mind (*citta-dāna*): although one may provide offerings with the aforementioned things, if the mind is not harmonious and wholesome, it is not called giving;
when the mind is wholesome and harmonious, and one generates profound devotion in making the offering, this is called giving with the mind.
When one casts off this body and receives another, one attains a mind of clarity and a mind free from delusion or madness;
in the future, upon attaining Buddhahood, one attains the mind of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*). This is called the fifth fruit of the gift of the mind.

The sixth is the gift of beds and seats: when one sees parents, teachers, elders, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas, one spreads out a bed or seat for them to sit upon, even using what one uses oneself to invite them to sit.
When casting off this body and receiving another, one will always obtain a noble and precious throne of the seven treasures;
upon attaining Buddhahood in the future, one will obtain the Lion Dharma-throne—this is called the sixth retribution.
The seventh is called the gift of dwellings: when one enables parents, teachers, elders, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas to come, go, sit, and lie within a house, this is termed the gift of dwellings.
Upon casting off this body and receiving another, one obtains natural palaces and dwellings;
when one attains Buddhahood in the future, one obtains the abodes of all dhyānas. This is called the seventh retribution, and these are called the seven kinds of giving.
Although no wealth or property was expended, a great karmic fruit was obtained. 77.

The Story of King Kapphina Obtaining Rain by Bathing the Buddha During a Drought (77). If one plants even a small amount of merit in a fertile field of blessings, one will certainly obtain its reward later.
In the distant past, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a king named Kāpa who ruled over eighty-four thousand kingdoms within Jambudvīpa.

The king had twenty thousand consorts, yet he had no offspring. He prayed and made offerings to the deities for many years until his chief consort gave birth to a crown prince named Candana. He became a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) who ruled over the four continents; later, weary of worldly life, he left the home and attained perfect enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi).
At that time, the various physiognomists in that country all said:
"A great drought shall last for twelve years; by what means and stratagems can this calamity be warded off?"
They then deliberated together, saying:

"We should now construct golden basins and place them in the marketplace, fill them with scented water to bathe the Buddha, distribute the scented water, and erect stupas and temples; thus we may eliminate calamities."

He immediately invited the Tathāgata to bathe in scented water; taking the remains of the World-Honored One’s bathwater, he fashioned eighty-four thousand precious jars and distributed them to eighty-four thousand kingdoms, so that they might erect stūpas and temples, making offerings and cultivating merit.

By virtue of the causes and conditions of creating stūpas and temples to cultivate merit, the heavens sent down great rain, the five grains ripened in abundance, and the people lived in peace and happiness.

At that time, there was a person who, upon seeing these stūpas and temples, felt joy in his heart; he immediately took a handful of flowers and scattered them over the stūpa, thereby obtaining a great and wholesome reward.
The Buddha said:

"With my Buddha-eye, I observe that distant past; those who received transformation under the Sandalwood Tathāgata and his fragrant-water stūpas and temples have all long since attained Buddhahood and entered nirvāṇa."
The one named Huashi was my own self.
Because of these causes and conditions from days past, I have now, at the very end, attained Buddhahood by myself.
Therefore, a practitioner should diligently cultivate all meritorious virtues and must not harbor thoughts of inferiority regarding even small acts of goodness. 78.

The Story of the Elder Inviting Śāriputra the Elder (78) In the past, within the city of Śrāvastī, there was a great elder whose family was immensely wealthy, possessing immeasurable riches and treasures. He would regularly invite a śramaṇa from the monastic roster to his home to provide offerings.
At that time, according to the order of seniority in the Saṃgha, it was Śāriputra’s turn and then Mahallaka’s to visit the house of the elder. Upon seeing them, the elder was filled with great joy.
On that very day, merchants who had gone out to sea returned home safely, having acquired a vast amount of precious treasures.

At that time, the king divided a village and bestowed it as a fief upon the elder. His wife was pregnant and subsequently gave birth to a son; thus, all these occasions of joy coincided. When Śāriputra and his companions entered the house, they accepted the elder’s offerings.
When the meal was finished, the elder served water and spread out a small seat before the Venerable One. Śāriputra offered a blessing, saying: "Today is an auspicious time;

excellent rewards have been obtained. Wealth, profit, and joyful matters have all gathered. With hearts leaping with joy and delight, faith has surged forth as we contemplate the One of Ten Powers. May it be so today, and may it always be thus hereafter."

At that time, having heard the verses of benediction, the elder was filled with great joy; he immediately offered two pieces of exquisite, high-quality cotton cloth to Śāriputra, yet he did not give any to the mahallaka alone.
At that time, the mahallaka returned to the monastery despondent and thought to himself:
"The reason Śāriputra has obtained this gift is precisely because his incantations and blessings suited the wishes of the elder; therefore, he received this offering."
"I should now seek this prayer of benediction.
He then said to Śāriputra,
"The prayer you offered just now, please grant it to me as well."
He replied to him, saying:
"This incantation for making aspirations is not to be used at all times; there are times when it may be used and times when it may not.
The mahallaka then entreated him with great earnestness:
"I pray that you will certainly grant it to me.
Śāriputra could not refuse his earnest request and immediately bestowed the incantation and its blessing.
Having received the instruction, he promptly began to recite it, mastering it until it was perfectly fluent, and then he reflected as follows:
"When shall it be that my turn comes and I obtain the position of *sthavira* so that I may employ this prayer?
At that time, by virtue of the monastic succession, he arrived at the house of a lay donor and was able to serve as the *sthavira*.

At that time, the elder had gone out to sea as a merchant and lost his precious treasures; the elder’s wife encountered legal trouble, and their son died. Yet the mahallaka continued to recite his original incantations and prayers, saying they would always be so in the future.
At that time, having heard these words, the elder was filled with resentment and anger; he immediately beat him and pushed him out the door.
Having been struck by the man's rage, he was deeply distressed and entered the king’s field of sesame, where he trampled the sesame plants, breaking and crushing the crops.
The guardian of the sesame was incensed by this and further beat him with a whip, subjecting him to extreme toil and humiliation.
Having been beaten severely once more, the mahallaka asked the assailant,
"What fault have I committed that you beat me so?"
At that time, the guardian of the sesame field described in detail how he had trampled the sesame seeds and pointed out the path.
They proceeded forward along the road, and before many li had passed, they encountered someone harvesting wheat, which had been piled up into a stack.

At that time, according to their secular customs, one circumambulated the funeral pyre clockwise while providing food and drink in order to seek a bountiful harvest; if one circumambulated counter-clockwise, it was considered inauspicious.
At that time, the mahallaka circumambulated the stack of grain counter-clockwise; the owner of the barley became incensed and struck him again with a club.
The mahallaka asked him once more:
"What crime have I committed that you should strike me so unjustly?"
The owner of the barley replied,
"When you circumambulated the barley heap, why did you not turn to the right and recite the mantra 'May there be much [grain]'?
Because you have violated my rule, I have struck you."
He then showed him the way.

After proceeding a short distance further, they encountered a burial site; [the monk] circumambulated the other's grave mound as he had previously done with the barley sheaves, reciting these words of incantation and aspiration:
"Enter deeply! Enter deeply!"
The master of the funeral was incensed; seizing his staff once more, he struck him and said to him:
"When you see the deceased, you ought to feel compassion for them. You should say, 'From this day forward, do not act like this again. Why, instead, do you say, 'More, more'?"
The mahallaka said, "From this day forward, I shall act according to your words.
He proceeded further and saw another wedding; he spoke as one who had been instructed by those attending a funeral:
"From this day forward, do not act in such a manner again.
At that time, the bridegroom and bridegroom’s party, enraged by this, beat him with canes until his head was split open.

He then moved forward again, running wildly as he was being beaten; encountering a hunter catching wild geese, he became terrified and panicked, crashing into the nets. Because of this, he startled and scattered the other geese, and the hunter, filled with rage, seized him and beat him again.
At that time, the mahallaka, having been beaten until he was utterly exhausted, said to the hunter:

"I traveled by the direct path, but I repeatedly stumbled and fell; my mind became confused and my steps grew frantic, causing me to strike against your net. I pray you will grant me your clemency and allow me to proceed."
The hunter replied, "You are extremely clumsy; why do you act so deceptively? Why not crawl along slowly?
He then stepped forward onto the path and, as the hunter had said, crawled along on his belly.

Furthermore, while on the road, he encountered a washerman; seeing him crawling on his elbows, the man thought he intended to steal his clothes, so he immediately seized him and beat him with a staff.
At that time, the Mahallaka, having encountered this dire distress, recounted the aforementioned events in full and was granted release.
Upon arriving at Jetavana, he said to the bhikṣus:
"The day before yesterday, while reciting the *śarīra* dhāraṇī and *praṇidhāna*, I suffered great anguish."
He himself declared that his body had been beaten until it was mangled, nearly losing his life.
The bhikṣus then led the mahallaka to the Buddha’s presence and related in detail the circumstances of how he had been beaten.
The Buddha said, "This mahallaka has not only had this causal condition today.
In the past, there was a king’s daughter who fell ill; the court astrologer divined her condition and declared that she must go to a cemetery to have it resolved."
At that time, the king’s daughter, taking her attendants with her, went toward the cemetery.
As they were traveling along the road, there were two merchants who, upon seeing the king’s daughter and her solemnly adorned retinue, became filled with fear and fled to the cemetery.
One of them was a servant attending the princess, whose ears and nose were cut off;
the other, seized by sudden terror, hid within a corpse and feigned death.

At that time, the princess, wishing to remove her ailment, selected the skin of a recently deceased person whose flesh had not yet decayed; she sat upon it and bathed to treat her illness. She then sent someone to check, who happened to be a merchant.

As he touched her body with his hand, it was still warm, so he thought she was newly dead. He immediately smeared mustard seeds on her body and bathed upon her. The pungent scent of the mustard entered the merchant’s nose; though he tried to restrain himself, he could not control it, and he suddenly sneezed loudly and sprang up.

At that time, the attendants, thinking him to be a *vetāla* (reanimated corpse), feared he might bring about various calamities or epidemics; they closed the gates to resist him, and the princess seized him urgently, refusing to let him go.
At that time, the merchant told her the truth,
saying, "I am truly not a ghost. Thereupon,
the princess immediately went with the merchant to the city, called for the city gates to be opened, and fully related the facts of the matter.

At that time, the king, the father of the girl, although he heard these words, still harbored disbelief; he arrayed his troops and weapons, opened the gate to go and look, and only then realized it was not a ghost.
Then the father king said,
"The physical form of a woman does not appear twice.
He then gave his daughter to him as a wife.
The merchant was filled with joy, celebrating his immeasurable good fortune.
The Buddha said:
"The merchant who obtained the king’s daughter at that time was Śāriputra."
The one who had his ears and nose cut off was this Mahallaka.
Such was his karmic connection from former lives;
it is not merely the case today. From this day forward, O Bhikṣus!

If you wish to preach the Dharma or offer prayers of aspiration, you should understand the appropriate timing; you ought to cultivate generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. Regarding sorrow, lamentation, joy, and happiness, you must know when it is the proper time and when it is not, and you must not speak recklessly.
*Sarvadharmapravacanasaṃgraha-sūtra*, Scroll Six;
*Sarvadharmapravacanasaṃgraha-sūtra*, Scroll Seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Ki-carya of the Western Regions during the Yuan Wei Dynasty, together with Tanyao.
The account of a Brahmin who gave a wish-fulfilling jewel to the Buddha, renounced the householder’s life, and attained the Way;

the account of Daśabala Kāśyapa using truthful words to stop the blood from the Buddha’s foot; the account of Māra Pāpīyas intending to come and disturb the Buddha while he was beneath the Bodhi tree;
the account of the Buddha preaching to the bhikṣus on the calamities of gain and offerings; and the account of bandits approaching.

The story of one who was being executed seeing the Buddha from afar, rejoicing, and thereby taking birth in heaven; the story of a man whose hands and feet were severed feeling the Buddha’s grace and attaining birth in heaven;
the story of an elder offering fine honey-milk to a traveler and thereby attaining birth in heaven;
the story of King Prasenajit sending a messenger to invite the Buddha, whereby the messenger attained birth in heaven; and the story of King Prasenajit exhorting others to practice almsgiving.

The story of a poor man who gave a piece of cotton cloth to the King and thereby attained rebirth in heaven; the story of an elder brother who constantly exhorted his younger brother to serve and cultivate the Triple Gem, yet the brother lacked faith and respect while the brother attained rebirth in heaven;
the story of a father who, upon hearing that his son had attained the Way, rejoiced and immediately attained rebirth in heaven;
the story of a son who was compelled by his father to leave the household life and attain rebirth in heaven; and the story of the Arhat Jīvaka who drove away an evil dragon.
78. The Story of Two Bhikṣus Who Entered the Ocean Far Afar and Saw Kṣemadatta Attain Rebirth in Heaven;
79. The Story of the King of the Yuezhi Seeing Kṣemadatta; The Story of the King of the Yuezhi Forming a Virtuous Friendship with Three Wise Ministers; 79.
The Story of a Brahmin Who Offered a Cintāmaṇi Jewel to the Buddha, Left Home, and Attained the Way. (79) Brahmin.
The Story of the Gatekeeper Who Attained the Way by Giving a Cintāmaṇi Jewel to the Buddha and Leaving Home:

When the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was at that time a Brahmin in South India who was skilled at distinguishing *cintāmaṇi* jewels. Carrying a *cintāmaṇi*, he traveled from South India to East India, visiting all the various kingdoms, yet there was no one capable of identifying it.
Proceeding in this manner, he arrived at the kingdom of Śrāvastī and went to King Prasenajit, saying:
"Who is able to distinguish and identify this pearl?"
King Prasenajit assembled his various ministers and all those who were wise men, yet none among them could identify it.
King Prasenajit went together with them to the presence of the Buddha.
The Buddha said to the brahmin, "Do you know the name of this pearl?"
"Do you know the origin from which this jewel was produced?
Do you know the power and durability of this jewel? He replied:
“I do not know,” [the king] replied.
The Buddha said, “This pearl comes from within the brain of the Makara great fish. The body of this fish is two hundred and eighty thousand li long; this pearl is named Vajra-dṛḍha (Diamond-Firm).”

Possessing the foremost power of endurance, it causes all those who have been poisoned to see their poison entirely vanish upon seeing it; furthermore, when its light touches their bodies, it likewise neutralizes the poison.
The second power is that when those afflicted by fever see it, they are cured; even if its light touches their bodies, they likewise recover.
The third power is that if a person has immeasurable hundreds of thousands of enemies, one who holds this jewel will cause them all to become friends.

When the brahmin heard these words, he was filled with great joy; realizing that the Tathāgata was truly an omniscient one, he immediately offered this jewel to the Buddha and requested to leave the household life.
The Buddha said,
"Welcome, Bhikṣu!
His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, the Dharma robes were donned upon his body, and as the Buddha preached the essentials of the Dharma for him, he immediately attained Arhatship.
The bhikṣus said,
"The Tathāgata is well able to distinguish this jewel and is further able to preach the Dharma so that beings may attain the realization of the Way.
The Buddha said:
"It is not only today; it was likewise in the past.
Long ago, in the kingdom of Kāśī, on the Mountain of the Seers (Ṛṣigiri), there was a seer possessing the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā).
At that time, a certain brāhmaṇa, holding a single tree leaf, asked the seer:"
"What kind of tree leaf is this?

The rishi replied, "This tree is named Golden Summit (Suvarṇamūrdhan). If a person is afflicted by poison and their life is at its end, should they sit beneath this tree, the poison will be immediately eliminated."
If those suffering from feverish diseases rely upon this tree, they too shall be cured.
Should the leaves of this tree touch a person's body, all toxic vapors as well as fevers shall be entirely eliminated.
The brahmin was filled with joy and requested to become the seer’s disciple; he practiced his teachings and likewise attained the five supernormal powers.
At that time, the seer who possessed the five supernormal powers was none other than myself.
The Brahmin who held the tree leaves at that time was this very Brahmin here.
At that time, I instructed him so that he attained the five supernormal powers; now, I have likewise delivered him from the perils of birth and death, and he has attained the state of an Arhat.

80. The Account of Daśabala-Kāśyapa Stopping the Blood from the Buddha’s Foot with Words of Truth (80). At that time, the Tathāgata was pierced in his foot by a *kaṭhalla* thorn; blood flowed and would not stop. Although various medicinal herbs were applied, they could not heal it.
The Arhats went to Mount Gandhamādana to fetch medicinal herbs for anointing and treatment, yet the bleeding still did not cease.
Daśabala Kāśyapa went to the World-Honored One and spoke these words:
"If the Buddha, the Tathāgata, maintains a mind of equality toward all sentient beings, without distinction between Rāhula and Devadatta, then the blood from his feet should stop."
Immediately the blood ceased and the wound was healed.
The bhikṣu sighed in admiration and said:
"Though various wonderful medicines were applied and treated, they did not stop it; yet at Kāśyapa’s truthful words, the blood immediately ceased."
The Buddha said, "Not only today,
but in a past life as well, it was just like this. Long ago,
there was a brahmin who had a son named Ahimsaka (Harmless), who spoke to his father, saying:"
"While walking among the fields, do not harm any living beings.
The father said to his son:
"Do you wish to become a rishi?"
"What is the way of life? How does one avoid insects?
The son replied, "I now hope for peace and happiness in this life and peace and happiness in future lives; if you do not follow my words, what is the use of living?"
He immediately sat down by the side of the Poisonous Dragon Spring, intending to seek death.
There was a poisonous dragon there that would harm anyone who saw it.
At that moment, the Brahmin’s son beheld the poisonous dragon; its venom spread through his entire body, and his life was on the verge of ending.
At that time, the father was filled with grief and distress, not knowing where his son was, so he immediately went out to search for him.
Seeing his son on the verge of death, the father went to his side and spoke these words:
"My son has never before harbored a harmful intent; therefore, this poison should be neutralized."
Having spoken these words, the poisonous vapor was immediately dispelled, and he recovered as before.
He who was the father at that time was Daśabala Kāśyapa;
he who was the son at that time was my own self.
In past lives, you were able to speak words of truth that eliminated my illness; in this present life as well, you shall cure my illness through truthful speech.

81. The Circumstances of Māra Pāpīyān’s Attempt to Disturb the Buddha While He Was Under the Bodhi Tree (81). Regarding the circumstances of Māra Pāpīyān’s attempt to disturb the Buddha while he was under the Bodhi Tree: In the past, when the Tathāgata was beneath the Bodhi tree, the evil Māra Pāpīyān, leading a host of eight billion followers, came intending to destroy the Buddha.
He went to where the Tathāgata was and spoke these words:
"Gautama! You are all alone; how can you sit here?"
"You must depart at once.
If you do not go, I shall seize your feet and hurl you beyond the sea.
The Buddha said:
"I observe the world and see no one capable of casting me beyond the sea.

In a previous life, you merely built a single temple, observed the eight precepts for a single day, and offered a bowl of food to a Pratyekabuddha; therefore, you were born in the six heavens as a great Māra king."

I have, however, extensively cultivated merit over three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. During the first *asaṃkhyeya* kalpa, I made offerings to immeasurable Buddhas; during the second and third *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I did likewise, making offerings to innumerable śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. Throughout the entire great earth, there is not even a space the size of a needle that has not been my own bone.
The Māra said: "Gautama!
You say that in the past I observed the precepts for a single day and gave food to a pratyekabuddha; this faith is indeed true, as I myself know it and you also know me."
"As for what you have said yourself, who can testify to it?
The Buddha pointed to the ground with his hand and said,
"This earth shall bear witness for me."
When these words were spoken, the entire great earth shook in six ways. The Earth Deity immediately emerged from the Diamond Foundation and, with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I bear witness to this; since this earth first came into being, I have always remained within it."
"What the World-Honored One has spoken is true and not false.
The Buddha said to Pāpīyas:
"If you can first move this water jar, only then will you be able to hurl me beyond the sea."
At that time, Pāpīyān and his assembly of eight billion could not cause [the Buddha] to waver; the host of Māra’s army fell headlong into confusion, shattered and scattered.
The bhikṣus said,
"For a long night, Pāpīyān has troubled and disturbed the Tathāgata, yet he has not prevailed.
The Buddha said:
"It is not only today; it was likewise in the past.

Formerly, in the kingdom of Kāśī, on Mount Ṛṣigiri, there was a seer possessing the five supernatural powers who taught the youths of the city of Vārāṇasī, causing them all to leave the household life and attain the path of the seers."
At that time, the city deity became extremely enraged and said to the rishi:
"If you enter the city and continue to save people, I shall seize your feet and hurl you beyond the sea."
The seer took up a water jar and said to the city deity, "Move this jar first, and only then may you hurl me.
Though the deity exerted all its supernatural power, it could not move the jar; filled with shame, it submitted and retreated.
"The rishi at that time was my own self.
The city deity at that time was Pāpīyān. 82.
The Buddha’s Discourse to the Bhikṣus on the Perils of Gain (82) At that time, the Tathāgata was staying in Śrāvastī, feeling weary and averse to gain and offerings.
There was a deep forest named Lobha-alaṃkāra (Adornment of Greed); having fled from gain and offerings, he went into that forest.
Within the forest was a monastery, where at that time a certain arhat named Nakaka served as its abbot.
When the Buddha arrived at that forest, it was past midday; there were many people there holding robes as offerings, filling the woods, who spoke these words:
"We have no need for gain and honor, yet this gain and honor constantly follow after us."
There were also twelve thousand bhikṣus who arrived at that place.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"Gain and offerings are a great calamity; they can create obstacles and hindrances, even for an arhat, who may likewise be obstructed and hindered by gain and offerings."
The bhikṣu asked,
"What kind of obstacle can it create?
The Buddha said:
"The harm of gain and honor destroys the skin, destroys the flesh, destroys the bones, and destroys the marrow.
How does it destroy?
It destroys the skin of ethical discipline, the flesh of meditative concentration, the bones of wisdom, and the marrow of the subtle, virtuous mind."
Twelve thousand bhikṣus uniformly maintained the three robes and six requisites, practiced as forest-dwellers (āraṇyaka), and accepted no other items.
The Buddha then praised them, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
One is able to practice the dharma of the forest hermitage (āraṇyaka).

This dharma of mine is the dharma of few desires, not of many desires; it is the dharma of contentment, not of discontent; it is the dharma of delighting in tranquility, not of delighting in bustle and noise; it is the dharma of diligence, not of indolence; it is the dharma of right mindfulness, not of wrong mindfulness; it is the dharma of a concentrated mind, not of a distracted mind; it is the dharma of wisdom, not of delusion.
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they all attained arhatship.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said:
"It is not only today; it was likewise in the past.
Long ago, in the kingdom of Kāśī, there was a minister named Yakṣa."
The son of a yakṣa, named Yakṣadatta, deeply realized the impermanence of existence and left the household life to study as a rishi.

The various rishis were full of desire and all vied with one another for fruits and grasses. In order to cause them to become less desirous, Yakṣadatta abandoned his soft grass and took their coarse grass; he abandoned his sweet fruits and took their sour fruits; he abandoned his own fresh fruits and took their old ones. Having thus practiced this giving and taking of fruits, he immediately attained the five supernatural powers.
When twelve thousand rishis saw this, they likewise practiced few desires and no longer sought much; they also all attained the five supernatural powers.
Nyaṅkudāta gradually employed skillful means to instruct and transform these sages.
After his life ended, he was reborn in the Place of No Use.
At that time, Datta was my own self;
the twelve thousand seers at that time are now these twelve thousand bhikṣus.

83. The Story of the Robber Who Was About to Be Executed Seeing the Buddha from Afar, Rejoicing, and Reborn in Heaven (83). At that time in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, King Prasenajit beat the drum and issued a proclamation, saying:
"If anyone commits robbery, they shall be executed upon capture."
At that time, there was a man who captured a thief and brought him before the king; the king then dispatched men to take him out and execute him.

While on the way outside the city, he encountered the Tathāgata on the road and felt great joy in his heart. Upon reaching the place of execution, he submitted to the king’s law and immediately attained rebirth in heaven.

Having fully cultivated the three mindfulnesses and known [the truth] thereby, he was on the verge of being executed when he saw the Buddha; filled with joy at his death, he was reborn in heaven. Moved by the Buddha’s benevolence and virtue, he descended to make offerings. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
The bhikṣu asked:
"By what karmic conditions was he born in this celestial palace?
The Buddha said:
"In a former life among humans, he was killed by a king; at the moment of death, he beheld the Buddha with joy.
By virtue of this wholesome cause, he was reborn in that celestial palace. Having encountered me once more, he heard the Dharma and attained realization, realizing the stage of Srotāpanna."

84. The Story of the Man with Severed Hands and Feet Who Attained Rebirth in Heaven through Gratitude for the Buddha’s Kindness (84). In the past, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a man who violated the king’s law; his hands and feet were severed and he was cast by the roadside.
The Buddha saw him while traveling and went up to his side, asking:
"What is your suffering today? The man who had had his feet cut off replied:
"I am suffering most from hunger.
He immediately commanded Ānanda to give him food.

That man who had been deprived of his feet died and was reborn in heaven; moved by the Buddha’s profound kindness, he descended to make offerings. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
A bhikṣu asked,
"By what karmic actions is one born in the heavens?
The Buddha said:

"Formerly, while among humans, he had his hands and feet cut off and was cast by the roadside. When the Buddha arrived at that place, He commanded that food be given to him; his heart was filled with joy, and upon the end of his life, he was reborn in heaven. Now, being in my presence, he has heard the Dharma and attained the Way."

85. The Story of the Elder Who Offered Fine Honey-Water to a Traveler and Attained Rebirth in Heaven (85) In the past, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was an elder who sought a secluded plot of land within the Jeta Grove, intending to build a dwelling there.

When the elder Sudatta had completed his work everywhere and there was no space remaining, he prepared a beverage at the main gate of the Jeta Grove using pure water mixed with various kinds of honey and various kinds of parched grain flour, providing it to all travelers.
After ninety days, the Buddha also accepted her.

Thereupon, she passed away and was reborn in the heavens, possessing great majesty and virtue. Riding upon a celestial palace, she came to make offerings to the Buddha; the Buddha preached the Dharma for her, and she attained the stage of *srotāpanna*.
The bhikṣu asked,
"By what karmic actions was this birth in the heavens attained, such that one's majestic power is like this?
The Buddha said:
"In his former life as a human being, at the gate of the Jetavana Monastery, he prepared various kinds of beverages and gave them to all; the Buddha himself also accepted them.
By this causal condition, he was reborn in the heavens, and furthermore, in my presence, he heard the Dharma and attained the Way."

86. The Story of King Prasenajit Sending a Messenger to Invite the Buddha, and How the Messenger Was Reborn in Heaven (86). Once, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, King Prasenajit and the elder Sudatta had not seen the Buddha for a long time; their hearts were filled with longing and devotion. Following the conclusion of the summer retreat (*varṣā*), they dispatched a messenger to invite the Buddha.
The messenger went to where the Buddha was, paid his respects, and said to the Buddha:
"The King and the elder wish to see the Tathāgata;
I pray only that the World-Honored One will mount this carriage and proceed to Śrāvastī."
The Buddha said, "I have no need for a chariot; I possess my own supernormal powers (ṛddhi).
Although he spoke these words, for the sake of her merit, he proceeded through the air above the chariot.
The messenger went ahead to inform the King and the Elder.
The King and the Elder came out in person to welcome him, and the messenger, together with the King, returned to see the Buddha.

At the end of his life, he was reborn in the heavens; immediately mounting a precious chariot, he came to where the Buddha was. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
A bhikṣu asked:
"By what causes and conditions were you reborn in the celestial palace and mounted this precious chariot?"
The Buddha said, “In the past, while among humans, I was sent by a king to the presence of a Buddha to offer him a carriage for him to ride.

By the causal conditions of this karma, I have now been born in heaven and constantly drive a precious chariot. Having come before me with great reverence, I heard the Dharma and attained awakening, realizing the stage of Srotāpanna.”

87. The Story of King Prasenajit Encouraging Almsgiving: How a Poor Man Gave a Piece of Cotton Cloth to the King and Attained Rebirth in Heaven (87) In the past, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, King Prasenajit spoke thus:

“The elder Sudatta is already able to exhort and transform all the people to perform various meritorious deeds; I too should now, for the sake of sentient beings, instruct them in almsgiving so that they may obtain merit.”
Thereupon, he traveled about to convert others, begging for alms from place to place.
At that time, there was a man who was so poor and destitute that he possessed only a single cotton cloth (*karpāsa*). He immediately offered it as a gift to King Prasenajit;
having received the cloth, the king in turn presented it to the Buddha.

Thereafter, the poor man passed away and was reborn in the heavens; moved by the Buddha’s great kindness, he came to make offerings to him. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
The bhikṣu asked:
"What karma did he perform in the past to be born in that heaven?
The Buddha said:
"When he was among humans, he encountered a king’s exhortation to practice charity and immediately gave a white cotton cloth as an offering.
By virtue of this wholesome cause, he has now attained birth in the heavens; consequently, in my presence, he has heard the Dharma and realized the fruit."

88. The Story of the Elder Brother Who Constantly Exhorted His Younger Brother to Serve and Practice the Triple Gem, Yet Whose Brother Lacked Faith and Respect, Resulting in the Elder Brother’s Rebirth in Heaven (88). The Story of the Elder Brother Who Constantly Exhorted His Younger Brother to Serve and Practice the Triple Gem, Yet Whose Brother Lacked Faith and Respect, Resulting in the Elder Brother’s Rebirth in Heaven: Long ago, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there were two brothers. The elder brother devoted himself to the practice of the Buddha-dharma, while the younger brother served Pūraṇa Kāśyapa.

The elder brother constantly exhorted his younger brother to serve the Triple Gem, but the younger brother did not comply; they were always at odds and their feelings were not in harmony, so they eventually lived apart.

The first person made offerings to the Buddha; subsequently, when his life came to an end, he was reborn in the heavens. He then came to the Buddha’s presence to offer a return gift of gratitude. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
The bhikṣu asked,
"What karma did you perform in the past to be born in this celestial palace?
The Buddha said:

"In former lives among humans, his mind delighted in the True Dharma and he reverently cultivated the Triple Gem. By virtue of these meritorious causes, he has now attained birth in the heavens; furthermore, having heard the Dharma from me, he has gained faith and understanding, thereby realizing the fruit of the Path."

89. The Story of the Father Who Attained Rebirth in Heaven Out of Joy upon Hearing His Son Had Attained the Way (89). Once, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there were two brothers who constantly delighted in quarreling and harbored mutual resentment and malice toward one another. They went together to the king, seeking a judicial decision.
While on his way, he encountered the Buddha, who preached the Dharma for him; he attained the path of Arhatship.

When his father heard that his son had met the Buddha and attained the Way, his heart was filled with joy; he then passed away and was reborn in the heavens. He came to where the Buddha was, and the Buddha preached the Dharma for him; he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
The bhikṣu asked:
"What karma did you perform in the past to have been reborn in heaven now?
The Buddha said:

"In the past, while among human beings, they heard me preaching the Dharma for the sake of their children and others; they leaped with joy and were born in the heavens upon the end of their lives. There, they again heard the Dharma from me, attained faith and understanding, and realized the fruits of the Path."

90. The Story of the Son Forced by His Father to Leave Home and Be Reborn in Heaven (90). In the past, there was a man in Śrāvastī who compelled his son to leave home and serve the Buddha. The Buddha immediately ordained him, but he was constantly made to sweep the ground. Unable to endure the hardship, he abandoned the path and returned to lay life.
His father said to him, "Just go forth into the religious life; from this day forward, I shall sweep the ground for you.
The father then went with his son to that Jetavana Monastery.
When the boy saw the vihāra and its purity, his heart was filled with joy, and he spoke these words:
"I would rather sacrifice my life to leave the household life and sweep this ground than ever return to secular life."
Subsequently, when his life ended, he was reborn in the heavens. He immediately came to where the Buddha was, and the Buddha preached the Dharma for him; he attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
A bhikṣu asked:
"By what karmic conditions was he reborn in the heavens?"
The Buddha said:
"In a previous life among humans, he was unable to endure hardship and wished to return home.
His father would not permit it; instead, he took over his labor and duties and forcibly compelled him to leave the household, whereupon he finally became joyful."
"At the end of his life, he was reborn in heaven, and furthermore, in my presence, he heard the Dharma and attained the Way. 91.

The Story of the Arhat Jīvaka Driving the Evil Dragon into the Sea (91). The Story of the Arhat Jīvaka Driving the Evil Dragon into the Sea: Formerly, there was a venerable Arhat named Jīvaka who appeared in the kingdom of Kaśmīra seven hundred years after the Buddha had passed away.
At that time, in the kingdom of Kaśmīra, there was an evil dragon king named Arina who frequently caused calamities and tormented the worthy sages;
the people of the land were all afflicted by him.
At that time, there were two thousand arhats, each exhausting their supernatural powers to drive this dragon away from the boundaries of the kingdom.
Among them, one hundred arhats moved the earth with their supernormal powers;
another five hundred emitted great radiance.
Furthermore, there were five hundred people who had entered meditative concentration while walking to and fro.
Though each of them exerted their supernatural powers to the utmost, they could not cause him to move.
Then the Venerable Kṣemadatta went last to the place of the dragon pond and snapped his fingers three times, saying:
“Nāga! Depart now; you must not remain here.
The nāga immediately departed, not daring to stay.
At that time, two thousand arhats said to the Venerable One:

"We and the Venerable One have both attained the exhaustion of outflows and liberation of the dharma-body; we are all entirely equal. Yet, each of us has exerted our supernatural powers to the utmost, yet we were unable to cause it to move."
"Venerable sir, how did you cause the Naga Arina to retreat far into the great ocean with a mere three snaps of your fingers?
The Venerable replied, "Since I was still an ordinary person, I have upheld the prohibitive precepts;

even regarding a minor offense such as a *dukkaṭa*, I have guarded them with an impartial mind no differently than the four grave offenses (*pārājika*). Now, as for why these people here cannot move this Naga—it is because their spiritual power is not equal to mine, and therefore they cannot move him."
At that time, the Venerable Kṣemadatta, together with his disciples, was traveling toward Northern India. On the road, he saw a crow and looked up with a smile.
His disciples asked him, "We do not know for what reason, Venerable One, you smiled?"
"I pray that you will explain its meaning.
The Venerable One replied, "The time for this has arrived; I shall speak."

Thereupon he proceeded forward and arrived at the city of Śilāvatī. Having reached the city gate, his countenance grew somber; when the time for the meal had come, he entered the city to beg for food. Once he had obtained the food, he returned and exited through the city gate, his countenance again becoming somber.
The disciples knelt for a long time and addressed him, saying:
"We do not understand for what reason you smiled just now,
nor why you subsequently changed your expression to one of such sorrow."
Then the Venerable Kṣemadatta replied to his disciples, saying:
"In the past, ninety-one kalpas ago, after the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Vipaśyin, I was the son of a householder."
At that time, he sought to leave the household life, but his parents would not permit it and said to their son:
"The affairs of our family business are weighty; if you were to leave the household life, who would continue the lineage?"
"I shall take a wife for you and produce an heir for you; then I will permit you to leave the household life.
He was then married.
Once he had taken a wife, he again requested to leave the household life, and his parents spoke once more:
"If you give birth to one more breath [a son], I shall allow you to leave the household life.
Not long thereafter, she gave birth to a son.
Once the boy was able to speak, he addressed his parents again, saying:
“‘I pray that the Honored One will first grant permission for me to leave the home life.
At that time, his parents, fearing they would contradict their previous words, secretly instructed the wet nurse to say to the infant:
‘When your father wishes to go forth into homelessness, you must stand at the gate and seize him, saying:’”
“Since you have already brought me up, do you now wish to abandon me and go forth into homelessness?
If you must go, I pray that my father will kill me first, and only then depart.”
His father immediately became somber and his feelings changed, and he said to his son:
"I shall stay now; I will not go further.
It was because of this that they wandered through birth and death.
With my eye of the Way, I observe past lives; whether among devas and humans, or within the three evil realms, it is extremely difficult to encounter one another!
It is extremely difficult to encounter one another!
Now I have seen him for the first time.
That crow you saw earlier was none other than that grandson at that time.
The reason my countenance turned so somber was that, by the side of the city, I saw the son of a hungry ghost who spoke to me, saying:
"I have been by this city for seventy years; my mother has entered the city on my behalf to seek food, yet she has never once returned.
I am now hungry and thirsty, and am in great distress. I pray that the Venerable One will enter the city, find my mother, and speak for me, saying:
'Come quickly to see me!'"
At that time, as I entered the city, I saw a mother of hungry ghosts and said to her:
"Your son is outside; he is in great peril from hunger and thirst, longing to see you."
Then the mother of the hungry ghosts replied to him, saying:

"I have been entering this city for more than seventy years. Because of my own meager merit, compounded by the fact that I have recently given birth, I am emaciated with hunger and lack strength. Although there is impure food such as pus, blood, mucus, saliva, and excrement, those who possess great power take it away first, so that I cannot obtain it."
Finally, he obtained one mouthful of impure food and wished to take it out the door to share with his son; however, there were other powerful ghosts at the gate who would not allow it to pass.
"I only pray that the Venerable One will take pity on me and lead me so that mother and son may see each other and share this impurity.
Then the Venerable One led the hungry ghost mother out through the city gate; mother and son saw one another and shared the impurity.
At that time, the Venerable One asked the ghost:
"How long have you been dwelling here?
Then the ghost replied:
"I have seen this city form and perish seven times.
At that time, the Venerable One sighed and said,
"The long lifespan of hungry ghosts is a most grievous suffering."
At that time, when the disciples heard these words, they all grew weary of birth and death and immediately attained the fruit of the Path.

92. The Story of Two Bhikṣus Seeing Ghyata Who Attained Rebirth in Heaven (92) At that time, in South India, there were two bhikṣus who, having heard that Ghyata possessed great majestic virtue, came toward Kaśmīra and arrived at his dwelling place.
As they were passing beneath a tree on the road, they saw a bhikṣu whose physical form was extremely emaciated,
tending a fire before a hearth. Those two bhikṣus asked him,
"Do you know the Venerable Śāriputra?"
He replied, "I know him. That bhikṣu said:
"Where is he now? He replied,
"He is in the third cave above."
Those two bhikṣus immediately climbed the mountain and went to the cave, where they saw the bhikṣu who had previously been tending the fire.
At that time, the two bhikṣus were filled with doubt and wonder;
the bhikṣus said, "Since you possess such renown and virtue, why did you worry about being unable to come here earlier?"
Then a certain bhikṣu, seeking to resolve his doubt, asked him:
"Venerable One, possessing such majestic power as this, why does fire arise spontaneously?
The Venerable One replied:

"I recall the suffering of birth and death in the past; if my head, hands, feet, or body could be used as fuel, I would still offer them to light fires for the sake of the Sangha, let alone burning firewood."
Then the two bhikṣus immediately asked, "We do not yet understand the nature of the suffering of birth and death in the past; what were its circumstances?
We wish to hear about it."
The Venerable One replied:
"I recall that in five hundred past lives, I was born among dogs; I was constantly tormented by hunger and thirst, and only at two times did I obtain sufficient food to satisfy myself."
First, I encountered a drunken man who had vomited his wine upon the ground, whereby I obtained food and was satisfied with comfort.

Second, I encountered a husband and wife living together; the husband went to the fields while the wife remained behind to prepare food. At that time, the woman went out briefly on some business, and I immediately entered and stole her meal.

Because the mouth of that food vessel was narrow, although his head had initially managed to enter, it was difficult to extract later; thus, while he achieved a single full meal, he endured great hardship. When the husband returned from the fields, he immediately cut off the head while it remained inside the vessel.
At that time, the two bhikṣus, having heard his preaching of the Dharma, grew weary of birth and death and attained the stage of *srotāpanna*. 93.

The Story of King Moṣadha Seeing the Arhat Kṣemadatta In the kingdom of Moṣadha there was a king named Candana-Kaniṣka. Having heard that in the kingdom of Kaśmīra there was a venerable Arhat named Kṣemadatta who possessed great renown, he desired to see him. He immediately prepared his own carriage and, accompanied by his ministers and attendants, traveled to that country.
On the way, he thought to himself:

"I am now the king, ruling over the world; among all the people, there is none who does not revere and submit to me. Unless one possesses great virtue, how could they be worthy of receiving my offerings?"
Having formed this thought, he proceeded forward and went directly to that country.
Someone informed the Venerable Kṣemadatta, saying:
"The King of the Yuezhi, named Candana-Kaniṣka, has come from afar with his ministers and attendants to meet you."
"I only pray, Venerable One,
that you will adjust your robes and together we shall welcome and receive him.
At that time, the Venerable One replied:

"I have heard the Buddha’s words: for one who has left the household life, the Way is honored above the mundane; one should devote oneself solely to virtue. How could one receive [a guest] with elaborate finery?"
He then remained silent, sitting upright and not emerging.

Thereupon, the King of the Yuezhi went to his dwelling place and beheld the Venerable Kṣemadatta; seeing his majestic virtue, his reverence and faith redoubled, and he immediately approached to prostrate himself, then withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, as the Venerable One was about to spit, the King of the Yuezhi unconsciously stepped forward and offered him a spittoon.
Thereupon, the Venerable Śāṇakavāsin addressed the King, saying:
"This humble monk is not yet worthy to serve as a field of merit for Your Majesty; why have you deigned to trouble your august personage by coming here in person?"

At that time, King Moṭṭāyana felt profound shame and said, "I had recently harbored a slight thought, yet he knew my mind. Were it not for his divine virtue, how could he have been capable of such a thing?"
He conceived a renewed sense of reverence toward the Venerable One.
Then, the Venerable Śāṇakavāsin briefly expounded the teaching for the king, saying:
"The path was good when you came, O King; it will be so when you depart from the Tathāgata."
Having heard these instructions, the king immediately returned to his kingdom.
Upon reaching the middle of the road, his ministers spoke with grievance:
"We have followed our Great King from afar to that country, yet in the end we have heard nothing and are returning home empty-handed."
Then King Candraprabha replied to his ministers, saying:
"Do you now reproach me for having nothing to attain?
Previously, the Venerable One preached the Dharma for me."
"The road was good when the King came; it will be the same when he departs.
Do you not understand this?

It is because in the past I maintained the precepts, practiced giving, constructed monasteries, and established stupas and temples; through these various merits, I have cultivated the royal lineage and now enjoy this position.
"Now you have again cultivated merit and extensively accumulated manifold virtues; in a future life, you will surely receive abundant blessings. Therefore, he cautioned me, saying:
'When the King comes, the road is good; when he departs, it is as when he came.'"
Having heard this, the ministers bowed their heads in prostration and apologized, saying:
"We, your humble servants, are of shallow wisdom and dull intellect; we have privately conceived a false understanding, taking what we have practiced to be the path."
"The Great King’s divine virtue perfectly accords with the profound meaning of the teachings; it is through the seeds sown by his accumulated merit that he enjoys this royal station.
The ministers rejoiced, and having spoken, they withdrew.

94. The Story of King Moṭṭāla and the Three Wise Ministers of the Yuezhi Kingdom (94) Regarding the story of King Moṭṭāla and the Three Wise Ministers of the Yuezhi Kingdom: At that time, there was a king in the kingdom of the Yuezhi named Candana-Kaniṣka. He maintained close friendships with three wise men: the first was the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa; the second was a high minister named Moṭṭāla; and the third was a skilled physician named Caraka. These three men were the king’s trusted friends; he treated them with great honor and they remained constantly by his side, attending to him in all his movements.
The Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa addressed the king, saying:
"If you would follow my words, it shall cause the king in future lives to always be accompanied by goodness, forever free from all calamities, and eternally depart from the evil realms."
The second minister again addressed the king, saying:
"If Your Majesty employs my secret counsel and does not leak it, all within the four seas can be conquered."
The third excellent physician again addressed the king, saying:

"Great King, if you can follow my words, I shall ensure that throughout your life you never suffer an untimely death; you shall have a hundred flavors according to your heart's desire, and you shall remain in perfect health without affliction."
The king acted according to these words and never suffered even the slightest ailment.

Thereupon, following the counsel of his great ministers, the king’s military might overawed all whom it confronted; none failed to submit, and three of the four quarters were already pacified. Only the eastern quarter had not yet come to surrender. He immediately arrayed his army, intending to go and punish them.

He first dispatched various Hu people and white elephants to lead the way at the head of the procession, while the King followed behind, intending to reach the Pamir Mountains and cross over the passes and precipices.
However, the elephants and horses he had previously ridden refused to advance. The King was greatly astonished and marveled, and spoke to the horse, saying:
"I have mounted you before and after to campaign in conquest, and the three directions have already been settled; why do you now refuse to proceed on the road?"
Then the minister said:
"What I previously reported to you was a secret; since the King has now divulged it, his end is not far off.
Just as the minister had spoken, the King realized for himself that his death would surely come before long.

This king had previously and subsequently led military expeditions, killing more than three hundred million people. Knowing that his future retribution would be heavy and certain, he was struck with fear and immediately began to repent. He practiced generosity and maintained the precepts, constructed monasteries for the Sangha, and provided the four requisites without fail. He cultivated various merits with diligent and tireless effort.
At that time, there were certain ministers who said to one another:
"The King has extensively committed various crimes and carried out merciless slaughter; though he now performs meritorious deeds, what benefit can this bring to his past transgressions?"
When the king heard this, wishing to resolve his doubts, he immediately employed a skillful means and commanded his ministers:
"You must light a large cauldron and keep it boiling intensely for seven days and seven nights, without letting it cease."
The king then threw a finger-ring into the cauldron and commanded his ministers:
"I rely upon you to retrieve this ring from within the cauldron.
The ministers addressed the king, saying:
"I pray that you might incur further punishment and face death, for this ring cannot be obtained.
The king said to his minister,
"Is there any expedient by which it might be recovered?"
Then the minister replied, "Extinguish the fire below and pour cold water above; by this expedient, one's hand will not be injured, and it may be taken."
The king replied:

"In the past I committed evil, which was like that heated cauldron; now I cultivate various virtues, feeling shame and remorse as I repent and resolve never again to do evil. Why, then, does it not cease?"
"The three miserable realms can be brought to rest, and the states of humans and devas can be attained.
Upon hearing this, they immediately attained understanding; when the ministers heard it, there was none among them who did not rejoice, realizing that the words of the wise must not be disregarded.
The Sutra of the Storehouse of Miscellaneous Jewels, Volume Seven;
The Sutra of the Storehouse of Miscellaneous Jewels, Volume Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kiṭyāya of the Western Regions during the Yuan-Wei Dynasty, together with Tanyao.
The minister and his wife of the kingdom of Kuśinagara harbored ill will toward the Buddha, but the Buddha immediately transformed them through his guidance, and they attained [enlightenment].

The Srotāpanna: The story of the Buddha’s younger brother Nanda being urged by the Buddha to leave the household life and attain the Way; the story of a great strongman converting a band of thieves in the wilderness; the story of a prime minister hearing the Dharma and becoming free from desire; the story of a Nirgrantha throwing himself into a fire-pit and being saved by the Buddha; the story of five hundred white geese hearing the Dharma and being reborn in heaven; the story of Devadatta releasing the intoxicated elephant Dhanapāla with the intent to harm the Buddha; (95) the story of the prime minister and his wife in the kingdom of Kuśinagara conceiving ill-will toward the Buddha, and how the Buddha immediately transformed them through guidance so that they attained the stage of Srotāpanna. (95) The story of the prime minister and his wife in the kingdom of Kuśinagara conceiving ill-will toward the Buddha, and how the Buddha immediately transformed them through guidance so that they attained the stage of Srotāpanna: When the Buddha was in the kingdom of Kuśinagara, there was a Brahmin prime minister who was violent and fierce, always acting contrary to the Way; his wife was likewise deceitful and no different from him.
The husband instructed his wife, saying:
"The Śramaṇa Gautama is within our territory; if he comes here, close the door and do not open it.
One day, the Tathāgata suddenly appeared inside their house; upon seeing him, the Brahmin woman remained silent and did not speak to him at all.
The Buddha then said:
"You brahmins are foolish and hold false views!
You do not believe in the Three Jewels."
Upon hearing these words, the wife was filled with extreme rage; she tore off her pearl necklace, put on soiled and greasy clothes, and sat upon the ground.
When her husband returned from outside, he asked her:
"Why are you like this?"
He replied, “The śramaṇa Gautama insulted me, saying these words: ‘You, brāhmaṇa!…’”
They held wrong views and did not believe.
The husband said, "Wait until tomorrow; open the gates tomorrow and await the arrival of the Buddha."

On a subsequent day at noon, the Buddha appeared at his house. The brāhmaṇa immediately seized a sharp sword and struck at the Buddha, but he was unable to reach him. Seeing the Buddha suspended in mid-air, he felt deep shame and remorse; prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will..."
"Please descend and accept my repentance.
The Buddha immediately descended and accepted his repentance, preaching the essentials of the Dharma for him; both husband and wife attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
At that time, when the bhikṣus heard that the Buddha had converted such an evil person, they each said:
"The appearance of the World-Honored One in this world is truly marvelous and extraordinary!"
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"Not only today, but in the past as well, he was once tamed.
The bhikṣu said:
"I do not understand how he was subdued in the past.
The Buddha said:

"Long ago, in the kingdom of Kāśī, there was a king named Duḥśīla (Evil Reception). He practiced extreme unrighteousness, causing suffering and distress to the common people. Cruel and devoid of the Way, he seized all the rare treasures and superior goods from merchants from distant lands as taxes, without paying them their rightful value."
Because of this, the precious goods within the kingdom became exceedingly expensive; people spoke of it among themselves, and his ill repute spread abroad.
At that time, there was a king of parrots in the forest who, hearing travelers speak of the king’s wickedness, thought to himself:
"Though I am but a bird, I still know what is wrong. I shall now go to him to explain the path of virtue."
If that king hears my words, he will surely say:
"Even that king of birds possesses such virtuous speech; how much more so for a king of men? He must be reproached by him, so that he might perhaps reform his conduct."
He immediately flew high up and reached the king’s garden, where he circled and descended to perch upon a tree.
At that moment, the king’s consort entered the garden for a stroll; the parrot then beat its wings and cooed, addressing her:

"The king is now exceedingly tyrannical and unrighteous, harming the myriad people and extending his cruelty even to birds and beasts. All living beings cry out in distress; humans and animals are filled with resentment, and the sound of their sighs and lamentations resounds throughout the world."
"The Queen bears the burden of governance no differently than the King; as a parent to the people, how could she act in such a manner?
Upon hearing this, the Queen’s poisonous wrath flared up:
"What lowly bird is this that insults me with such profanity?"
He dispatched men to watch for and capture it.
At that time, the parrot was neither startled nor afraid; it entered the hands of the captors.
When the lady obtained it, she immediately presented it to the king.
The king said to the parrot,
"Why do you revile me?
The parrot replied:
"I spoke of the King's unrighteousness because I wished to benefit you; I did not dare to revile you.
At that time, the King asked, "What was unrighteous?"
He replied,
"There are seven matters that are contrary to the Dharma which can endanger the king's life.
The king asked:
“What are the seven? He replied:
“The first is to be addicted to and obsessed with female beauty, failing to strive for chastity and rectitude.”
Second, they are addicted to wine and intoxicated by disorder, showing no concern for state affairs.
Third, they are greedily attached to chess and gambling, failing to cultivate ritual and instruction.
Fourth, they engage in hunting and killing, possessing no compassion whatsoever.
Fifth, they delight in uttering evil words and never speak well.
Sixth, they impose taxes, labor services, and punishments at double the usual rate.
Seventh, they plunder the people's wealth without any sense of righteousness or principle.
"There are these seven matters that can endanger the king's person.
Furthermore, there are three matters that bring ruin to the kingdom.
The king asked again:
"What are the three things? He replied:
"The first is to associate with those who are wicked, sycophantic, and deceitful."
Second, he does not associate with the worthy and sage, nor does he accept loyal counsel.
Third, he delights in attacking other states and fails to nourish his own people.
Unless these three faults are eliminated, the time for his downfall will come either this morning or this evening.
Now, as for one who acts as a king, all within the realm look up to him in devotion; the king should be like a bridge, ferrying across the myriad people;
the king should be like a scale, treating both kin and strangers with impartiality;
the king should be like the Way, never deviating from the traces of the sages.
A king is like the sun, universally illuminating the world;
a king is like the moon, bringing refreshing coolness to all things;
a king is like parents, nurturing with kindness and compassion.
A king is like heaven, covering and protecting all;
a king is like the earth, supporting and nourishing the myriad things;
a king is like fire, for the sake of the myriad people, burning away evil afflictions.
"A king is like water, moistening and nourishing the four quarters.
He should be like the past Wheel-Turning Sage Kings, transforming and teaching sentient beings through the ten paths of wholesome action.
Upon hearing these words, the king felt deep self-reproach and shame.
"The words of this parrot are most sincere and earnest.
As I am a king of men, my conduct has been devoid of the Way.
He requested to follow its instructions, to honor it as his teacher, and to receive its teachings for the cultivation of correct practice.

At that time, as the governance and moral instruction were established within the realm, ill repute was extinguished; the ladies of the court and the ministers all gave rise to loyalty and reverence, and there was not a single person among the populace who did not rejoice. It was like a bull-king crossing a river: when the leader is upright, those who follow are likewise upright.
At that time, the parrot was my own self.
At that time, the wicked King of Kāśi was this present prime minister.
At that time, the queen was this present wife of the prime minister.

96. The Circumstances of the Buddha’s Younger Brother Nanda Being Urged by the Buddha to Leave Home and Attain the Way (96) The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kapilavastu. He entered the city to beg for alms and arrived at the house of Nanda. At that time, he encountered Nanda applying cosmetic ointments to his wife, specifically painting between her eyebrows. Hearing that the Buddha was at the gate, Nanda wished to go out to see him. His wife made an agreement with him, saying:
"Go and see the Tathāgata, but return here before the ointment on my forehead has even dried."
Nanda immediately went out, prostrated before the Buddha, took the bowl toward his house, and filled it with food to offer to the Buddha.
The Buddha did not accept it; he passed it to Ānanda, but Ānanda also did not accept it.
Ānanda said to him, "From whom did you receive this bowl? Return it to its original place."
Thereupon, taking his bowl, he followed the Buddha until they reached the Nyagrodha Monastery.
The Buddha then commanded the barber to shave Nanda’s hair.
Nanda was unwilling; clenching his fist in anger, he spoke to the barber, saying:
"All the people of Kapilavastu, you may now shave their hair.
The Buddha asked the shaver:
"Why have you not shaved [yours]?"
He replied, "I am afraid, and therefore do not dare to shave him.
The Buddha, together with Ānanda, went to his side; out of fear, Nanda did not dare to refuse to shave him.
Although he had been granted permission to shave his head, he constantly desired to return home; yet whenever the Buddha took him along on his travels, he was unable to leave.

Later, on one day, as it was his turn to guard the dwelling, he rejoiced to himself, thinking, "Now I have truly found the opportunity to return home. Once the Buddha and the assembly of monks have all departed, I shall go back to my family."
After the Buddha had entered the city, he thought to himself:
"I shall draw water to fill my bathing flask, and then I will return. He immediately drew water;
one flask was just filled when another overturned. This continued for some time, yet he could not fill the flasks. Then he spoke these words:
"Neither can be filled; let the bhikṣus come back and draw water themselves. For now, I shall simply leave the jars inside the room and depart.
He then closed the door of the room, but as soon as he closed one leaf, the other leaf opened again; as soon as he closed one panel, another panel opened again.
He then thought further: "Neither can be closed; I shall leave them as they are and go."
"Even if the robes and belongings of the bhikṣus are lost, I possess abundant wealth and treasure, sufficient to provide compensation.
He then left the monastic quarters and thought to himself, "The Buddha will surely come by this path; I shall depart by a different route."
The Buddha, knowing his intention, also came by a different path. Seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, he hid behind a large tree.
The tree spirit lifted the tree into the air and stood it upright in the open space.
The Buddha saw Nanda and, leading him back to the vihāra, asked him:
"Do you still think of your wife?
He replied:
"Reflect truly.
He then led Nanda toward Anāpāna Mountain and asked him again,
"Is your wife beautiful?"
He replied, "She is beautiful.
In the mountains there was an old, blind monkey who asked again:
“Your wife Sundarī has a face and features of such exquisite beauty; how can she be compared to this monkey?
Nanda was distressed and thought to himself:
“My wife’s beauty is peerless among men; for what reason does the Buddha now compare my wife to this monkey?”

The Buddha again led him up to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, visiting all the celestial palaces together to observe them; there they saw the sons of gods and the goddesses enjoying themselves in mutual delight.
He saw within one palace five hundred celestial maidens, but no celestial youths.
Upon his return, he questioned the Buddha,
who said, "Go yourself and ask."
Nanda went and asked, "In all the other palaces there are devaputras; why is it that there are none here?
The goddess replied:

"Within Jambudvīpa, there is the Buddha’s younger brother Nanda. Because the Buddha urged him to leave the household life, by virtue of that cause and condition of renunciation, he will, at the end of his life, be reborn in this celestial palace as my son among the devas."
Nanda replied, “It is I myself.
As he was about to remain there, the celestial maiden said to him:
"We are devas and you are now a human; having relinquished your human lifespan and been reborn here, you may now dwell in peace.
He then returned to the Buddha's presence and reported all that had occurred in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha said to Nanda,
"How does your wife’s beauty compare to that of a celestial maiden?
Nanda replied:
"Compared to those celestial maidens, she is like a blind monkey compared to my wife.
The Buddha then led Nanda back to Jambudvīpa; for the sake of being reborn in heaven, Nanda diligently maintained the precepts with great resolve.
At that time, Ānanda, he spoke these verses for him:
"Just as rams fight, advancing only to retreat again,
so too is your practice of upholding the precepts."

The Buddha led Nanda back to the hells once more; he saw various cauldrons of boiling water, all of which were cooking people, yet there was only one cauldron that remained empty while bubbling and boiling.
Wondering at the reason for this, he came to question the Buddha. The Buddha told him, "Go yourself and ask.
Nanda immediately went there and questioned the wardens of hell, saying:
"All these cauldrons are used to boil and punish sinners; why then is this cauldron empty and contains nothing being boiled?

He replied, "Within Jambudvīpa there is a younger brother of the Tathāgata named Nanda. By virtue of his merit from leaving the household life, he was destined to be reborn in heaven; however, due to the circumstances of his desire to abandon the path, his heavenly lifespan ended and he fell into this hell. Therefore, I am now heating the cauldron and waiting for him."
Nanda was terrified, fearing that the hell-wardens would detain him, and he immediately said: "Namo Buddhāya!
I pray only that you will protect me and lead me back to Jambudvīpa."
The Buddha said to Nanda,
“Diligently uphold the precepts and cultivate your heavenly merit.
Nanda replied:
"I do not wish to be born in heaven; I only pray that I may not fall into this hell.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and within seven days, he became an Arhat.
The bhikṣus exclaimed:
"The appearance of the World-Honored One in this world is most marvelous and extraordinary!
The Buddha said:
"It is not only today; it was also thus in the distant past.
The bhikṣus asked, "If it was also so in the past, what were those events?"
"Please explain this to me.
The Buddha said:
"In the past, there was a king of Kāśī named Pūrṇamukha. In the kingdom of Videha, there was a courtesan who was exceptionally beautiful and graceful."

At that time, the two kingdoms were constantly at odds with one another out of mutual resentment and jealousy. A sycophantic minister, addressing the King of Kāśī, praised the beauty of a courtesan in the rival kingdom, saying she was of such exquisite form as to be rarely seen in the world.
