Upon hearing these words, the king’s mind became filled with confusion and attachment; he dispatched a messenger to demand [the person] from him, but that country would not give him up.
He sent another messenger with this message:
"I request to see him for a short while; within four or five days, I shall send him back."
At that time, the king of that country commanded the courtesan:
"Your physical charms and all your artistic skills are perfectly complete; cause the King of Kāśi to become infatuated with you so that he cannot distance himself from you for even a moment."
He immediately sent her away; after four or five days had passed, he summoned her again and said:
"I wish to perform a great sacrifice and require this girl; let her return for a short while, and I shall send her back again later."
The King of Kāśi immediately sent him back. Once the great sacrifice was completed, he dispatched a messenger to demand his return, to which the reply was:
"He shall be sent tomorrow.
When the next day arrived, he was still not sent.
Thus he spoke these falsehoods for many days.

The king’s mind became deluded and attached; taking only a few attendants with him, he intended to go to that country, yet though his ministers exhorted and remonstrated with him, he refused to accept their counsel.
At that time, in the mountains of the Rishis, there was a monkey king who was intelligent, erudite, and possessed great knowledge; his wife having recently died, he took a female monkey as his mate.
The entire troop of monkeys became angry and rebuked him, saying, "This lustful monkey belongs to the whole community; for what reason do you claim her alone?
Then the monkey king, taking his female companion, fled into the kingdom of Kāśī and sought refuge with the king, while the rest of the monkey troop pursued them together.
Having reached the city, they tore down roofs and demolished walls, making it impossible to repair.
The King of Kāśī said to the monkey king,
"Why do you not now return a female monkey to the other monkeys?"
The monkey king said, "My wife has died, and I have no other wife; why does Your Majesty now wish to send me back?
The king spoke to him, saying:
"Now you, monkey, have brought ruin and disorder to my kingdom; how can you not return?
The monkey king said, "Is this matter not unfavorable?"
The king replied,
"It is not good.
Thus he spoke a second and a third time, yet the king still said it was not good.
The monkey king said:
"In your palace there are eighty-four thousand ladies; you take no pleasure in them, yet you wish to go to a hostile kingdom to pursue a courtesan."
"I currently have no wife; I would take this one alone, yet you say she is not good enough.
All the people of the myriad clans depend on you for their livelihood; how can you abandon her for the sake of a single courtesan?"

Great King, you should know that the matter of sensual desire brings little pleasure and much suffering; it is like holding a blazing torch against the wind—if a fool does not let go, he will surely be burned and harmed.
Sensual desire is impure, like a heap of excrement;
sensual desire manifests its outward form, yet it is covered by a thin skin;
sensual desire is devoid of gratitude, like a venomous snake smeared with dung.
Desire is like a hostile thief, feigning intimacy with people;
desire is like a borrowed object, which must inevitably be returned;
desire is loathsome, like flowers growing in a latrine.
Desire is like a scabies rash; when one approaches a fire to scratch it, the irritation only intensifies.
Desire is like a dog gnawing on a dry bone; as its saliva mingles with it, the dog deems it flavorful, yet its lips and teeth are worn away without ever knowing satisfaction.
Desire is like a thirsty person drinking salt water; it only serves to increase their thirst further.
"Desire is like a piece of meat, which various birds vie to seize;
desire is like a fish or a beast, which, out of greed for flavor, follows it until death—its affliction is truly great.
At that time, the monkey king was none other than myself.
The king at that time was Nanda;
the courtesan at that time was Sundarī.
At that time, I sought to pull Nanda out from the mire of desire, and now I likewise pull him out from the suffering of birth and death.
97. The Story of the Great Strongman Transforming the Bandits of the Wilderness (97). At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
Between the two kingdoms of Rājagṛha and Vaiśālī, there were five hundred bands of bandits.
King Bimbisāra, being compassionate, benevolent, magnanimous, and virtuous, governed the world with the Dharma of grace and did not harm living beings. He then issued a proclamation, saying:
"Whoever can go and convert these five hundred bands of thieves so that they cease their thievery shall be granted high rank and rewards."
At that time, there was a strongman who came to respond to the king's recruitment; he went to that wilderness and pacified the bandits, immediately enabling them to cease their thievery forever.
Having been able to subdue them, he established a great city and settled them there; as they gradually gathered and many people came to rely upon him, it eventually became a great kingdom.
The people of that country each spoke these words:
"We have now received the grace of being nurtured by this great strongman; let us gather together and make this solemn agreement:
'From this day forward, whoever takes a new wife shall first offer her to the strongman.'"
He went immediately to where the Mallas were and said to them, "We have made an agreement:
whoever has newly taken a wife shall present her to the Mallas for two reasons; first, because they desire fine offspring who will resemble the Mallas."
"Secondly, it is to repay the kindness of the Malla.
The Malla replied,
"What need is there for this?"
The crowd was insistent and thus complied with their wishes.
While they were practicing this rite for some time, there was a woman who took no pleasure in it; she stood naked before the assembly to urinate.
The crowd all rebuked her, saying, "How can you be so shameless? Why do you stand to urinate in front of everyone?"
The woman replied, "When women urinate naked even in the presence of other women, what shame is there?
This entire country consists of women; only the great wrestlers are men. If it were before them, one ought to feel abashed, but before you all, what cause for shame is there?"
From this, the multitude of people began to say to one another,
"What this woman has said is precisely the truth.
At that time, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were traveling through a wilderness with five hundred disciples.
The Malla knew of this and invited the two Venerable Ones along with their five hundred disciples, providing them with lodging and supplying them with food and clothing.
After three days had passed, the people of the country gathered for a festival; having become excessively drunk from drinking wine, they surrounded the house of the Great Malla and set it on fire.
The Malla asked, "For what reason have you done this?"
The crowd replied, "When women first marry, they all pass through you; we are human beings and could not bear this matter, so we have come to burn you."
The Malla replied, "I did not consent; you all forced me.
They would not listen, so they burned him until he died. As his life was about to end, he made this vow:
"By virtue of the merit from my offerings to Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, I have been born here in this wilderness as a powerful spirit-ghost (yakṣa) to destroy these people."
Having spoken these words, his life was immediately severed; he then became a magically born ghost (*upapāduka-preta*) in the wilderness, emitting a great poisonous vapor and killing many people.
When they reached the middle ground, a wise man said to the ghost together with the others:

"You have now slaughtered immeasurable people, yet you cannot finish eating their flesh; it would be in vain to let it rot and stink. We pray that you will allow us to slaughter oxen and horses instead, providing you with one person every day."
Thereupon, throughout the kingdom, everyone together drew lots, with each person taking their turn for one day.
In this manner, it came to a certain elder’s daughter-in-law, Sūdarśanā; she gave birth to a son who was virtuous and handsome, yet his turn had arrived to be food for the ghosts.
The elder thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata has appeared in the world to rescue and deliver all sentient beings from suffering and distress.
I only pray that the World-Honored One [will grant me his presence]!"
"Protect my son from his calamity today!
The Buddha, being in Rājagṛha, knew the elder’s thoughts and immediately went to sit within the palace of the forest spirit (yakṣa) in the wilderness.
A yakṣa from the wilderness came to see the World-Honored One; filled with extreme rage, he said to the Buddha, "Śramaṇa, depart!
The Buddha then departed.
The ghost entered the palace, and the Buddha returned inside.
This happened three times; on the fourth occasion, the Buddha did not come out, whereupon the ghost spoke these words:
"If you do not come out, I shall cause your mind to become inverted, and I will seize your feet and hurl you into the Ganges."
The Buddha said to him,
"I do not see anyone in the world— whether among the devas, Māras, or Brahmās— who could seize me and treat me in such a manner.
The wilderness spirit said:
“Just so, just so. The Tathāgata has granted me permission to ask about four matters;

you should explain them to me. First, who is able to cross the swift current? Second, who is able to cross the great ocean? Third, who is able to abandon all suffering? Fourth, who is able to attain purity?”
The Buddha replied:
"Faith can cross the swift current; heedfulness can cross the great ocean; diligence can abandon suffering; and wisdom can attain purity."

Having heard these words, he immediately took refuge in the Buddha and became a disciple of the Buddha. Taking the young boy by the hand, he placed him inside the Buddha’s alms bowl; consequently, the boy was named Kalandaka (Wilderness-Hand). As he gradually grew up, the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stage of Anāgāmin.
The bhikṣus said:
“It is truly rare for the World-Honored One to appear in this world!
That such a malevolent spirit of the great wilderness could be subdued by the Buddha and become a lay follower (upāsaka) is marvelous.”

The Buddha said, "Not only today, but in the past as well, there was once a vast wilderness between the two kingdoms of Kāśī and Videha. There dwelt an evil spirit named Śaṭhala who cut off the roads, so that no people at all could pass through."
There was a caravan leader named Siṃha who, leading five hundred merchants, intended to travel along this road; the men were terrified, fearing they could not pass through it.
The merchant leader said:
"Do not be afraid!
Simply follow behind me."
Thereupon he proceeded forward, arrived at the place where the ghost was, and said to the ghost:
"Have you not heard my name?
The ghost replied:
"I have heard your name, and thus I have come wishing to fight.
He asked, "What are you capable of?"

He immediately seized his bow and arrows and shot at the ghost; five hundred arrows were released, all of which sank into the ghost’s belly. His bow, sword, and other weapons also entered the ghost’s belly. He stepped forward and struck with his fist, but the fist also went inside. He pressed with his right hand, but the right hand also stuck; he stamped with his right foot, but the right foot also stuck; he stamped with his left foot, but the left foot also stuck;

he then struck with his head, but the head also stuck. The ghost spoke in verse: “You have used your hands, feet, and head— Every single thing has become stuck. What else do you have that does not stick?”
The merchant leader replied with a verse:
"My hands, my feet, and my head, All my wealth and my weapons— Only diligence does not cling to you; If diligence shall never rest..."
"I shall never cease contending with you; now that I am practicing diligence without rest, I shall never give rise to fear toward you.
At that time, the ghost replied:
"I have now, for your sake, released all five hundred merchants.
At that time, the lion was my own self;
at that time, the Śaṭha was the wilderness spirit.
98. The Story of the Minister Who Heard the Dharma and Became Free from Desire (98). The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
The king had a chief minister who frequently went with the king to the place where the Buddha was, there to listen as the Tathāgata taught the Dharma on becoming free from desire.
Later, he did not visit his wife very often; she conceived a malicious intent, sought out poison, placed it in food and drink, and invited the Buddha, intending to give it to him.

The husband realized that his wife harbored ill intentions; when he asked her for food and drink, she refused to give him any and instead offered him different food. When the Buddha arrived, the husband said to the Buddha, "This food is unfit to be eaten."
The Buddha asked,
"Why may it not be eaten?
They replied:
"It is poisonous.
The Buddha said, "In this world, there are no poisons greater than the three poisons; since I have already eliminated these, what minor poison could possibly harm me?"
The Buddha then ate the food, and it was in every way no different from usual.
At that time, the wife of the prime minister gave rise to faith; the Buddha preached the Dharma for her, and both husband and wife attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
The bhikṣus marveled at this unprecedented event!
The Buddha said:
"Not only today, but in the past as well, I have transformed them."
In the past, the King of Kāśī had a wise minister named Bṛhaspati, who constantly assisted the king and all his ministers with the teachings of the Dharma, causing them all to cultivate goodness.
At that time, there was a dragon king named Vairocana who frequently came and went to the abode of Bhṛgu to listen to and receive the words of the Dharma; he also visited his wife only rarely.
The nāga wife, filled with rage, spoke these words:
"Only by obtaining the heart of Bhituḥi to offer as a sacrifice to the fire, and by drinking his blood, can you be restored to life.
At that time, there was a yakṣa who was on friendly terms with this nāga king and his wife; hearing the nāga wife's words, he immediately replied:
"I can obtain it. Taking the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) from the dragon lady, he disguised himself as a merchant and traveled to the kingdom of Kāśī.

Upon arriving before the king, he played at dice with him, wagering the wish-fulfilling jewel. The king staked his kingdom, his treasury, and his *bimbisāra* [palace] as the counter-bet against that jewel.
The yakṣa was victorious; he did not seek the kingdom or its treasuries, but took only Bhituḥi and gave him the jewel to the king.
The king asked Bhituḥi, "Do you wish to leave?"
He replied,
"I wish to go.
As the yakṣa was leading him away, Piṭhika asked the yakṣa:
“Why have you come to seek me? What is your purpose?
The yakṣa did not answer.
When he questioned him thus persistently and repeatedly without ceasing, the yakṣa finally spoke to him:
"The Dragon King’s wife wishes to obtain your heart to offer it as a sacrifice to the fire, and she wishes to obtain your blood to drink. Bhituḥi said:
"If they were to kill me and take my heart and blood away, since the heart-blood of all people is of one kind, how would one know whose it was?"
Do not kill me now; take me away instead. If you need my heart, you desire my wisdom; if you need my blood, you desire my Dharma.
Having heard these words, the yakṣa thought to himself, "He is truly a wise man," and immediately led him to the place where the nāga was.
Upon seeing him, the nāga rejoiced and immediately preached the Dharma for him.
The dragon king and his wife, along with their retinue, gave rise to a mind of reverent faith and fully received the five precepts; the hosts of yakṣas likewise received the five precepts.
At that time, the nāgas and yakṣas of Jambudvīpa brought a great abundance of rare treasures to present to Bhitu-he.
Having received these treasures, Bhitu-he offered them to the king and distributed them among the people.
Thereupon, the people of Jambudvīpa, as well as the nāgas and ghosts, received and upheld the five precepts and practiced the ten wholesome actions.
At that time, I myself was Vituḥi.
The Dragon King Mingxiang at that time was the minister Shanjian;
the dragon wife at that time was the minister’s wife;
and the king at that time was Śāriputra.
"The yakṣa at that time was Maudgalyāyana. 99.
The Story of the Nirgrantha Throwing Himself into a Mass of Fire and Being Saved by the Buddha (99). The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Tathāgata subdued the six heterodox teachers of wrong views and their followers, causing them all to be utterly defeated.
The five hundred Nirgranthas thought to themselves:
"Our entire assembly has been completely shattered and dispersed; it would be better for us to burn our bodies and attain an early rebirth in the next world."
He immediately gathered wood and grass, intending to burn his body.
Out of great compassion, the Tathāgata wished to uproot his suffering and caused the fire not to ignite.
The Buddha stood by his side and entered the *tejodhātu-samādhi* (the samādhi of the fire-element).
When the Nirgranthas saw the great mass of fire, their hearts were filled with joy, and they spoke these words:
"We have no need to kindle a fire; let us all throw ourselves into it together."
Once he had entered the fire, his body became cool and refreshing, and he experienced supreme bliss; seeing the Buddha therein, his joy redoubled, and he sought to leave the household life.
The Buddha said, “Welcome, Bhikṣu!
His beard and hair fell away, and the Dharma robes appeared upon his body. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained arhatship.
The bhikṣus said:
"How extraordinary, World-Honored One!
You have been able to uproot the suffering of these Nirgranthas who were self-immolating and cause them to become arhats."
The Buddha said, "Not only today;
in the past, there were five hundred merchants in the kingdom of Śrāvastī who went to sea to gather treasures."

At that time, there was a merchant leader named Viśākha who, leading a multitude of merchants, traveled with a favorable wind until he reached a place of treasures, which he then gathered and loaded onto his ships.
The merchants, greedy for precious jewels, loaded their ship with an excessive weight.
At that time, Viśākhā said to the traders,
"Do not overload yourselves with jewels, lest you lose your lives."
At that time, the merchants did not heed his words; they would rather die with their treasures than diminish them.
The merchant leader then cast the ship’s treasures into the water and took the other merchants onto his own vessel. Those treasure ships were then submerged in the sea.

When the Sea God saw that this merchant leader was able to renounce his precious treasures to save the other traders, he felt great joy in his heart. He took the treasures discarded by the merchant leader, carried them while flying ahead, and once they had safely emerged from the sea, he returned them to the merchant leader.
The merchants said, "Why should we not take our own lives right here at this place of treasure?

Seeing their distress, Viśākha felt deep compassion; he shared all the precious jewels he had obtained with them and then practiced the way of renunciation according to the non-Buddhist outsiders, attaining the five supernormal powers.
The merchants said:
"A great being such as this does not covet wealth or treasures, but cultivates his own resolve and thereby attains great benefit; we should follow his example."
Each of them renounced their precious treasures and went to the place where the seer was, practicing his dharma until they all attained the five supernormal powers.
At that time, the one named Viśākhā was none other than myself.
"At that time, the five hundred merchants were these five hundred Nirgranthas. 100.
The Story of the Five Hundred White Geese Hearing the Dharma and Rebirth in Heaven. The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the Pañcāla kingdom presented five hundred white geese as an offering to King Prasenajit, who then sent them to the Jetavana Monastery.
When the community of monks was taking their meal, each person went out to beg for alms. Seeing the assembly of monks gathered, the goose came forward and stood before them.
The Buddha preached the Dharma with a single voice, yet all sentient beings each understood it according to their own kind.

At that time, the flock of geese also understood the Buddha’s words; hearing the Dharma, they were filled with joy and called out to one another in harmony as they returned to the pond. Later, when their feathers had grown long, they flew to other places, where a hunter covered them all with a net and killed them.

When they were caught in the net, one goose let out a cry and all the geese joined in harmony; this was called the sound of listening to the Dharma, and by virtue of this wholesome mind, they were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Regarding the dharma for rebirth in heaven, there are three recollections:
first, recollecting where one originally came from;
second, recollecting in which place one will certainly be born.
Third, he reflects on what karma he previously performed to have been reborn in the heavens;
he then contemplates within himself and perceives his past causes, seeing that there was no other merit, only having listened to the Dharma from the Buddha and the Sangha.
Having formed this thought, five hundred devaputras immediately descended and stood beside the Tathāgata; the Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they all attained the stage of Srotāpanna.
King Prasenajit, having come to the place where the Buddha was, usually saw five hundred geese arrayed before the Buddha;
on this day, however, they were not to be seen, so he asked the Buddha, "Where have all these geese gone?"
The Buddha asked,
"Do you wish to see the geese?
The king replied:
"I wish to see him.
The Buddha said, "The goose first flew away to another place, where he was killed by a hunter; at the end of his life, he was reborn in heaven."
"These five hundred sons of gods, who now wear fine celestial crowns and are so exceptionally handsome and distinguished, have today heard the Dharma and all attained the stage of Srotāpanna."
The king asked the Buddha,
"By what karmic conditions did these geese fall into the realm of animals, and yet at the end of their lives were reborn in heaven, and today have attained the Way?"
The Buddha said:

"In the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, five hundred women all received the precepts together. However, their resolve was not firm; they violated the precepts they had received. Due to these causes and conditions of breaking the precepts, they fell among the animals and were born with the bodies of these geese."

"Because he received the precepts, he was able to meet the Tathāgata, hear the Dharma, and attain the Way; through the causal conditions of listening to the Dharma while in the body of a goose, he was reborn in the heavens.
101. The Circumstances of Devadatta Releasing the Intoxicated Elephant Dhanapāla to Harm the Buddha (101). The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, Devadatta released the intoxicated elephant Dhanapāla, intending to harm the Buddha; five hundred arhats all flew into the air, while Ānanda alone remained behind the Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha raised his right hand; the white elephant Dhana-pāla saw five hundred lions, and the elephant became terrified, yet he immediately became tamed and submissive.
All five hundred bhikṣus abandoned the Buddha and departed, with the sole exception of Ānanda, who remained behind the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Not only today, but it was also so in the past.
Long ago, in the kingdom of Kāśī, there were five hundred geese who lived together as a flock. At that time, the king of the geese was named Ratha, and the king had a minister named Sumana."

At that time, this king of geese was captured by a hunter; the flock of five hundred geese all abandoned him and flew away, but only Soma followed him closely and would not leave. She spoke to the hunter, saying:
"Please release my king; I shall take his place with my own body this day."
The hunter would not listen and eventually presented the king of geese to King Brahmadatta.
The king asked the king of geese,
"Are you safe and well?"

The king of geese replied, "I have received Your Majesty’s great kindness; having obtained Your Majesty’s clear water and excellent grass, my life is sustained and I dwell in peace within your realm."
"I only pray, Great King,
that you release all these geese so that they may be free from fear.
Then the flock of five hundred geese, positioned above the king’s palace in the air, let out a cry.
At that time, the king asked,
"What kind of goose is this?
The goose king replied:
"These are my attendants.
The king immediately granted them fearlessness and issued a proclamation throughout his inner and outer domains:
"It is forbidden to kill geese."
The king of geese addressed the king, saying: "Now you must govern the kingdom with the True Dharma.

The world is impermanent, like mountains from the four directions. For example, a great mountain from the east, its summit boundless, might suddenly descend; the same would occur from the south, west, and north. These mountains would grind the world to dust, and all sentient beings, including humans and spirits, would be utterly extinguished. There would be no place to escape, nothing to rely upon, and no means of salvation."
At that time, what can one rely upon? One should simply reflect thus:
"I ought to nurture all beings universally with a compassionate heart, practice the True Dharma, and perform all manner of meritorious deeds."
Great King, you should know:
all wealth and nobility are crushed and shattered by decline; coming from the four quarters, they lead to ruin and loss.
All vigor and strength are likewise beset by various diseases; arriving from the four quarters, they destroy and annihilate robust health.
All youthfulness is like a mountain of frailty and disease that comes from the four directions to destroy it;
all life is like a great mountain of death that comes from the four directions to annihilate it.
These four mountains are common to all; among gods, dragons, humans, ghosts, and all classes of living beings, there is none who can escape them.
For this reason, one should constantly cultivate a mind of loving-kindness and diligently practice the True Dharma.

If one is able to do so, one will have no regrets at the time of death; because the mind is without regret, one will be reborn in a good realm, where one will surely encounter noble sages and saints. Having encountered these noble sages and saints, one shall attain liberation from birth and death.
The King asked Soma,
"Why are you silent? Soma replied:

"Now, as the Goose King and the Human King, these two kings converse together; if there were to be any interference in their speech, it would not accord with the rules of propriety, and there would be no heart of reverence and respect between superior and subordinate."
The king said,
"Truly it is rare! Though you have the body of a goose,
you are able to practice such loyalty as a minister, surpassing what humans can achieve, and are able to sacrifice your own life to take the place of the goose king."
"Furthermore, he was humble and compliant, refraining from idle speech; such a bond between sovereign and minister as yours, O Goose King, is rare in this world.
He then gave him a golden *kinkinī* (necklace) to fasten around his neck and placed a fine white silk cloth upon the head of the Goose King before dispatching him, saying:
"Go and preach the True Dharma for me."
He then released them.
"The king of the geese at that time was I myself;
Soma at that time was Ānanda."
"The king of men at that time was my father, King Śuddhodana;
the hunter at that time was Devadatta.
— *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka Sūtra*, Volume VIII.
The Sutra of the Storehouse of Various Jewels, Volume Nine.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kiṭāya of the Western Regions together with Tanyao during the Yuan Wei Dynasty.
The Circumstances of Kātyāyana Explaining Eight Dreams for King Caṇḍapradyota.

The Causes and Conditions of the Golden Cat; the Causes and Conditions by which King Duṣprasaha Obtained Five Hundred Bowls. [End of Volume] Within the subsequent text, there are further eight causes and three causes. 102. The Causes and Conditions of Kātyāyana Explaining Eight Dreams for King Duṣprasaha (102). The Causes and Conditions of Kātyāyana Explaining Eight Dreams for King Duṣprasaha: Formerly, King Duṣprasaha practiced cruelty, lacked a heart of compassion, and his false views were rampant.

The Tathāgata, out of great compassion, dispatched his disciples to convert all nations universally. Kātyāyana was of the Brahmin caste in the kingdom of King Caṇḍapradyota; the Buddha subsequently sent Kātyāyana back to convert that king, as well as his subjects.
At that time, the Venerable Kātyāyana, having received the Buddha’s instruction, immediately returned to his native country.
At that time, King Candaśoka, not beholding the true and right path, served heterodox ways; every morning, he was unwilling to see anyone and would first pay obeisance at the temples of the gods.

At that time, Kātyāyana, wishing to convert King Aśoka, rose early at dawn and manifested himself as a stranger; appearing like a foreign envoy with a dignified and handsome countenance, he arrived at the king’s gate.
When the king saw him, he returned to his original form and appeared in the likeness of a śramaṇa.
The king felt an even greater hatred toward the Daoist who had shaved his hair, and in great rage, the king said:
"You shall surely die now!"
He immediately dispatched men to take Kātyāyana, intending to inflict harm upon him.
Kātyāyana addressed the king, saying:
"What transgression have I committed that you should seek to kill me?"
The king spoke again, saying, "You are a shaven-headed man;
those who see you are ill-omened. For this reason, I now wish to kill you.
Venerable Kātyāyana then replied to him, saying:
"What is currently inauspicious pertains to me, not to the King. Why is this?

Although the King has seen me, he has suffered no harm whatsoever; yet when I see the King, he desires to have me killed. Judging by this, that which is called inauspicious resides precisely within me."
The king, being naturally intelligent, understood the meaning of these words as soon as he heard them; he released Kātyāyana and harbored no ill will.
He secretly dispatched two men to follow behind him to observe where he stayed and what food and drink he consumed.
He saw Kātyāyana sitting beneath a tree, eating almsfood; whenever he obtained food, he shared it with two others, and when there was a small remainder left over, he poured it into the river.
Once the two had returned, the king immediately asked them about the Venerable’s dwelling place and his food. The two reported everything they had seen to the king exactly as it was.
On a subsequent day, the king invited the Venerable Kātyāyana and provided him with coarse and unpalatable food; he then sent a messenger to ask:
"Is this food now to your liking?"
The Venerable replied,
"The power of that food has already sufficed. Later,
when he was given fine, delicately prepared food, the king again sent a messenger to inquire:
"Is it sufficient? He replied,
"The power of this food is already quite sufficient."
Later, the king asked the Venerable One:
"Regarding the food I have given, regardless of whether it was coarse or fine, everyone said it was sufficient.
What does this mean?"
The Venerable Kātyāyana then replied to the king:

"As for the body and speech, they are like a furnace: it burns sandalwood as well as filth and excrement. The body and speech are likewise; whether food is coarse or fine, the limit is simply being fully satisfied."
He then spoke in verse:
"This body is like a chariot; It makes no distinction between the beautiful and the foul.
Whether it be fragrant oil or stinking fat, They are all equally used for its maintenance."
When the king heard these words, he recognized the great virtue of the venerable one and immediately offered both coarse and fine food to the brahmins.
When the brahmins first received the coarse food, they were all filled with indignation and, assuming angry expressions, reviled him;
but when the fine food was later served, they rejoiced and offered their praise.
When the King saw that the brahmins and others felt joy and anger toward the food and drink, he conceived even greater faith and reverence for Kātyāyana.
At that time, the Venerable One had a maternal niece who previously lived in a brahmin village outside the city and possessed very beautiful hair.

As the time for the summer retreat arrived, he conceived a desire to make offerings; he cut his own hair and sold it, obtaining five hundred gold coins, with which he invited Kātyāyana to receive his summer retreat offerings.
When the Venerable Kātyāyana had completed his summer retreat, he returned to the city.

At that time, a pheasant that had suddenly died appeared at the gate of King Caṇḍapradyota’s palace; it was like the pheasant consumed by a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin), and King Caṇḍapradyota immediately desired to eat it.
At that time, a wise minister addressed the king, saying, "This pheasant should not be eaten immediately; it ought to be tested first.

The king followed his advice and immediately sent a man to cut off a small morsel to give to a dog. Once the dog had received the meat, he became greedily attached to its flavor and swallowed it whole with his tongue, until he eventually died.

Furthermore, he cut off a small piece of flesh to test one person; once that person had eaten the meat, they also became attached to its flavor, until they eventually came to devour their own hands and died.
Having seen this, the king was struck with deep terror. Then he heard someone say:
"As for this meat, only a Wheel-Turning Sage King, or one who has attained the Way through untainted wisdom, may eat it."
He immediately sent someone to prepare a delicious meal and deliver it to the Venerable Kātyāyana.
When Kātyāyana had finished eating this food, his body became at ease.
On a later day, the king dispatched people to observe him; they saw that Kātyāyana’s countenance was serene and joyful, appearing twice as radiant as usual.
Upon hearing this, the king felt profound wonder and increased his respect for him, while growing increasingly disdainful toward the non-Buddhist Brahmins and others.
The King asked Kātyāyana,
"Venerable One, where did you observe the summer retreat this year?
Is it only now that you have arrived?"
The Venerable One related in detail how she had sold her hair to a foreigner for money to provide offerings for the Sangha. Upon hearing these words, the king said:

"In my palace, even those with the most beautiful hair fetch no more than a few copper coins; yet now you say this woman's hair is worth five hundred gold pieces—this woman’s beauty of hair must be extraordinary, and her appearance surely exquisite."

He immediately asked for the names of the girl's parents and promptly dispatched a messenger; upon arriving there, he personally beheld the girl’s person, and her beauty was indeed as extraordinary as he had anticipated.
The king immediately dispatched a messenger to betroth her as his wife; however, her family demanded a vast amount of precious goods from the cities and villages. The king then reflected:
"If I grant these to them, when the girl arrives, she shall still belong to me."
He immediately gave her to him, and she was taken as his consort.
On the day of her initial reception, the entire kingdom rejoiced and celebrated, all declaring it a great auspiciousness.

On the following day, he again issued a general amnesty and bestowed upon her the title of Queen Śivakusā. The King held her in great affection and respect; subsequently, she gave birth to a crown prince named Gopāla.
At that time, while the king was sleeping, he saw eight things in a dream:
first, his head was ablaze with fire;
second, two snakes were constricting his waist.
Third, his body was entwined by three fine iron nets.
Fourth, he saw two red fish swallow both his feet.
Fifth, four white cranes flew toward the king.
Sixth, walking through blood-mud until the mud reaches his armpits;
seventh, ascending Mount Great White;
eighth, the crane with a head like a *mañjiṣṭhā* flower.
Having awakened from the dream, he considered it an ill omen and became sorrowful and dejected; he immediately went to consult various Brahmins.
When the Brahmins heard of the king's dream, they already harbored resentment toward him and were envious of the Venerable One; taking advantage of this dream, they said:
"Great King, this is inauspicious. If you do not perform rites of expiation and warding off, calamity will befall your person."

When the king heard these words, he believed them to be true; his grief and distress increased all the more, and he immediately asked him, "If you are to perform the rites of averting calamity, what items will you require?"
The brahmins said, "Whatever you require is what the king holds most dear; if we were to speak of it, the king would certainly not be able to grant it.
Then the king replied:
"This dream is most ominous; I fear a great calamity will befall my person. Aside from myself, there is nothing else I hold dear; please tell me what you require."
When the brahmins saw his earnestness and knew that his heart was sincere, they spoke to the king, saying:
"Regarding what is required, this dream has eight [elements]; it is essential that eight things be obtained to avert the calamity:
first, the killing of the queen Śivakūṣā, whom the king honors."
Second, he killed the king’s beloved crown prince, Jīvaka;
third, he killed the chief minister;
fourth, he killed the king’s vassal official.
The fifth, King Śaśaka, can travel three thousand li in a single day on an elephant;
the sixth, King Śaśaka, can travel three thousand li in a single day on a camel;
the seventh, King Śaśaka, possesses excellent horses.
"Kill the eight bald-headed Kātyāyanas.
Seven days hence, if you kill these eight and collect their blood, enter into it and walk; thus you shall be able to eliminate the calamity."
When the king heard these words, he granted his permission immediately because of the gravity of his own life.
Upon returning to the palace, he was filled with grief and distress.
The queen asked the king:

"Why is this so? the king replied to his consort, recounting in detail the inauspicious dream he had previously related, as well as what was required for the Brahmins to perform the rites for averting the dream's ill omen.
Having heard this, the lady spoke these words:
"If only Your Majesty’s person remains safe and free from affliction, what need is there to speak of this wretched body of mine?
She then addressed the king, saying:
"In seven days from now, I shall return and die; permit me to go to that venerable Kātyāyana for six days to observe the fast and listen to the Dharma."
The king said, "No.
If you go there, you might speak the truth; if he were to find out, he would abandon me and fly away."
The lady was so insistent that the king could not refuse her; he immediately granted her permission to go.
Once the lady had arrived at the residence of the Venerable One, she paid her respects and inquired after his well-being, remaining there for three days.
The Venerable One asked in wonder:
"The King’s consort has never before stayed here for even a single night; why is she now different from her usual self?
The consort related in detail the King’s evil dream, saying: "In seven days, he intends to kill us to avert this calamity. Our remaining lives are few; therefore, we have come to hear the Dharma."
He then recounted the king's dream to the Venerable One, and the Venerable Kātyāyana said:
"This dream is most auspicious!
There shall be cause for celebration; there is no need for concern."

As for the fire burning upon one's head: it signifies that the kingdom of the Lord of Jewels shall produce a celestial crown worth one hundred thousand taels of gold, which will come as tribute to the King; this dream was precisely for this reason.
The queen was in a great hurry; as the seven days were drawing to a close, she feared being too late for the King’s execution and asked the Venerable One, "When will you arrive?"
The Venerable One replied:
"This very day, at the hour of *pradoṣa*, he will surely arrive.
As for the one with two snakes coiled around his waist, he is the King of the Yuezhi; he shall present a pair of swords worth a hundred thousand taels of gold, and he will arrive as the sun sets."

As for those whose bodies are entwined with fine iron nets, they are the kings of the Great Qin; they shall present pearl necklaces worth one hundred thousand taels of gold, and they shall arrive tomorrow morning.

Regarding the one who swallowed the feet of the Crimson Fish: the Lion King’s kingdom shall present a lapis lazuli jeweled sandal worth one hundred thousand taels of gold; it shall arrive at the time of the meal on the following day.
As for the four white cranes that have come, they are the King of the Vṛji kingdom, who shall present a chariot of gold and jewels; he will arrive later this very day at noon.

As for the one in the bloody mud, he is the King of An-shi (Parthia), who shall present a *kambala* cloak of deer-hair worth a hundred thousand taels of gold; he will arrive later this very day at sunset.
As for those who ascend Mount Taibai: the King of the Kingdom of Kuangye shall present a great elephant, arriving at the hour of *bū* on the following day.
As for the crested crane: the King and his consort shall have a private matter; this shall be known of itself on the following day.
Just as the Venerable One had said, when the appointed time arrived, all that had been offered by the various kingdoms arrived, and the King was greatly delighted.

Queen Śivakusā already possessed a celestial crown; she then layered upon it the celestial crown offered by the kingdom of Ratnapati. During a playful jest, the King removed one layer of the celestial crown worn by Queen Śivakusā and placed it upon the head of Queen Suvarṇamālā.
At that time, Lady Śivakusā spoke with indignation:
"If there were any misfortune, I would have been the first to suffer it; yet now, having obtained this celestial crown, she has put it on instead."

He then took a vessel of curd and threw it onto the king’s head; the king’s head was completely smeared with it. Greatly incensed and enraged, the king drew his sword, intending to strike the lady. Fearing the king, she fled into a room and immediately bolted the door, so that the king could not advance.
The king soon realized for himself:
"The Venerable One’s interpretation of the dream spoke of a secret matter; this must indeed be it.

The king and his consort then went to the Venerable Kātyāyana and recounted in detail how they had previously believed the unlawful and evil words of heretics, nearly committing great wickedness toward the Venerable One, their wife and children, their ministers, and their cherished possessions.

"Now that we have received the Venerable One’s exposition of the truth, which has opened our blinded eyes and allowed us to behold the right path and depart from evil deeds, we entreat the Venerable One to accept our respectful offerings.
We shall expel all these Brahmins and others far beyond the borders of our kingdom."
He then asked the Venerable One:
"By what causes and conditions have these various kingdoms each offered me their most precious treasures?
The Venerable One replied:
"In the distant past, ninety-one kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin.

When that Buddha appeared in the world, there was a kingdom called Bandhumatī. The crown prince of that kingdom was faithful, joyful, and diligent; he went to the place where the Buddha was, made offerings and prostrations, and immediately presented to that Buddha the celestial crown he wore, his precious sword, his necklaces, his great elephant, his jeweled chariot, and his kṣauma garments."
"By virtue of this merit and auspiciousness, you shall be honored and noble in every birth; whatever precious things you desire shall come to you spontaneously without being sought.
Having heard this, the king conceived deep faith and reverence toward the Triple Gem, prostrated himself, and returned to his palace.

103. The Story of the Golden Cat (103). Once, while King Caṇḍapradyota was touring the pleasure groves, he saw a golden cat upon the terrace in the garden, entering from the northeast corner and exiting through the southwest corner.
The king immediately dispatched men to excavate once more, whereupon they discovered a bronze jar with a capacity of three *shu*. It was filled with gold coins.
As they gradually dug deeper, they obtained another jar; continuing in this manner, they successively found three layers of jars, each with a capacity of three *shu*.
Gradually digging further to the side, he also found a copper jar; continuing to dig without ceasing, throughout a distance of five li, he discovered nothing but copper jars filled with gold coins.
King Canda-pradyota, struck with deep wonder, went at once to the Venerable Kātyāyana and related to him in detail the circumstances and causes of how he had obtained the money:
"I wish now to use this, but will there not be some calamity or misfortune for me and my people?"
The Venerable One replied, "This is the meritorious reward obtained through the king's past causes; it is used merely for the sake of non-suffering.
The king then asked:
"I do not understand the past causes; what were those events?
The Venerable One replied, "Listen attentively, listen attentively!"

In the past, ninety-one kalpas ago, during the period of the bequeathed Dharma of Vipaśyin Buddha, there were certain bhikṣus who, at a crossroads, set up a great high seat and placed an alms bowl upon it, saying:

"Who among the people of this world is able to take wealth from the secure treasury? If one enters this treasury, water cannot sweep it away, fire cannot burn it, kings cannot seize it, and thieves cannot plunder it."

At that time, there was a poor man who had previously earned three coins from selling firewood; having heard these words, he gave rise to a heart of joy and immediately placed those coins back into the bowl, making a vow with a sincere mind.

Five *li* from his home, as he was returning, he felt joy at every step; upon reaching his gate, he turned toward the place where he had been teaching and made a sincere vow, only then entering his house.
The Venerable One said:
"The poor man of that time is now this king.

Because of the causal conditions of his gift of three coins in the past, he has been noble and honored in every lifetime, constantly obtaining such jars of triple-layered coins. Due to the joy he felt at every step within the five *li*, he has always possessed these gold coins throughout those five *li*."
Having heard of his past karmic conditions, the king departed with joy. 104.
The Story of King Caṇḍapradyota Obtaining Five Hundred Bowls (104). Once upon a time, King Caṇḍapradyota resided in the city of Ujjayinī.

At that time, when the gatekeeper opened the gates at dawn, there were suddenly five hundred chariots outside the gates, each carrying a precious bowl filled to the brim with golden grain; all were sealed and inscribed with the words:
"These bowls are for King Canda-pradyota."
At that time, the gatekeeper informed the King, saying:
"Outside there is a precious bowl inscribed with the words 'Given to the King. I do not know whether you should take it now or not."
The king reflected to himself:
"This treasure has appeared suddenly; perhaps it is an omen of ill fortune. If I were to take it, would it not bring calamity upon my family and kingdom?"
Having had this thought, he immediately went to the Venerable Kātyāyana and asked him:

"This morning, when the gate was opened, I suddenly saw a precious bowl with an inscription upon it that reads, 'Given to King Canda-pradyota. I do not yet know whether this is auspicious or inauspicious; should it be taken or not?"
The Venerable One replied, "This is the fruit of the King's past merit; simply take it without hesitation.
The King said to the Venerable One:
"What merit did I cultivate in past causes to bring about this retribution?
The Venerable One replied,
"In the past, ninety-one kalpas ago, on Mount Ṛṣigiri, there was a Pratyekabuddha who, encountering rain, slipped and broke his clay alms-bowl."
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha went to the potter’s house and begged for an earthen bowl.
The potter immediately took five vessels, filled each with water, and joyfully offered them as alms.

Having attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha, he cast his alms bowl into the air and leaped upward, soaring through the void and performing the eighteen miraculous transformations. When the potter’s wife and children, as well as those who had purchased the tiles, witnessed these supernatural feats, they were all filled with boundless joy and exultation.
The potter at that time was the King himself;
the wife at that time was Queen Śivakusā;
and the son at that time was Prince Gopāla.
"At that time, the one who purchased the tiles was the minister Pūrṇa;
the woman who purchased the tiles was the wife of the minister.
The King asked again:
"I wonder whether this bowl appeared spontaneously or if it came from somewhere?
The Venerable One replied, "This bowl did not appear spontaneously; it came from the dragon palace within the waters of the Ganges River."
How is this known?
In the distant past, there was a Brahmin who was the maternal uncle of King Rāma; he practiced pure conduct on the banks of the Ganges.
At that time, King Rāma daily sent food in a precious bowl to his uncle.
According to the dharma of the brahmins, vessels are not used twice; having finished eating, he discarded his bowl into the Ganges River.
A blind nāga retrieved the precious bowl, filled it with golden grains, and placed it within his own palace.
As these discarded items accumulated day by day, they gradually increased until five hundred cartloads of bowls were obtained.

When the blind nāga passed away, there was no son to inherit and take charge of these bowls. Knowing the king’s past causes and conditions regarding the gift of the bowls, Śakra, Lord of Devas, left them as a legacy to the king.

Upon hearing these words, the king immediately took the precious bowl and used it to cultivate merit; he extensively practiced giving and made offerings to the Triple Gem. By virtue of these causes and conditions, he was later reborn in a favorable realm.

105. The Story of the Deva King Pīṭhaka’s Aspiration for Great Wealth Once upon a time, there were two brothers whose household was in poverty. The elder brother constantly worshipped the deva king Pīṭhaka morning and evening with diligent devotion, aspiring to attain great wealth, while he sent his younger brother to plow the fields and cultivate crops.
Thus he entreated for a long time.
Then, the King of the Vimala Heaven transformed himself into his younger brother and went to his elder brother’s side.
The elder brother spoke angrily to his brother:
"Why do you not cultivate the land?
Why have you come here?
At that time, the younger brother replied:
"Your elder brother was at Ten-ji Temple, praying day and night in hopes of attaining great wealth;
today, your younger brother likewise wishes to follow his example, observing the fast and making a vow in hopes of obtaining great wealth."
The elder brother said to his younger brother,
"If you do not plow the fields and sow the seeds, by what means can wealth and grain be obtained?
The younger brother replied to his elder brother:
"Is it truly because of the seeds sown that the harvest is reaped?
The elder brother was unable to reply.
Thereupon, the god Vemacitrin restored his celestial form and spoke to him, saying:
"My power can now assist you; if you practice generosity today, you may thereafter become wealthy.
However, because you did not practice generosity in the past, you have been made poor."
Although you now strive with diligence day and night seeking my abundant wealth and treasures, how could they possibly be obtained?
It is like the *āmra* tree: if it is in winter, even if one were to serve a hundred thousand celestial deities in hopes of obtaining fruit, no fruit can be found.
You are just like this: having previously failed to cultivate the causes, you wish to seek great wealth from me, yet it cannot be obtained;
but when the fruit is ripe, it is obtained spontaneously without seeking.
And he spoke in verse:
“Meritorious deeds are like fruit that has ripened; they are not obtained through sacrificial offerings.
A person who mounts the chariot of moral discipline shall, in the end, reach the heavenly realms.”
When the wisdom of meditative concentration is like a lamp extinguished, one attains the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Since everything is obtained through practice, what is the use of seeking rebirth in heaven?

106. The Story of Hārītī Losing Her Son (106). Regarding the story of Hārītī losing her son: Hārītī was the wife of the elder king of the ghost spirits, Pañcika; she had ten thousand sons, all of whom possessed the strength of great wrestlers.
Her youngest son was named Bhīṣaṇaka; this daughter of the Mother of Ghosts (Hārītī) was fierce, malevolent, and tyrannical, killing children and devouring them herself.
The people were distressed by her and appealed to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One took his son Piṅgala and placed him at the bottom of his alms bowl.

The Mother of Ghosts searched throughout the world for seven days, but could not find him; she was filled with grief and distress, until she heard it said of others that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possessed all-encompassing wisdom.
He immediately went to where the Buddha was and asked for his son’s whereabouts.
At that time, the Buddha replied:
"You have ten thousand sons; you have lost but one. For what reason do you distress yourself with grief and sorrow, searching for him?"
"The people of the world have some with but one son, or others with five or three sons, yet you have killed them.
The Mother of Ghosts addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If I may now obtain Pīṅgala, I shall never again kill the children of worldly people."
The Buddha then caused Hārītī to see that Piṅgala was beneath his alms bowl; though she exerted all her supernatural powers, she could not take him away, so she returned to seek the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"If you can now receive the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, and refrain from killing for the rest of your life, I shall return your child to you.
The Mother of Ghost Children then followed the Buddha's command and received the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts.
Having completed the recitation and upholding [of the precepts], he immediately returned his son to him.
The Buddha said:

"You must maintain the precepts well. During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, you were the seventh youngest daughter of King Kṛkin; although you performed great meritorious deeds, because you did not maintain the precepts, you have received this form as a ghost."
107. The Story of the Lord of Sacrifices (107). Once upon a time, there was a brahmin who served the deity Maheśvara, attending upon him day and night.
The deva then asked,
"What do you seek?
The brāhmaṇa replied:
"I now seek to become the presiding master of this sacrifice for the gods.
The deity said, "He has a herd of cattle; you should ask the one who is at the very head of the procession."
He then went to question that ox, just as the deva had instructed:
"What do you now consider to be suffering and what do you consider to be happiness?
The ox replied:
"It is an extreme suffering; my two ribs are pierced and my back is broken and twisted. I am yoked to pull a cart, bearing a heavy load without rest.
Then he asked again:
"By what causes and conditions have you received this ox form?"
The ox replied to him, saying:
"I was once the master of that celestial sacrifice; indulging my every whim and consuming the sacrificial offerings, I died and was reborn as an ox, undergoing this suffering."
Having heard these words, he immediately returned to his celestial abode.
The deity then asked him:
"Do you now wish to become the Lord of Devas?"
The brahmin said,
"Having witnessed this matter, I truly dare not do it.
The deva said:
"Whether a person performs good or evil deeds, they shall receive their own retribution.
The Brahmin repented his faults and immediately cultivated various virtues.

108. The Story of the Tree-Spirit (108): The Story of the Tree-Spirit. Long ago, there was an old man whose family was immensely wealthy. This old man desired to eat meat, so he devised a deceptive stratagem. Pointing to a tree at the edge of a field, he said to his sons:
"The reason our family business has prospered and attained such wealth is due to the grace and blessings of this tree deity.
Today, you all should select a sheep from among your flocks to use for sacrifice."
Then the sons, receiving their father’s instructions, immediately slaughtered sheep to offer prayers and sacrifices to this tree, and there, beneath the tree, they erected a temple for the deity.
Later, when his father’s lifespan had ended and his life was over, he was drawn by the force of his past karma and was reborn within the flock of sheep in his own home.

At that time, the sons were about to sacrifice to a tree spirit; they selected a sheep, and it happened to be his father. As they were about to slaughter him, the sheep began to laugh loudly and said, "What kind of spiritual power does this tree possess?"
"In the past, for the sake of meat, I falsely incited you to perform sacrifices; together with all of you, I ate this meat.
Now, to repay the karmic retribution for my transgressions, I alone shall first bear its consequences."

At that time, there was an Arhat who encountered him while begging for alms. Seeing that his deceased father had been reborn with the body of a sheep, he lent the householder the divine eye of the Path so that he might observe for himself; thus he recognized it was his father. Filled with anguish, he immediately destroyed the tree spirit, repented, cultivated merit, and ceased killing living beings forever.

109. The Story of a Woman Who Left Home Out of Weariness with Desire (109) Once there was a woman of exceptionally beautiful and refined countenance who left home to practice the Way within the teachings of the non-Buddhist sects.
People of the time asked, "With such a countenance as this, you ought to remain in the secular world; for what reason have you left the home life?
The woman replied:
"As for me today, it is not that I am not handsome; rather, because I have long since grown weary of sensual desire, I have now gone forth into homelessness.

When I was at home, because of my handsomeness, I was quickly given a position and soon fathered a son. As the boy grew up, his beauty became peerless, yet he has lately become increasingly emaciated, as if he were ill."
I immediately questioned my son about the cause and symptoms of his illness, but he was unwilling to speak. As I continued to press him without ceasing, he had no choice but to say to his mother:
"If I do not speak at all, I fear my life will not be spared;
yet if I wish to explain it fully, it would be most deeply shameful."
He then said to his mother,
"I desired to have private sexual relations with you, but because I did not obtain them, I am ill.
His mother then spoke to him, saying:
"Since ancient times, how could such a thing have ever occurred?
He further thought to himself:
"If I do not comply, my son may well die; it would be better now to violate principle in order to preserve my son's life."
He immediately called his son, wishing to follow the son's wishes.

As the son was about to go up onto the bed, the ground split open; my son instantly fell into it with his body still alive. I was struck with terror and, reaching out my hand, pulled at my son, seizing him by the hair.
"Yet my son's hair remains even now within my embrace.
Moved by this poignant matter, I have therefore left the household life. 110.
The Story of the Filial Son Receiving a Suffering Retribution (110). Once, in the village of Kūṭaśālmali in the kingdom of Kāśmīra, there was an old woman who had only one son.
His son was rebellious and failed to cultivate benevolence and filial piety; out of anger toward his mother, he raised his hand against her and struck her once, whereupon he departed that very day.

Encountering bandits, he had one arm severed; the retribution for his filial impiety manifested immediately, and his suffering was such as this—yet the sufferings of hell that follow are beyond measure.

111. The Discourse on King Nanda’s Discussion with Nāgasena (111) The Discourse on King Nanda’s Discussion with Nāgasena: Once, King Nanda was intelligent and widely learned; there was no matter he had not mastered. Relying on his own knowledge, he believed there was no one who could challenge him, and so he asked his ministers:
"Is there any person of wisdom and eloquence who, when consulted on matters of doubt, can respond to me?"
At that time, there was a minister whose family had long supported an elderly bhikṣu who maintained pure conduct but had not studied extensively; the minister spoke of this man to the king.
The King asked him, saying,
"As for one who attains the Way, is it attained while remaining at home, or is it attained by leaving the home life?
At that time, the elderly bhikṣu immediately replied to him:
"Both have attained the Way.
The king asked again,
"If both have attained it, what is the use of leaving the household life?"
That elderly bhikṣu remained silent, not knowing how to respond.
At that time, King Nanda became even more arrogant.
Then the ministers addressed the king, saying:
"Nagasena is of peerless intelligence and currently resides in the mountains.

At that time, wishing to test him, the king immediately dispatched a messenger carrying a jar of ghee, filled to the brim and perfectly level. The king thought to himself, "My wisdom is already complete; who else could possibly add anything further to me?"

Nāgasena, having obtained the ghee, immediately understood its significance; from among his disciples, he selected five hundred needles and used them to pierce the ghee, yet the ghee did not overflow. He then promptly sent it back to the king.
Once the King had captured him, he immediately understood his intention and promptly dispatched a messenger to invite Nāgasena.
Nāgasena then went to the King’s summons. Nāgasena was tall and large in stature;

leading his assembly of disciples, he stood out prominently among them. The King, being arrogant and haughty, made the pretext of going on a hunt and encountered him along the way. Seeing that he was exceptionally tall and handsome, the King immediately shook his finger at him, took a different path, and departed without speaking a word, silently wishing to disparage him; yet none of the elders present knew anything of this.
Then Nāgasena immediately pointed with his own finger to his chest and said, "I alone know.

King Nanda intended to invite him into the palace, so he had a small hut excavated with a doorway made extremely low, hoping that Nāgasena would have to bow down and stoop as he entered. However, Nāgasena, realizing the king intended to humiliate him, stepped back and refused to submit to such an indignity.
At that time, King Nanda immediately prepared food and drink, offering several kinds of coarse fare. After eating five or three spoonfuls, he said he was full.
When finer and more delicious food was subsequently served, he then ate again. The king asked him once more:
"You said earlier that you were full; for what reason do you still continue to eat now?"
Sena replied, "I have previously been sufficient in coarseness, but not yet sufficient in subtlety.
He then spoke to the king:
"Now, let all people be gathered upon the king's palace terrace until it is completely full.
Immediately, people were summoned until they filled every space, leaving no room for anyone else.

The king arrived later and was about to ascend the hall; because all the people were struck with awe, they were completely cowed and submissive, so that the space within became much wider and could accommodate many more people.
Then Sena immediately said to the king:
"Coarse food is like the common people, while fine food is like the king; when the people see the king, who would not yield the way?"
The king asked again,
"Between one who has left the household life and one who remains at home,
which attains the Way? Sona replied:
"Both have attained the Way.
The king asked again,
"If both have attained the Way, why is it necessary to leave the household life?"

Sena replied, "Suppose one were to travel more than three thousand li from here; if one were to dispatch a young and robust man, mounted on a horse, carrying provisions and holding a weapon, would he be able to arrive quickly?"
The king replied,
“I have. Sona spoke again:
"If one sends an elderly man riding a lean horse, and furthermore provides no provisions, will he be able to reach his destination?
The King said, "Even if he were provided with provisions, I fear he would not reach it; how much more so without provisions?"
Sena said, "To attain the Way while living as a renunciant is like being in one's youth; to attain the Way while remaining at home is like being an old man.
The king asked again:
"I now wish to ask about matters concerning the body: Is it permanent or impermanent? Answer according to your own inclination.
Sona replied with a counter-question:
"In the royal palace, there is a mango tree; are its fruits sweet or sour?"
The king said, "In my palace, there are no such trees at all; how can you ask me about the sweetness or acidity of their fruit? Sena replied:
"I am now likewise so.
Since all five aggregates are themselves without self, why do you ask whether I am permanent or impermanent?
At that time, the king asked again:
"In all the hells, those whose bodies are dismembered by swords and scattered in every direction still remain alive; does this truly exist?
Sena replied, "It is like a woman who eats cakes, meat, melons, and vegetables; her food and drink are entirely digested."
"As for the state of pregnancy, when it is at the stage of the *kalala*, it is like a minute speck of dust; how does it grow so large without being digested?
The King replied, "This is the power of karma."
Sena replied, "In that hell as well,
it is by the power of karma that the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is maintained.
The king asked again:
"The sun above has but one body; why is it that during summer it is extremely hot and during winter it is extremely cold? Why is it that in summer the days are long and in winter the days are short?"
Sena replied: "Mount Sumeru has upper and lower paths.
During the summer, the sun travels upon the upper path; because the route is long and its progress slow, it illuminates the Golden Mountain for a prolonged duration, and thus it is hot."
"In winter, the sun travels along the lower path; because its route is short and its movement swift, it illuminates the waters of the great ocean.

For this reason, the days are short and the cold is extreme. 112. The Story of the Unfilial Wife Who Intended to Harm Her Mother-in-law but Instead Killed Her Husband (112). The Story of the Unfilial Wife Who Intended to Harm Her Mother-in-law but Instead Killed Her Husband: Long ago, there was a wife whose nature was perverse and who did not conform to the rules of propriety. In all her actions, she constantly opposed her mother-in-law; having incurred her mother-in-law’s anger and reproaches, she harbored perpetual resentment.
Her anger grew ever more intense, and she plotted to kill her mother-in-law. Later, she devised a scheme and instructed her husband to kill his own mother.
Her husband was foolish and, following his wife’s words, took his mother to the wilderness, bound her hands and feet, and was about to inflict harm upon her.
The gravity of his transgressions moved Heaven above; clouds and mist gathered from all sides, and a thunderbolt struck down, killing his son.
The mother immediately returned home, and when her daughter-in-law opened the door, she thought it was her husband and asked:
"Is he dead yet?"
The mother-in-law replied,
"I have already killed him.
It was not until the following day that she learned her husband had died.
The retribution for the sin of filial impiety is such in this present life; hereafter, one enters hell and undergoes immeasurable suffering. 113.

The Story of the King of Vārāṇasī Hearing the Call from the Cemetery (The Elder Bhikṣu Obtains the Four Fruits through the Occasion of the Call; the Woman Attains the Fruit of the Path through Sincerity). Regarding the story of the King of Vārāṇasī hearing the call from the cemetery: In all phenomena, that which can be sought may be obtained if one employs skillful means;
however, that which cannot be sought cannot be acquired at all, even if one desires to obtain it by force.
It is like pressing sand to extract oil or churning ice to seek butter; since these cannot be obtained, one merely exhausts oneself in vain.
Long ago, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta who, every night at midnight, heard voices calling out from among the tombs, crying:
"Ho, King! Ho, King!"
In this manner, he heard that sound three times during the single night.
Hearing these strange sounds, the king was deeply alarmed; the voices did not cease for a long duration.
The king assembled the brahmins, the chroniclers, and the physiognomists, and consulted them, saying:
"Every night, I have heard the sound of someone calling my name from among the graves; I am constantly terrified and, out of fear, do not dare to respond."
The people replied, "There must be some malevolent spirit in that cemetery making these sounds; we should now dispatch a messenger who is bold and brave to go to the cemetery and investigate."
The king immediately issued a proclamation:
"If there is anyone who can go to the cemetery at night, I shall reward them with five hundred gold coins.
At that time, there was a man who was solitary and fatherless; his family was extremely poor, yet he possessed great courage and strength, and so he immediately responded to the call.
Clad in armor and grasping a sword and staff in hand, he went to a cemetery at night and, hearing the sound of someone calling for the King, immediately shouted:
"Ho! Who are you?"
He replied,
"I am the treasure-keeper Śaṅkhaśravaṇa," and spoke to the solicitor, saying:
“O valiant man, I constantly call out to that king at night; if that king should respond to my call, I wish to go into his treasury.”
However, that king is timid and has never responded to me; as for me, I am now accompanied by seven followers, and tomorrow at dawn, I shall come to your house.
The recruiter asked,
"When you come tomorrow, with what shall I welcome you? Śaṅkha replied:

“You need only sprinkle and sweep the interior of the hall, remove all filth and impurities, and adorn it with fragrant flowers until it is utterly pure. Prepare eight vessels each of grape flour, sweet wine, and rice porridge with ghee and milk. There are eight men of the Path; you shall strike the head of the senior monk with a staff and say, ‘Enter the corner,’ and in this manner, drive them all in turn into the corner.”
Once the person who had been recruited learned of this, he immediately returned home.
He requested five hundred gold coins from the king to use for the preparations of the offering.
The king asked him, saying:
"What kind of thing is that sound?
The person who had been hired replied deceptively, "It is a malevolent spirit.
Having heard these words from the shell-eared man, the hired man felt private joy and invited a barber to adorn himself.
When the next day arrived, the provisions for the meal were prepared. Eight practitioners of the Way came to partake of the food.

Once they had finished eating, he struck the head of the assembly, driving him into a corner, where he immediately transformed into a single bowl of gold coins. He drove them in one after another, until there were eight bowls of gold.
At that time, the barber, seeing him obtain the treasure from within the keyhole, thought to himself in silence:
"I understand this method; let me try to imitate and perform it."

Thereafter, having prepared everything as before, he invited eight practitioners of the Way; once the meal was finished, he closed the doors and barred the gates, then struck the head of the senior monk, hoping to obtain a hoard of precious treasures just as he had done previously.
However, this practitioner of the Way had his head split open and blood dripping, staining the bedding and seat; he was driven into a corner, where, in his desperation, he lost control and defecated.

Next, seven men were all beaten with clubs and rolled about on the ground. Among them, one man possessed great physical strength; he immediately pulled his hand free, rushed out to the exterior, and cried out at the top of his voice:
"This master wishes to harm us!"
Then the king of that country dispatched men to investigate; they immediately seized the host and questioned him thoroughly regarding the circumstances of the matter.
At that time, the barber related all the aforementioned events in detail to the king.

The king soon dispatched men to the house where the man was staying to inspect his gold and treasures; just as they were about to seize them by tax, [the treasures] transformed into venomous snakes and changed into a mass of fire.
The King then said:
"This is the fruit of your merit.

The foolish commoners of the world are likewise; by possessing diligence and observing the eight precepts, they obtain wholesome karmic rewards, gradually practice the Eightfold Noble Path, and attain the fruit of outflowlessness (*anāsrava*).

They then wish to emulate others by undertaking the eight precepts; yet, lacking sincerity within, they seek only profit and pleasure. Since there is no virtuous fruit, they instead incur calamity and blame, being no different from those foolish people.

114. The Story of the Elder Bhikṣu Attaining the Four Fruits (114) The Buddha-dharma is vast and its salvation is boundless. For those who seek the Way with a sincere heart, there are none who do not attain the fruits; even for those who act in jest, their merit is never in vain.

In the past, there was an elderly bhikṣu whose years had advanced and whose faculties were clouded and obstructed. Seeing the young bhikṣus preaching the Dharma in various ways and hearing them speak of the four fruits of spiritual realization, he felt envy and admiration in his heart. He said to the young bhikṣus:
"You are all wise and intelligent; I pray that you will bestow upon me these four fruits."
The young bhikṣus mocked him, saying, "We possess the four fruits [of the śramaṇa];
we shall give them to you only after we have obtained some fine food.

When the old bhikṣu heard these words, joy arose within him; he immediately untied his *kambala* (woolen garment) to trade for what was required, and promptly prepared various kinds of delicacies. He then invited the young bhikṣus and requested that they grant him the four fruits.
After the young bhikṣus had finished eating their food, they pointed at one another and teased the elderly bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable One!
Sit here in a corner of this house, and we shall give you some fruit."
When the elder bhikṣu heard this, he was filled with joy and sat down as instructed.
The younger bhikṣus then struck him on the head with a leather ball and said to him,
"This is the fruit of srotāpanna."
Upon hearing this, the elderly bhikṣu focused his mind without distraction and immediately attained the first fruit [of the path].
The younger bhikṣus again teased him, saying:

"Although you have just attained the fruit of srotāpanna, you still have seven more births and seven more deaths ahead of you. Move one corner over, and next we shall grant you the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin."
At that time, because the elder bhikṣu had attained the first fruit [of the path], his mind became further refined and he immediately moved his seat again.
The young bhikṣus struck him on the head with a ball and said to him:
"We give you the second fruit."
At that time, the elderly bhikṣu applied himself with even greater single-mindedness and immediately realized the second fruit [of the path].
The younger bhikṣus again teased him, saying:

"You have now attained the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin; yet you still face the hardship of coming and going through birth and death. Move your seat further away, and we shall grant you the fruit of an Anāgāmin."
Then the elder bhikṣu moved his seat as he was told; the younger bhikṣus struck him again with a ball and said to him, "We now grant you the third fruit."
When the elder bhikṣu heard this, he was filled with joy; redoubling his sincerity, he immediately realized the fruit of *anāgāmin*.
The younger bhikṣus again teased him, saying:

"You have now attained the fruit of *anāgāmin*, yet you will still receive a contaminated body within the realms of form and formlessness. It is impermanent and subject to decay; every moment is suffering. Move your seat once more, and we shall next grant you the fruit of *arhat*."
Then the elder bhikṣu moved his seat as he had been told. The young bhikṣus again struck him on the head with leather balls and said to him:
"We now bestow upon you that fourth fruit."
At that time, the elderly bhikṣu focused his mind in contemplation and immediately realized arhatship.

Having attained the fourth fruit, he was filled with great joy; he prepared various delicacies and diverse fragrant flowers, invited the junior bhikṣus to repay their kindness, and together with them, discussed the factors of the path and the untainted merits.
The young bhikṣus found their speech faltering and obstructed.
Then an elder bhikṣu spoke to them, saying,
"I have already realized the fruit of arhatship."
When the junior bhikṣus heard these words, they all repented and apologized for their previous offense of mockery.
Therefore, practitioners should maintain mindfulness of the wholesome; even through mere mockery, one may still obtain a real retribution—how much more so when acting with a sincere heart!

115. The Story of the Woman Who Attained the Fruit of the Path through Sincerity (115). Regarding the story of the woman who attained the fruit of the path through sincerity: If a person seeks the Way, it must rely on earnest sincerity; when earnest sincerity moves [the divine], one can obtain the fruit of the Way.
