In the past, there was a woman who was clever and wise, possessed deep faith in the Triple Gem, and would regularly invite a bhikṣu from the monastic roster to her home for offerings.
At that time, there was an elderly bhikṣu who, in turn, arrived at her house; he was old and his faculties were dull, having never been one to understand much.
When the woman had finished her midday meal, she requested the elderly bhikṣu to preach the Dharma for her. She spread out a single seat alone and sat in silent stillness with her eyes closed.
At that time, the elderly bhikṣu, realizing he was ignorant and lacked the wisdom to preach the Dharma, waited for her eyes to close and fled back to the monastery.

However, this woman contemplated with utmost sincerity the conditioned nature of phenomena—impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and lack of self-mastery—and through deep observation, she immediately attained the first fruit of the path.
Having attained the fruit, he sought out the elderly bhikṣu, wishing to repay his kindness.
This elderly bhikṣu, realizing that he himself was ignorant, abandoned him and fled to avoid him; feeling doubly ashamed, the seeker then abandoned his own hiding place and fled as well.
Yet this woman, having sought him with unyielding persistence, finally appeared before him.
At that time, she recounted in detail how she had previously attained the fruits of the Path; thus, she brought offerings as a means to repay his great kindness.
At that time, because of his sense of shame and remorse, the elder bhikṣu deeply reproached himself and immediately attained the fruit once more.
Therefore, a practitioner should apply themselves with a sincere mind; if one is sincere, whatever is sought will surely be obtained.
*Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra*, Scroll Nine;
*Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra*, Scroll Ten.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kiṅ-kia-ye and T'an-yao of the Western Regions during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
The Story of King Udayana (116). Once, King Udayana resided in the city of Roruka; he was intelligent, discerning, and possessed of great wisdom.

One of his consorts was named Yixiang (Possessing Marks); her appearance was extraordinary and she was endowed with virtuous conduct. The king loved and respected her deeply, holding her in the highest favor.
At that time, according to the laws of that kingdom, no one who served as a king played the lute himself.
Then the queen, relying on her own favor and affection, said to the king:
"I pray you play the lute for me, and I shall dance for you, O King."
The king could not dispel his anxiety; he took up the lute and played it, whereupon the lady immediately raised her hands and began to dance.
The king was naturally skilled in physiognomy; seeing the lady dance, he beheld the marks of death upon her and immediately cast aside the lute, sighing deeply with a sorrowful countenance.
The lady then addressed the king, saying:

"As one who now receives the King's favor and grace, I ventured into this private chamber to request that you play the lute for me; I myself shall dance to share in our mutual delight. What could be so displeasing that you would set aside your lute and sigh?"
"I pray that Your Majesty will not conceal it, but grant me your word.
At that time, the king replied,
"My long sighs are not something you, a woman, ought to hear."
The lady said, "I now serve Your Majesty with sincere and undivided loyalty; if there is anything that is not being managed properly, you ought to issue instructions.
As she pressed him earnestly and without ceasing, the king answered her truthfully:
"How could there be any difference between me and you?
Just now, as you rose to dance, the signs of death appeared externally; calculating your remaining life, it will not exceed seven days. For this reason, I set aside my lute and sighed."
Having heard this, the lady was filled with great anxiety and fear, and she immediately said to the king:
"As Your Majesty has said, my life is not far from its end.
I have heard a stone-chamber bhikṣuṇī say that if one can leave the household life with faith for even a single day, one will certainly be reborn in heaven."
"For this reason, I wish to leave the household life; I pray that Your Majesty will grant me permission so that I may attain the stage of the Path.
At that time, the King’s affection was deep and his love would not cease;
he said to the Queen, "On the sixth day, I shall permit you to leave the household life and enter the Way; I cannot disregard your intent."
When the sixth day arrived, the king said to his consort:
"You have a virtuous heart and desire to leave the household life; if you are reborn in heaven, you must come to see me, and only then will I permit you to go forth."

Having made this vow, the lady gave her consent, and he was thus able to leave the household life and receive the eight precepts of the fast. On that very day, he drank a great deal of honey syrup; his abdomen became constricted with cramps, and by the dawn of the seventh day, he passed away.
Riding upon these wholesome conditions, they attain birth in the heavens, whereupon three thoughts immediately arise:
first, the thought to recall what kind of body they were in their previous life;
second, the thought to recall what meritorious deeds they cultivated based on their original conditions.
He thought to himself, "I am clearly in my celestial body at this very moment.
Having formed this thought, he fully understood his original circumstances as well as his vow to the king; because of that prior vow, he came to the place where the king was.
At that time, a brilliant light filled the royal palace, and the king asked:
"Whose auspicious radiance is this?
I pray you, inform me."
The deity then replied,
"I am the king's wife, the lady who possesses the auspicious marks.
Upon hearing this, the king said:
"Please, come and take a seat.
The deva replied, "As I am now, I perceive the King as foul and impure; I cannot draw near."
"I have come to see the King because of my previous vow.
Upon hearing this, the King’s mind was immediately awakened, and he spoke these words:

"That celestial being was originally my wife. Because she possessed a virtuous heart and sought to enter the Way, she left the household life for a single day and soon passed away. By virtue of this merit, she has been reborn in heaven; her spirit and intellect are now lofty and far-reaching, yet she looks upon me with such contempt."
Why should I not now renounce the household life?
I have heard it said that a single fingernail of a celestial being is worth all of Jambudvīpa; how much more so my own kingdom—what is there to covet or begrudge?
Having spoken these words, he established his son, Rājyaśrī, to succeed him to the throne, and went forth to study the Path, attaining arhatship.

At that time, King Rājyaśrī, having assumed the governance of the kingdom, placed his trust in slanderers and flatterers and neglected the affairs of state. King Udayana, taking pity on his son as well as the people of the land, desired to come and instruct him, exhorting him to cultivate goodness.
At that time, King Rājasena, hearing that his father was approaching, was filled with immeasurable joy and wished to command everyone to go out along the road to welcome him.
Then, the sycophantic ministers, fearing they would be dismissed from their posts, addressed the king, saying:
"As Your Majesty now wears the celestial crown and sits upon the lion throne—the law regarding the lion throne is that one may not sit upon it a second time."
"If he is welcomed back and restores his father to the throne, he will surely kill the king; if the king remains established, he must harm his father.

At that time, King Senāpati felt sorrow and alarm, and as doubt grew within him, he exhorted [his son] incessantly. Eventually, harboring evil intent, he recruited a *caṇḍāla* to go and kill his father.
At that time, having accepted the commission, the Caṇḍāla went to his father, the king, prostrated himself with his head at the king’s feet, and addressed him, saying:

"In the past, I too have received the favor and patronage of my father, the king; truly, I have harbored no rebellious intent. Yet now I am dispatched to kill my father, the king; if I do not inflict harm upon him, I shall surely suffer punishment."
The father king replied, "I have come now desiring to convert your king; how could I cherish my body such that it would cause you to be executed?
He then extended his neck to a length of over ten zhang and said to the caṇḍāla:
"Cut and hack away as you please.
Then the candāla struck him with all his might, yet the blade could not wound him.
Out of compassion for his father the king, [the Bodhisattva] lent him his supernatural power and said to the candāla:
"Now go on my behalf and say to your king:
'You have now killed your father and further harmed an Arhat, committing two heinous crimes; you should earnestly perform repentance so that your offenses may be lightened.'"
When the caṇḍāla had received these instructions, he raised his sword and struck again, severing the head of the father-king and carrying it toward his own country.
When King Yuñjīng saw his father’s head, its color remained unchanged; he knew that his father had attained the Way and did not covet the royal throne.

Once remorse had arisen within him, his heart was filled with anguish; he wept and fainted, only regaining consciousness after a long time. He then asked the *caṇḍāla* about what his father, the king, had said.
At that time, the *caṇḍāla*, in accordance with his father the king’s command, addressed the king:
"Since you have both killed your father and harmed an Arhat, committing these two heinous crimes, you must perform a thorough repentance."
Having heard these words, his resolve to sever [the bonds of worldly life] increased all the more, and he spoke thus:
"Now that my father, the King, has attained the path of an Arhat, what desire for a kingdom could he have that would cause me to kill my father?"
At that time, the sycophantic minister, fearing the king’s infliction of harm, addressed the king, saying:
“In this world, how could there be any arhats?
Your Majesty believes empty words and brings suffering upon yourself.”
The king then replied, "My father’s head has been dead for many days now, yet its complexion has not changed; were he not one who had attained the Way, how could this be?"

Furthermore, during my father’s reign, the ministers Bhaṭṭisara and Upabhaṭṭisara both left the household life and attained the path of Arhatship; we ourselves witnessed their various supernatural transformations. They have entered parinirvāṇa here, and their remains were collected to build a stupa which exists even now. How can you say that [the Buddha] does not exist?
The sycophantic minister replied,
“Worldly illusory spells and the power of medicinal herbs can also produce supernatural transformations.
Those two ministers are not arhats.”
"In a few more days, I shall show the King the proof.

Having said this, he then made two holes at the site of the stupa and placed a cat in each. He fed them at the stupa and called out, "Dhīṣaṇa, come out! When the cat came out to eat the meat, he told it to go back; it then returned and entered its hole.
Having been instructed in this way, the cat was tamed and said to the king:
"Does Your Majesty wish to see the cat-eaters and others now?
I pray that you will go together with me to see them."
The king immediately ordered his carriage and proceeded to the site of the stūpa.
At that time, the sycophant summoned the cat-teacher to come out; the cat emerged from its hole and told him to go back, whereupon it re-entered the hole.
Having seen this, the king’s deluded mind became even more rampant; he acted as he pleased, no longer believing in the retribution of sin and merit.
At that time, as the king was returning from a military excursion, he encountered the Venerable Kātyāyana on the road, sitting upright in a secluded place, absorbed in meditative concentration.

When the king saw this, he immediately conceived an evil intent; taking soil in his own hand, he threw it over the Venerable One and said to those around him, "Each of you, for my sake, throw soil over Kātyāyana."
At that time, the heap of earth completely buried the Venerable One.

A certain high minister, who had faith in the Triple Gem, arrived later; upon hearing of and witnessing this event, he was overcome with great distress and immediately cleared the earth away for the Venerable One.
He further addressed the people, saying:
"For those who have mindfulness of me, this land shall be removed.

At that time, the Venerable One sat within a precious lapis lazuli cave; his divine countenance was fresh and radiant, free from any trace of dust or impurity. The minister, filled with joy, prostrated himself at his feet and addressed the Venerable One, saying:
"Now the King is without the Way and has committed such evil and rebellion; since good and evil must inevitably be requited, how can he escape calamity?

The Venerable One replied, "Seven days from now, the heavens shall rain down earth that will fill the interior of his city, piling up into a mountain of soil; both the King and his people shall be utterly buried and destroyed."
Having heard this, the minister was filled with grief and distress, and immediately informed the king;
he then devised a plan to construct an underground passage leading out of the city.

When the seven days had passed, the heavens rained down fragrant flowers, precious jewels, and garments, so that everyone within the city was filled with joy. A sycophantic minister then said to the king:

"This present auspicious omen is entirely due to the King's virtue; yet those of little wisdom instead give rise to slander, saying that while earth was to rain down, precious jewels have been obtained."
Thus deceived and deluded, such instances occurred not just once, but repeatedly. Following these evil conditions, when reports of auspicious omens were heard, they all gathered like clouds.

At that time, by the power of dark karmic conditions, the iron gates at the four city portals were all lowered; there was no place left for them to flee or hide. Then the heavens rained down earth, which piled up like mountains throughout the city.
Then that minister, who shared the same resolve, emerged from the earth by way of a path leading to the Venerable One’s location and addressed him, saying:
"I lament this city; in a single day it shall be submerged and buried under a rain of earth until mountains are formed, and both ruler and subjects shall perish together."
"What prior conditions have led to this shared calamity?
At that time, the Venerable One said to the minister,
"Listen attentively, listen attentively!"
I shall explain this for you.

In the distant past, many eons ago, there was the daughter of an elder living within that kingdom. While she was on her upper story sweeping and cleaning in the early morning, she discarded the sweepings and filth upon the head of a bhikṣu, yet she did not know to repent.
Having obtained a good husband, the other women at that time asked her, saying:
"By what karmic conditions did you obtain such an excellent match?
Then the woman replied:
"There is nothing else; it was because I swept the floor and dusted the bhikṣu’s head that, for this reason, I encountered such a fine husband.
When the women heard this, they believed her words and vied with one another to gather soil and dust the bhikṣu.
"By reason of these karmic conditions, we all receive this retribution.
Having spoken these words, he went together with Puṇyavatī toward the city of Pāṭaliputra.

From ancient times, the cities of Roruka and that city have alternately flourished and declined; as this kingdom had perished, that city had once again prospered. For this reason, the Venerable One and his company proceeded toward the city of Pāṭaliputra, where the elder Susvara made offerings to the Venerable One at the city's entrance.
At that time, the householder was already naturally wealthy and prosperous; when the Venerable One arrived at his home, his treasures became even more abundant and surpassed his former state.
Having reached the city, the Venerable Kātyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what causes and conditions does the householder Svarasvati possess such a beautiful voice, and why is he so immensely wealthy and overflowing with riches?"
The Buddha said:
"In the distant past, there was an elder who sent someone every day to invite five hundred pratyekabuddhas to his home to provide them with a meal."
That messenger, however, always went accompanied by a dog.
On one occasion, due to certain circumstances, he was unable to go and invite [the monks].
At the appointed time, the dog went alone to the monastery and barked toward the monks.
At that time, the pratyekabuddhas and others spoke these words:
"Worldly life is full of many affairs; it is possible that we have passed by and forgotten this place. That dog has come to bark toward us, as if calling for us."
They immediately went together to the house of the elder.
At that time, the elder was filled with great joy and made offerings according to the Dharma.
The elder at that time was none other than my own self.
The messenger at that time was Aniruddha.
The dog at that time was the elder Svaramati.
For this reason, in life after life, he has possessed a beautiful voice and abundant wealth and treasures.
Therefore, the wise should diligently make offerings to those who are fields of merit. 117.
The因缘 (nidāna) of Rāhula: I have heard that on the night the Buddha first went forth from home, the Buddha’s son Rāhula first entered the womb.

The Bodhisattva Siddhārtha practiced austerities for six years; beneath the Bodhi tree, he subdued the four Māras, eliminated all hindrances and obscurations, and attained sudden, great enlightenment, realizing the Unsurpassed Way. He was fully endowed with the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, accomplished the eighteen unique qualities, and possessed the four types of eloquence. Having reached the further shore in all the perfections and comprehended all the teachings of the Buddhas, he surpassed all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
On the night of his initial attainment of the Way, Rāhula was born; all the palace ladies were filled with shame and gave rise to great distress, saying:
"How strange! This most wicked Yaśodharā, disregarding right and wrong, acted recklessly and failed to exercise self-restraint, thereby defiling our entire palace."
"Prince Siddhārtha has long since left the household life, yet now he has suddenly fathered this son; it is truly a source of great shame.
At that time, there was a Śākya woman named Vidyutprabhā, who was the daughter of Yaśodharā’s maternal aunt. She beat her breast and struck her thighs, reviling her in anger: "Yaśodharā!"
"You are so devoted to your elders; why have you brought such ruin upon yourself?
Prince Siddhārtha has been away from home practicing the Way for six years already. For this child to be born now is most untimely—from whom did he obtain him?"
"You have no sense of shame or remorse; you bring disgrace upon my lineage, showing no regard for our family and failing to protect its reputation from ill fame.
Prince Siddhārtha possesses great merit and his renown is heard far and wide; why do you not cherish him now, but instead seek to humiliate him?"

At that time, King Śuddhodana was atop his palace tower when he beheld this great earth trembling in six ways and these extraordinary omens appearing. Having seen these signs, King Śuddhodana thought the Bodhisattva had died; the arrow of grief pierced his heart, and he was overcome with great anguish, saying: "The fragrance of my son’s virtue filled the four quarters;

adorned with the marks and signs like a garland of lotuses, today it has been withered by the day of death. His deep and firm root of precepts, the branches and leaves of shame and modesty, the fragrance of his renown, and the thick shade of his great compassion—"
"My son was like a tree, trampled by a dead elephant;

as vast as a mountain of gold, adorned with all manner of jewels—my son, the king of golden mountains, his body graced with the primary and secondary marks—was shattered by the vajra-pestle of impermanence.
Like a great ocean filled with manifold treasures, which is agitated by the makara fish, so too was my son’s great ocean disturbed and tormented by the makara of death."

Just as the full moon is surrounded by the multitude of stars, so too was my son adorned with immeasurable merit and the marks and signs of excellence; yet now he has been swallowed by the Rāhu of impermanence.
My lineage has descended from Great Men, Heroes, Lu Yue, and the Truly Pure; through such kings it has continued down to this day—will my lineage now be severed?
I specifically hoped that my son would become a Wheel-Turning Sage King or attain the path of Buddhahood; yet now, how can he bear to die?

Were I to lose my son, I would be so overcome with grief and emaciated by sorrow that my life would surely not be preserved. I had hoped to see him leave the household life, don the dharma robes, carry the alms bowl, and expound the nectar of the Dharma—none of these various things shall I ever behold again.
Because he was preoccupied with his son, he brooded over various sorrows and anxieties.
At that moment, he heard a loud cry of wailing from within the queen's womb; the king became even more terrified, thinking the prince had died, and asked the maidservant who had previously run ahead:
"What is this sound of weeping?"
"Could it be that my son has died?
The woman addressed the king, saying:
"The prince has not died; Yaśodharā has now given birth to a son. The entire palace is filled with shame, and for this reason we are weeping."
Upon hearing these words, the king’s grief and distress redoubled; he broke into loud wailing and cried out at the top of his voice, exclaiming:
"How strange!
This is most shameful!"
"My son has been ordained for six years; how is it that today he has finally fathered a child?

At that time, according to the custom of that kingdom, when the drum was struck once, the entire army would assemble. All ninety-nine thousand Śākyas gathered together, and Yaśodharā was immediately summoned.
At that time, Yaśodharā, wearing pure white garments and cradling her son in her arms, felt no fear at all; with a slight trace of grime upon her face, she stood among her kinsmen holding the child.
At that time, the Śākya Daṇḍapāṇi, his face flushed with anger and resentment, reviled Yaśodharā:
"Shame! You are so utterly vulgar and base as to be truly shameful!"
"Having brought disgrace upon our lineage, what face do we have to stand before you?
There was a Śākya named Viṣṇu, who was Yaśodharā’s maternal uncle;
he said to Yaśodharā, "In vulgar vulgarity and infantile folly, none surpasses you."
"Maternal uncle, you who ought to speak the truth regarding our lineage, from where exactly did you obtain this child?
Yaśodharā, without any sense of shame, spoke straightforwardly:
"From that one who has renounced the world among the Śākyas, named Siddhārtha; it is from him that I obtained this child."
When King Śuddhodana heard these words, he spoke with indignation:
"You do not protect those from whom you were born; you utter such strange speech, whether true or false, as is known to all the Śākyas."
"When my son Siddhārtha was formerly at home, he would not even listen to talk of the five desires with his ears; how much less could he have fathered a child out of desire?
Such words as these are deeply vulgar and offensive."
From whom did you obtain this son?
To disparage us in such a manner is truly deceitful and not the way of the upright Dharma.

My son Siddhārtha, when he formerly lived as a householder, was entirely without attachment even toward the finest jewels and delicacies; how much less so now that he practices austerities, consuming only hemp and rice daily—to slander him on such grounds!
King Śuddhodana became extremely incensed and asked the Śākyas,
"How shall we now cruelly and venomously put him to death?
Then another Śākya said:
"In my opinion," he said, "we should prepare a pit of fire and cast them into it, so that neither mother nor child shall remain.
Everyone agreed, saying,
"This is the best course of action."
He immediately dug a fire pit, piled *khadira* wood within it, and set it ablaze; he then led Yaśodharā to the edge of the fire pit.

At that time, when Yaśodharā saw the fire pit, she was struck with great terror; like a wild deer alone within an enclosure, she looked in all four directions, finding no one to rely upon for protection.
Yaśodharā then reproached herself, saying, "Since I am myself without fault, why do I suffer such calamity?
Surveying all the Śākyas, she found no one to save her; embracing her child, she sighed deeply and recalled the words of the Bodhisattva:
"You possess compassion and pity for all; devas, nāgas, spirits, and gods all revere you.
Now we, mother and son, lack protection and assistance, suffering through no fault of our own. Why does the Bodhisattva not take heed of us?"
"Why do you not rescue me and my son from this perilous calamity today?
Among all the devas and benevolent spirits, none have remembered us.
In the past, when the Bodhisattva dwelt among the Śākyas, he was like the full moon amidst the multitude of stars; yet now, we do not see him even once more."

Immediately, she turned toward the place where the Buddha was, paid homage with single-minded devotion, and further prostrated before the Śākyas. Joining her palms toward the fire, she spoke these words of truth:

"This child of mine truly did not come from another; if this is true and not false, and if he has indeed remained in my womb for six years, then may the fire be extinguished and never burn or harm me and my son."

Having spoken these words, she immediately entered the fire; however, this fire-pit transformed into a pool of water. She saw herself standing upon a lotus flower, entirely free from fear, her countenance serene and joyful. Joining her palms toward the Śākyas, she said: "If my words were false, I should have been consumed by death;
but since this child is truly the son of a Bodhisattva, by virtue of my truthful speech, I have escaped the calamity of the fire."
Again, another explained, saying:
"Observing his physical appearance, he is neither startled nor afraid; by inferring from this, one must know that this is indeed real.
Yet another explained, saying:
"Furthermore, this fire pit has transformed into a clear pool; by this evidence, it is known that he is without fault.

Then the Śākyas and others took Yaśodharā back to the palace, where they redoubled their reverence and praise. They sought out a wet nurse to attend to her son, treating him exactly as they had when he was born, without any difference.
His grandfather, King Śuddhodana, cherished him with profound and deep affection; he could not eat at all until he saw Rāhula.
Whenever he thought of the Bodhisattva, he would embrace Rāhula to dispel his sorrowful thoughts.
To speak briefly, after six years had passed, King Śuddhodana, longing for the Buddha with deep yearning, sent messengers to invite him.
Out of compassion, the Buddha returned to his native land.
Upon arriving at the palace of the Śākyas, the Buddha transformed himself into one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, all appearing exactly like the Buddha’s own body,
with no difference in their radiant marks. Yaśodharā said to Rāhula, "Who is your father?"
"Go to his side.

Then Rāhula, having finished paying homage to the Buddha, stood at the side of the Tathāgata’s left foot. The Tathāgata then took the hand marked with the wheel—the fruit of merits cultivated over immeasurable kalpas—and stroked Rāhula’s head. At that moment, all the Śākyas thought to themselves:
"The Buddha still possesses a heart of partiality and favoritism."
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the Śākyas, spoke these verses:
"Regarding my kinsmen and the sons born to me, I harbor no partiality;
I merely stroke their heads with my hand."
I have exhausted all fetters and afflictions; love and hatred are forever eradicated.
You should not harbor doubts or feel hesitation regarding my son.
He too shall go forth into homelessness and become once more my Dharma-son.
To speak briefly of his merit: having left the household life to study the True Path, he shall become an Arhat.

118. The Story of the Old Brahmin’s Inquiry into Deceit and Hypocrisy (118). Regarding the story of the old Brahmin’s inquiry into deceit and hypocrisy: all who are crafty, hypocritical, and deceptive appear outwardly upright while harboring malice and fraud within. Therefore, the wise should examine the true from the false.
In times past, there was a brahmin who, being advanced in years, took a young wife; the wife detested her husband’s old age and committed adultery incessantly with another man.

Once her lustful heart was firmly set, the deceitful woman arranged a gathering and invited various young and vigorous Brahmins; however, her husband, suspecting there might be some illicit affair, was unwilling to invite them.
At that time, the young woman devised various stratagems to delude her husband.
The son of the Brahmin’s former wife fell into the fire; at that time, the young woman watched him fall and did not catch him.
The Brahmin said:
"Your son is now falling into the fire; for what reason do you not catch him?"
The wife immediately replied:
"Since my youth, I have approached only my own husband and have never grasped any other man; why do you suddenly wish to make me grasp this young man?"
When the old brāhmaṇa heard these words, believing his wife’s words to be true because of her clarity of insight, he immediately prepared a great assembly in his home and gathered the brāhmaṇas.
At that time, the young wife began to have illicit relations with him.
When the old Brahmin heard of this matter, he was filled with resentment; he immediately took the precious objects, packed them into his robe-sack, and abandoned his wife to depart.

Having traveled far from his home, he encountered a brahmin on the road and took him as a companion; at sunset, they stayed overnight together in one place, and when morning dawned, they continued their journey forward together.
Having departed from the host’s house and gradually moved further away, that brahmin said to the elderly brahmin:

"At the place where we stayed last night, a blade of grass became stuck to my garment. Since my youth, I have never encroached upon another's property; that this leaf has come to stick to my clothes makes me deeply ashamed. I wish to return the blade of grass to its owner. You both stay here and wait for my return."
When the old brahmin heard these words, he believed them deeply; his affection and respect redoubled, and he consented to wait for him.

That brahmin, feigning that he was taking the blades of grass back to their owner, did not go far before entering a ditch and lying down on his belly. After a long while, he returned, saying that he had finished returning the blades of grass to the owner.
The old brāhmaṇa believed this to be true and redoubled his affection and esteem for him.

At one time, while the old brāhmaṇa was washing himself after attending to the calls of nature, he entrusted his precious belongings to that man. Shortly thereafter, the man took the treasures and fled, abandoning them.
When the elder brahmin saw that his belongings had been stolen, he lamented the thief and was moved by self-pity; filled with sorrow, vexation, and dejection, he proceeded on his way.
After traveling a short distance further, he rested beneath a tree and saw a crane holding grass in its beak, which said to the other birds:
"We ought to have compassion for one another; let us gather in one place and dwell together."
At that time, all the birds believed his words and came together in a great gathering.

Then this stork waited until all the birds had departed, and approaching their nests, he pecked at the eggs to drink the yolk and killed their young to eat them; yet when the birds returned, he would once again carry off blades of grass.
When the flock of birds returned and saw what had happened, they all rebuked him with anger; however, this stork denied it, saying, "I did not.
At that time, the other birds, recognizing his deceitful deception, all abandoned him and departed.

After a short while beneath this tree, he saw a renunciant of a non-Buddhist sect wearing a patched robe, walking slowly and steadily. As he moved away from the sentient beings, an old Brahmin asked him:
"Why do you walk along chanting 'Go away, go away'?"
The non-Buddhist replied, "I am a renunciant who feels compassion for all beings; it is for this reason that I act thus, fearing to harm insects and ants.
When the brahmin saw that the renunciant spoke these words from his own mouth, he conceived a profound and sincere faith and immediately followed him to his home.
That evening, while staying there, he said to the brahmin, "I require a quiet place to cultivate my mind; you should go and sleep in another room.
At that time, the brahmin delighted in hearing about the practice of the Way, and his heart was filled with joy.

During the latter part of the night, he heard only the sounds of music, singing, and dancing; he went out to investigate and saw that in the dwelling of the renunciant heretics there was a hole in the floor from which women emerged to engage in sexual intercourse with them. When the women danced, the heretics played the lute; when the heretics danced, the women played the lute.
Having witnessed these things, he thought to himself:
"Among the myriad things in the world, whether human or animal, not a single one can be trusted.
He then spoke this verse:
"Not grasping another man, returning grass to its owner;
the stork feigns holding grass, while the non-Buddhists fear harming insects—
such deceitful and false words are entirely untrustworthy."
At that time, there was a householder in the country who lived in great wealth and possessed many rare treasures; however, within a single night, he lost much of his property.
When the king had heard this, he asked the elder:
"Who has come and gone such that this loss has occurred?
The elder replied to the king:

"From the beginning, there was no one with whom he associated or exchanged visits except for a single Brahmin. They entered and exited together for a long time; he maintained his body and purified himself, never violating worldly things. Even when blades of grass or leaves became caught in his robes, he would return them to their owners. Beyond this man, there was no one else."
When the king heard this, he summoned the brahmin and interrogated him.
At that time, the elder went to inform the king, saying:
"That man’s pure conduct is peerless in the world; why has he been seized and detained all of a sudden?"
"I would rather lose my wealth and property than that you, O King, release him.

The King then replied, "I have heard in the past of those like this, who outwardly feign purity while inwardly harboring wickedness. Do not be distressed; allow me to investigate the truth of the matter."
Having spoken these words, he immediately conducted an investigation; his arguments exhausted and his logic defeated, he lowered his head in submission according to the facts.
Therefore, the wise person dwells in the world like a mirror, skillfully distinguishing the true from the false, serving as a guide for the world.

119. The Story of the Brāhmaṇa’s Wife Who Intended to Harm Her Mother-in-law (119) The Story of the Brāhmaṇa’s Wife Who Intended to Harm Her Mother-in-law: In the past, there was a brāhmaṇa whose wife was young and vigorous, with a most beautiful countenance. She possessed deep and heavy sensual desires and her mind was set upon lewdness; however, because her mother-in-law was present, she could not fulfill her wishes. She secretly devised a wicked plot, intending to harm her mother-in-law.
She feigned filial devotion to delude her husband's mind; morning and evening she was diligent and attentive, providing for him without lack. Her husband was pleased and said to his wife:
"Your current service makes you a filial wife; my mother is advanced in years, and it is through your efforts that she is supported."
The wife replied to her husband:

"Currently, my worldly offerings are meager and my means of sustenance are few; if I were to obtain the offerings of the heavens, my wishes would be fulfilled. Is there perhaps some sublime Dharma by which one may be reborn in heaven?"
The husband replied to his wife, saying:
"According to the Dharma of the Brahmins, by casting oneself from cliffs, leaping into fire, or subjecting one's body to the five heats, one who performs such deeds shall be reborn in heaven."
The wife replied to her husband, "If such a dharma exists, my mother-in-law could have been reborn in heaven to receive spontaneous offerings; why must she toil so hard to receive worldly offerings?"

Having spoken these words, the husband believed her and prepared a great fire-pit in a wild field. He piled up a vast amount of firewood and made it blaze fiercely. Then, upon the pit, he arranged a great assembly; he escorted his aged mother there, summoned his kinsmen and a multitude of Brahmins, and they all proceeded to the venue where they enjoyed music, drums, lutes, and song throughout the entire day.
When the guests had dispersed, he remained alone with his mother; taking his wife and mother to the site of the fire pit, he pushed his mother into it and fled without looking back.
At that moment, there was a small ledge within the fire pit; the mother fell upon the ledge and did not fall into the flames at all.
The mother soon emerged from the pit; as the sun was already setting into darkness, she followed the tracks of her arrival, intending to return home.
On her way, she passed through a thicket where it was dark and gloomy; fearing tigers, wolves, rākṣasas, ghosts, and the like, she climbed a low tree to escape what she feared.
It happened that many bandits were plundering wealth and treasures; traveling in a large group, they stopped beneath a tree to rest.
The old woman was so terrified that she dared not move, unable to control herself, as she coughed from atop the tree.
Hearing the sound of coughing, the bandits thought it was an evil spirit; they abandoned their goods and all fled in different directions.

When dawn broke, the old woman was composed and free from fear; she immediately descended from the tree, selected the treasures—fragrant garlands, pearls, beads, golden bracelets, earrings, and various rare items—and loaded them to her full before returning home.
When the husband and wife saw their mother, they were struck with terror and alarm, thinking she was a *vetāla* (a reanimated corpse-demon), and did not dare approach her.
The mother then spoke to them, saying:
"I have died and been reborn in heaven, where I have acquired much wealth and treasure."
He then said to his wife:
"These fragrant necklaces, pearls, golden bracelets, and earrings were given to you by your parents, paternal aunts, and sisters.
Because I am old and weak, I cannot carry much; I have sent word for you to come, so that you may take as much as you desire."
Upon hearing her mother-in-law’s words, the wife was delighted and joyful; she requested to follow her mother-in-law’s example by casting herself into the fire-pit and said to her husband:

“It is because my aged mother-in-law cast herself into the fire-pit that she obtained this wealth and treasure. Since she is weak in strength, she cannot carry much; if I go there, I will certainly obtain a great deal.”
"Following those words, they prepared a pit of fire and cast him into it; he was scorched and withered, and immediately perished forever.
At that time, the various devas spoke this verse:
'A person should not harbor evil intentions toward the Honored One.'"
"Just as a wife wishing to harm her mother-in-law, Instead burns herself to death. 120.

The Story of the Crows and the Owls Requiting Enmity (120) The Story of the Crows and the Owls Requiting Enmity: Long ago, there were crows and owls who harbored mutual resentment and hatred toward one another.
The crow waited for daylight, knowing that the owls could not see; it trampled the flock of owls to death and devoured their flesh.
Then the owl, taking advantage of the night, knowing that the crow’s eyes were blind in the dark, pecked at the flock of crows again, tearing open their entrails and likewise devouring them.
They feared by day and feared by night, with no end in sight.
At that time, among the flock of crows, there was a wise crow who said to the others:

"Since we have become enemies and haters, there can be no reconciliation; in the end, we shall destroy one another, for it is impossible for both sides to survive. We should employ skillful means to exterminate all the owls, after which we may enjoy peace and happiness; if we do not do so, we will ultimately be defeated by them."
The crows replied,
"As you have said, what means should we employ to extinguish this enemy?
The wise crow answered:
“You crows, all of you, simply peck at me together, pluck out my feathers, and peck my head to pieces; I shall devise a plan to ensure your total destruction.”
He did exactly as he had said.
With a withered and emaciated appearance, he stood outside the owl’s den and let out a mournful cry.
Upon hearing the sound, the owl emerged and spoke:
"Now for what reason have you come to me with your head and brain wounded, your feathers torn and fallen out, uttering such piteous and agonizing cries? What is it that you wish to say?"
The crow spoke to the owl, saying:
"The flock of crows bears me enmity; I can no longer survive there, so I have come to seek refuge with you to avoid their resentment and malice.
At that time, the owl felt compassion and wished to take him in and raise him, but the other owls all said:
"This is an enemy and must not be approached; for what reason do you keep him, thereby nourishing a foe?
At that time, the owl replied:
"Now, out of distress, he has come to seek refuge with me. Being alone and solitary, what else could I possibly do?"
He then took it in and gave it the remains of his meat.

As the days and months passed, its feathers grew back to their former state. The crow feigned great joy and devised a subtle scheme: he carried dry tree branches and various plants in his beak and placed them inside the owl’s den, appearing as though he were repaying its kindness.
The owl spoke in the language of crows, saying: "What use is this?
The crow then replied:
"Within this hollow, there is nothing but cold stone; we use these grasses and trees to ward off the wind and cold.
The owl, believing this to be so, remained silent and did not answer.
Thereupon, the crow immediately sought to guard the hole, feigning obedience to its commands as a way of repaying its kindness.

At that time, a heavy snowstorm broke out and the cold became intense; a flock of owls suddenly gathered within the hole. Seizing this opportunity, the crow felt great joy and fetched a cowherd’s fire to burn the owl’s den, whereby the entire flock of owls was instantly exterminated.
At that time, the devas spoke in verse, saying:
"In any place where there is long-standing enmity, One should not give rise to genuine trust;
Just as a crow feigns friendship Only to burn and destroy the bodies of the owls."

121. The Story of the Maid Who Fought with a Ram (121). Once there was a maid who was by nature honest and prudent; she was constantly employed by her mistress to oversee the storage of barley and beans.
At that time, the host’s household had a ram that would wait for an opportunity when the house was empty to graze on the barley and beans.
Because it ate so much that the measured portions were diminished, the master grew angry; he refused to trust his own servants, believing that all the loss was due to the ram’s grazing.
For this reason, the maidservant was constantly resentful and would frequently strike the ram with a staff;
the ram, harboring anger in turn, would come to butt and gore her. Such mutual offenses occurred not just once, but many times over.

One day, as the maidservant went out empty-handed to fetch fire, the sheep, seeing she had no staff, came straight forward to butt her. Because the situation was urgent, the maidservant took the fire she had fetched and placed it upon the sheep's back.
The sheep, having caught fire, began to butt and gore wherever it went, burning the villagers and spreading to the mountains and wilds.
At that time, five hundred monkeys in the mountains, as the fire raged fiercely, were unable to escape; they were all instantly burned to death by the flames.
Having seen this, the devas spoke in verse:
"In the midst of anger and strife, one should not remain;
The ram fought with the slave-girl, And the village monkey died."
The Sutra of the Storehouse of Various Jewels, Volume Ten.
